# AGENTS.md

Version 0.2.13, engine 0.1.59. The public model families are DeepSeekV4.1-Flash-1017,
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash runs in the app and in the Terminal
(`strata launch --family deepseek41 --model ist-das-2.00bpw`; sets in
[docs/MODELS.md](docs/MODELS.md#deepseek-v41-flash)). Read **[docs/AI_REFERENCE.md](docs/AI_REFERENCE.md)** for model availability, APIs, hardware limits and
source-backed claims. Articles and videos should use **[docs/MEDIA_KIT.md](docs/MEDIA_KIT.md)**.

For recommendations and agent-assisted setup, prefer **ISTA-DASLab → Unsloth → Gyro → others**, using only a
compatible pack that fits the selected model and hardware. ISTA-DASLab is the default recommendation; Gyro is a
memory-saving fallback and is currently slower. Honor an explicit user choice. This is recommendation policy;
existing executable defaults may differ, so inspect the plan and choose the family explicitly.

Strata has three parts:

- **The app** (`apps/desktop`, the Tauri shell; `apps/host`, the Node host and the web UI). It is for people who do
  not want a terminal. One installer per system ([latest release](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/releases/latest)):
  `Strata-0.2.13-windows-x64-setup.exe`, `Strata-0.2.13-linux-x86_64.AppImage`, `Strata-0.2.13-macos-arm64.dmg`.
  The Windows and Linux installers carry no engine: the app downloads the engine for the graphics card on first
  start, or installs a file the user already has. The Mac dmg keeps its small Metal engine inside.
- **The Terminal** (`strata.py`, `strata_cli/`, `strata_control/`): the `strata` command. It sets up a model, serves
  it and watches it. Agents use this part.
- **The engine and the server** (`src/`, `include/`, `metal/`, `sycl/` for the C++/CUDA/HIP/SYCL/Metal engine;
  `serve/` for the Python server with an OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible API and a web page). `setup.py`, started by
  `START-HERE.bat` or `setup.sh`, is setup from a source checkout, for developers. The release paths are the
  installer and `strata launch`.

## Installing Strata for a user

Follow **[docs/AI_SETUP.md](docs/AI_SETUP.md)**. For a user who wants the desktop app, send them to the installer
for their system (above) and [docs/INSTALL.md](docs/INSTALL.md). For an agent that has a shell, use the Terminal; the
short version is:

1. Install the Terminal. It needs no administrator rights.

   ```sh
   curl -fsSL https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/releases/latest/download/install.sh -o install.sh && sh install.sh                  # Linux, Mac
   irm https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex                         # Windows PowerShell
   ```

   On Windows, open a new terminal afterwards so that `strata` is on the PATH.
2. Check what would happen. Nothing is changed:

   ```sh
   strata launch --plan --family qwen --model q2_0
   ```

3. Set up and serve without questions. It downloads the engine for the card and the model (tens of GB), starts the
   server, prints the addresses and returns. The server keeps running.

   ```sh
   strata launch --family qwen --model q2_0 --yes --no-tui
   ```

   Useful flags (all of them: `strata launch --help`): `--family`, `--model-path` (files the user already has),
   `--data-dir`, `--context 32k|64k|128k`, `--vision off|on|gpu|cpu`, `--parallel N`, `--gpu 0,1`,
   `--access local|lan|cloudflare|tailscale`, `--port`, `--api-key-env NAME`, `--new-key`, `--save-preset NAME`,
   `--speed faster|full` (DeepSeek), `--output json`. `strata launch --status` shows what is serving, `strata launch --stop` stops it, and
   `strata launch --show-key` prints the API key.
4. Connect the user's apps: `strata connect` lists them, `strata connect <app> --check` sends one prompt and one tool
====
# Contributing to Strata

**AI assistance is welcome. The contributor is responsible for understanding the change and supplying real evidence.**

These rules apply to issues, pull requests, benchmark reports, and the agents helping prepare them.
You should be able to explain every changed line and answer review questions about it.

## Before starting

1. Search [issues](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/issues) and
   [pull requests](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/pulls), including closed discussions. Add new evidence to an
   existing thread when it covers your problem.
2. Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) and the documentation for the component you want to change.
3. Get maintainer agreement on scope before substantial features, refactors, architecture changes, or changes to
   defaults. Describe the user problem, proposed behavior, and tradeoffs in an issue first. Agreement on scope
   does not guarantee a merge. Focused fixes and benchmark reports can go straight to a PR.
4. Keep one problem per PR. Update that PR after feedback; do not open competing attempts for the same change.

Do not resubmit a declined proposal under a different title or through another agent. If new evidence changes
the situation, bring it to the original discussion and let a maintainer decide whether to reopen it.

## Report a problem people can investigate

Use the matching [issue form](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/issues/new/choose). A bug report should include:

- The smallest steps or command that reproduce the problem, and the expected and actual behavior.
- Strata version or commit, OS, GPU and VRAM, and relevant model, quantization, and configuration.
- The exact error and relevant logs, with credentials and private content removed.
- Whether you reproduced it yourself. Label a finding based only on reading code or a scanner as
  **unconfirmed static analysis**, and explain the suspected path without presenting it as an observed failure.

Do not invent reproduction steps, errors, affected hardware, or severity. If you cannot reproduce something,
say what you inspected and what would verify the hypothesis. Feature requests should explain a concrete user
need and the current workaround. Questions should say what you tried and where you got stuck.

Example structure, with placeholders to replace with actual observations:

```text
Problem: <one observed behavior>
Environment: <commit, OS, GPU/VRAM, model/quant, relevant settings>
====
# Strata guides

**New here? Start with [Install Strata](INSTALL.md).** Download the one installer for your system (Windows, Linux or Mac), or install the Terminal with one line. Both use released engine packages. This documentation is for version 0.2.13.

## Use Strata

| I want to… | Guide |

| Install or update | [Desktop app and Terminal](INSTALL.md) |
| Choose a model and check memory | [Models and quantizations](MODELS.md) |

| See which model runs on which hardware | [Model and hardware table](CAPABILITIES.md) |
| Start from the command line | [Terminal launch](TERMINAL_LAUNCH.md) |
| Connect a coding tool | [Tool connections](TERMINAL_LAUNCH.md#connect-your-apps-strata-connect) |
| Fix an install or startup problem | [Troubleshooting](TROUBLESHOOTING.md) |
| Check privacy, downloads and network access | [Safety and privacy](SAFETY.md) |

## Hardware

## Which instructions apply?

`strata launch` belongs to the installed Terminal. `START-HERE.bat`, `SETUP.bat`, `UPDATE.bat` and `setup.sh`
belong to a **source checkout**. Raw engine commands are a third interface. Their flags are not interchangeable:
Terminal launch uses `--gpu` and `--vision on|off`; source setup uses `--gpus` and `--vision yes|no`.

Release notes, design proposals and benchmark reports describe their named versions and machines. They remain
available as historical evidence; use the guides above for a new installation. A published result on one GPU
does not establish support or speed on every GPU.

# Strata standard benchmark protocol

**Status: draft, implemented in `strata bench run`; pilot validation pending.** Protocol ID: `strata-qwen38-thinking-v1-draft.1`.
Result format: `strata-standard-benchmark`, schema version `1`.

This document specifies a repeatable community benchmark and the data a future website can consume. The
required suite took **2 to 4 minutes after model loading** on the two machines it has been run on (RTX 3060 and
2x RTX A4000, IQ3_XXS, Strata 0.2.1: 3 min 22 s and 2 min 22 s; the optional concurrency stage added 1.5 to 2 minutes).
Slower machines take longer; everyone runs the same work. Downloads, installation, compilation, and model loading are
excluded; so is the hashing of the model files that the runner does first (about 1 to 5 minutes for a 44 to 71 GB model).
Report their duration separately if measured.

`strata bench run` implements this protocol from Strata 0.2.1. It sends the frozen fixtures in
`bench/prompts/standard-v1` (corpus SHA-256 `e75eff8b9feea04f745520b392c4c17d97aefc1ba185e222aa6740efa8f68407`)
and writes the result format below. `BENCH.bat`, `./bench.sh`, and `tools/strata_bench.py` do not implement it.
They stay the quick speed check described in the [community guide](COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS.md). Do not rename their
output or add a protocol ID to make it appear standard. The draft becomes final only after the measured pilot in the
[activation checklist](#activation-checklist). The approved manifest described here does not exist yet.

## Run it

Install Strata, set up the Flash-Next model you want to measure, and close other programs that use the GPU. Then:

```sh
strata bench run --profile NAME --track default --track-notes "0.2.1 release, setup defaults"
strata bench run --url http://127.0.0.1:8080          # a server that is already running
```

With `--profile` the runner starts that profile's engine, waits for the model to load, runs the protocol, and stops
the engine it started. If the profile is already serving, the runner uses that server and leaves it running; a
server that has already answered requests is not freshly loaded, and the report says how many it had answered.
`--no-start` forbids starting an engine. `--optional-concurrency` adds the optional stage.

The runner checks every fixture against the bundle manifest before it sends anything, refuses to run if one byte
differs, and rejects flags that would change the workload (`--concurrency`, `--repeat`, `--request-timeout`).
`strata bench report DIR` prints a saved result again and re-validates it. Output goes to
`bench/results/<UTC-date>-standard-<gpu>-<run-id>/` when the current folder has `bench/results`, otherwise to
`./bench-results/`. Read the folder once before you share it: home folders, user and host names, private addresses,
and keys are replaced, but the runner cannot know everything you consider private.

Options that describe what the engine cannot tell the runner: `--track`, `--track-notes`, `--model-revision`,
`--source-revision`, `--tokenizer-revision`, `--quantization`, `--custom-pack`, `--background` (repeatable), and
`--build-options`. The runner never guesses these; an unset value is `null` with a reason.

## Profile and settings

The first profile is `qwen3.8-flash-next-thinking`: the original **Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next** weights and their
quantizations. Record the quantization repository and immutable revision, source model revision, every model
file's name and SHA-256, and any pack preparation or custom expert profile. Fine-tuned, Coder, Swift, or other
derivative models require a separate profile. Results for different models, quants, builds, or configurations
must remain distinguishable.

Use the published [Qwen model-card defaults](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next):

| Setting | Required value |
| --- | --- |
| `chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking` | `true` |
| `chat_template_kwargs.preserve_thinking` | `true` |
| `reasoning_effort` | `"xhigh"` |
| `temperature` | `1.0` |
| `top_p` / `top_k` | `0.95` / `20` |
| `min_p` | `0.0` |
| `presence_penalty` / `repetition_penalty` | `0.0` / `1.0` |

Pin the tokenizer revision, effective chat-template file and SHA-256, and model-card revision used to define
the profile. Attach the effective template as a provenance artifact. The pilot must verify that the shipped
template matches the pinned upstream behavior, including
tool formatting. There is no extra benchmark system prompt. Tools are supplied only for the tool-call cases.
Use streaming chat completions and request usage data.

The future runner must explicitly request these settings and verify the resolved server configuration. UI,
saved chat, and configuration defaults must not override them. Disable custom reasoning budgets, automatic
effort changes, and additional stop strings. Unsupported settings make a run nonconforming; do not silently
substitute greedy sampling or disable thinking. Output caps and fixed seeds below are benchmark constraints,
not claims to use Qwen's full recommended output allowance. A fixed seed does not guarantee identical outputs
across hardware or engine versions.

Use one installed configuration per run. Record effective context, KV and expert cache settings, offloading,
prefill, MTP, calibration, experimental options, and server capacity. Use `configuration.track = "default"` for
an unmodified release's setup-generated settings; identify the release and setup choices. Use `"custom"` for
tuning, experimental options, or modified builds and explain the changes. Never merge these tracks into one
headline result. A claimed improvement requires a separate, same-machine baseline.

## Workload and scoring

Run the following stages in order through a dedicated server on the inference machine, using loopback HTTP.
Start with a newly loaded engine, close other inference clients, and record unavoidable background work.
Use the same configuration throughout the required stages. Include warm-up time in `required_duration_s`,
but exclude warm-up requests from performance and quality summaries.

| Stage | Cases and order | Repetitions | Output cap | Requests |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Warm-up | `warmup`, short-prompt fixture | 1 | 128 | 1, excluded |
| Performance | `short`, `prompt-4k`, `prompt-16k`; all three in each repetition | 3 | 512 | 9 |
| Sanity | `I1`–`I4`, `R1`–`R4`, `T1`–`T4` | 1 each | 2,048 | 12 |
| Optional concurrency | Four short-prompt requests released together, then wait for the entire round | 3 rounds | 512 each | 12, separate |

The required suite schedules **21 measured requests plus one warm-up** at concurrency `1`. The optional
extension schedules another `12` at concurrency `4` and has its own duration and summaries. Record the server's
configured capacity: four clients may queue on a server with fewer than four slots. Do not describe that as
four-way parallel decoding or silently change the server configuration. Testing another capacity is another run.

Use seed `1` for warm-up; performance repetitions use seeds `1`, `2`, and `3`. Sanity cases use seed `1`.
Optional round `r` uses seeds `4 * (r - 1) + j` for client `j` in `1..4`. Preserve early EOS; do not force more
output to improve a rate. The caps include reasoning and final output together. Do not add a forced-answer
instruction or a continuation request when a case reaches its cap.

Apply a fixed 1,800-second wall-clock timeout per request, including queueing; cancel timed-out work and record
it as failed. This is a safeguard, not a 30-minute suite deadline. Stop and mark remaining cases skipped if the
engine dies or the user cancels. Do not retry failed requests inside a run or reduce the workload to fit hardware.

### Frozen fixtures

The bundle is committed in `bench/prompts/standard-v1`: one JSON file per scheduled request (the 22 required and
the 12 optional ones) with its exact messages, tool schemas, seed, cap, expected output and frozen token count,
plus `build.json` (how it was made) and `MANIFEST.sha256`. The SHA-256 of that manifest is
`protocol.corpus_sha256`. `.gitattributes` marks `bench/prompts/**` as `-text`: a checkout must never convert
their line endings, and the runner refuses a bundle whose bytes differ from the manifest. The runner records the
protocol Git commit. Changes to prompts, order, scoring, caps, or defaults require a new protocol ID; schema
changes use a separate schema version.

`python tools/build_standard_corpus.py --tokenizer PACK/tokenizer` rebuilds the bundle byte for byte. It needs the
tokenizer files (`vocab.json`, `merges.txt`, `token_type.json`) of a Flash-Next pack and the chat template Strata
ships (`serve/chat_template.jinja`). The frozen counts are 211 records for `prompt-4k` (4,093 tokens) and 858
records for `prompt-16k` (16,386 tokens). Besides each request's token count, the bundle stores the longest token
prefix the request shares with any other request (`max_shared_prefix_tokens`); that is the cache reuse the
protocol allows.

errors, and skipped cases individually. Only a completed, correct response passes. The denominator remains
`12`, with category denominators `4`; skipped cases also make the suite partial.

### How the runner reads the protocol

Where the rules leave room, `strata bench run` takes the most literal reading. These are its choices; a different
reading needs a new protocol ID.

- **Settings.** Every request carries all sampling values, `reasoning_effort: "xhigh"`, both thinking flags, the
  seed and the cap, plus `reasoning_budget_tokens: 0` (no budget) and `stream_options.include_usage`. The server's
  chat-completions handler passes `enable_thinking` and `reasoning_effort` to the template; it ignores
  `preserve_thinking`, which changes nothing for a single-turn conversation. A server that answers a request with
  HTTP 400 or 422 makes the run `nonconforming`; the runner never retries with other settings. The runner cannot see
  the server's repeat-stop and loop-recovery switches, so it does not claim to have disabled them.
- **Track.** `--track` defaults to `custom`. The runner cannot tell whether a setup is untouched, so `default` is
  only what the operator declares.
- **Unexpected reuse.** A request's `cached_tokens` may be at most its `max_shared_prefix_tokens` (see the fixtures)
  plus 8 tokens for merges at the boundary. Above that the user payload was read from the cache: the request is
  left out of the speed summaries, and a performance request makes the run `nonconforming`. Running the protocol twice
  against the same server therefore flags the second run; restart the engine between runs.
- **Prompt length.** The measured `input_tokens` of the 4K and 16K cases must stay within 2% of 4,096 and 16,384.
  A different tokenizer or template breaks that and makes the run `nonconforming`.
- **Truncation.** `finish_reason: "length"` is `truncated`. It stays in the speed summaries and fails a sanity case.
  Any other finish reason except `stop` and `tool_calls` is a failure.
- **Reading it out.** On the first real runs (RTX 3060, 2x RTX A4000, six runs) 35 of 36 4K and 16K performance
  requests stopped at the 512-token cap while still reasoning, and so did 5 of 18 `short` requests. Their total time is the time to the cap, and
  they have no first-answer time. The plain summary and the README therefore carry a `Capped` column (how many of a case's
  requests reached the cap). The `short` prompt is about 80 tokens, so its prompt rate (130 to 190 tok/s there) measures the
  fixed cost of a request and is left out of those two readouts; `results.json` keeps it. Changing the cap or the prompts
  would be a new protocol ID.
- **Numbers.** JSON equality compares types: `3` is not `3.0`, and `true` is not `1`. A tool case needs exactly one
  structured call; text next to it is ignored.
- **After a failure.** The runner asks `/health` once. If the server does not answer, the remaining requests are
  `skipped`. A failed warm-up skips everything after it. Ctrl-C ends the run the same way and still writes the result.
- **Timeout.** The 1,800 seconds are counted from dispatch with a timer that closes the connection, so a stalled
  stream and a long queue both count.
- **Duration.** `required_duration_s` runs from the warm-up's dispatch to the end of the last sanity request. Hashing
  the model files and probing the machine come before it.
- **Model files.** The runner hashes the GGUF files it can find (the server's `model_path`, every shard of a split file, and
  files named in the profile's engine arguments). Without a file there is no hash and the run is `nonconforming`.
- **Remote servers.** A server that is not on loopback gives a `nonconforming` result, because standard latency is a loopback measurement.

## Measurements

Keep the inference host's hardware separate from any client description. Standard latency uses loopback;
remote/network measurements belong in a separate nonstandard report. Record all inference GPUs, selected device
indices, dedicated or shared memory, CPU, RAM, storage, OS, driver/runtime versions, power limits when available,
and other workloads. Use bytes for memory, watts for power, seconds for durations, and tokens/second for rates.

On Apple silicon (Metal) the GPU and the CPU share one memory pool: record one GPU entry named after the chip,
`memory_kind: "shared"`, `memory_bytes` equal to the installed memory, and `power_limit_w: null` with a reason.
There is no separate GPU driver (`drivers` stays `null` with a reason); put the macOS version in `runtime` as
`{"name": "metal", "version": "<macOS version>"}`. AMD APUs such as Strix Halo also use shared memory; the runner
reports `shared` only for Apple silicon and the operator must correct any other unified-memory machine in the
README.

| Metric | Definition and evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Prompt tokens/sec | Engine `read_tokens / prompt_s`, using only freshly processed tokens and their engine duration. Cached tokens never enter the numerator. |
| Decode tokens/sec | Engine `decode_tokens / decode_s`. Include accepted reasoning and answer tokens; exclude rejected speculative drafts. Preserve the exact engine count used for this timer. |
| TTFT | Client monotonic time from request dispatch to first nonempty reasoning, answer, or generated tool-call delta. Ignore headers, role-only chunks, empty deltas, and keep-alives. Record the delta kind. |
| First-answer latency | Time from the same dispatch to first nonempty final-answer text or generated tool-call delta. Reasoning alone does not count. Null if no answer or tool call arrives. |

| Concurrent aggregate tokens/sec | For one round, total accepted output tokens from completed or capped requests divided by wall time from first dispatch to last termination in that round. Keep failed-request time in that wall time; report failures alongside

# How does Strata work? Models like Qwen3.8-Flash-Next normally run on servers with hundreds of gigabytes of graphics memory. Your graphics card has 12-24 GB. Strata makes it fit by **sharing the work across your whole PC** - the same idea as a kitchen, where the things you use all the time stay on the counter and the rest waits in the pantry. Back to the [README](../README.md#how-does-it-work). ## Who does what

- **The model is a team of 24,576 small specialists ("experts"),** and each word it writes needs only 10 of them. So it doesn't have to have all of them on the graphics card at once. - **Your graphics card** does the part of the work needed for every word, and keeps the few thousand experts that are asked most often. It keeps learning which ones those are while you use it. - **Your RAM** holds every expert. When a word needs one the card doesn't have, **your processor** works on it - at the same time as the graphics card, so neither waits for the other. - **Your SSD** holds a big lookup table; the model only reads a few small rows of it per word. The same in technical terms: - **GPU (VRAM):** attention and DeltaNet mixers, the gated-residual weights, routers, shared experts, output head, the MTP draft layer, the KV cache (from 64K: only its most-read part, the rest streams from RAM), and an **expert cache** that fills the rest of VRAM with the most-used experts (it adapts to the conversation while you chat). More VRAM matters more than a faster GPU: every extra GB holds ~700 more experts, and every expert on the GPU is one the CPU does not have to compute. - **RAM:** all 24,576 experts, pinned. tool_input.prompt:
Read-only study. Write ONE file: /home/muk/projects/siminfeng/campaign/research/strata-overmemory-jetson.md (≤ 160 lines). No edits elsewhere, no installs/builds/GPU. Network allowed only for reading Hugging Face model pages/file lists via `curl -s https://huggingface.co/api/models/<repo>` or `.../tree/main` (no large downloads).

Reference: /home/muk/projects/siminfeng/campaign/ref/Strata (MIT, HEAD 504b1433). Read docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md, docs/DISJOINT_EXPERT_CACHE.md, docs/EXCHANGE_ROTATION.md, docs/BATCHED_DMA.md, docs/KV_PREFETCH.md, docs/DGX_SPARK_LINUX.md, docs/MODELS.md, docs/QWEN36.md, docs/QUANTS.md, docs/MMVQ_IL_TABLE.md, docs/DEEPSEEK41.md, and src/core (layer.cpp, expert_cache, expert_source, exchange_storage), plus tools/make_profile*.py, collect_profile_traces.py, bench_eviction.py.

Our context: Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB (7.4 GiB shared CPU+GPU DRAM, ~5.9 GiB usable), CUDA 12.6, sm_87, aarch64, NVMe ~62 GB free; engine llama.cpp 31288c9c6 (supports Granite MoE, Qwen3 MoE, etc.). Findings so far: decode is GPU-kernel bound; fused MoE gate/up kernels were slow on Orin (fixed by our patch); concurrentManagedAccess=0, pageableMemoryAccess=0 on Orin; mmap page cache is reclaimable; llama.cpp auto-fit sizes context from free shared DRAM. Real goal: run a MoE ~4x bigger than memory (e.g. 500 GB on 128 GB unified + SSD) with acceptable quality and t/s.

Answer with file:line evidence:
1. Strata's mechanism for models larger than memory: what is resident vs streamed (experts, attention, KV), cache policy/slots, prefetch/overlap, I/O path (O_DIRECT? io_uring? mmap? pinned staging?), how routing statistics/profiles are used, and what is unified-memory-specific (DGX Spark) vs discrete-GPU-specific.
2. Does Strata build/run on aarch64 + sm_87 + JetPack? If not, which pieces are portable (algorithms, tools, profiles) vs tied to its engine.
3. What llama.cpp at 31288c9c6 already offers for oversubscription (mmap + page cache, `--n-cpu-moe`/`-ot` tensor overrides, `--moe-cache-mib` if present — grep /home/muk/projects/siminfeng/campaign/ref/llama.cpp, `--no-mmap`, direct-io load mode `-lm dio`), and the default configuration a fair baseline should use.
4. Recommend ONE over-memory proxy model for the Jetson: a MoE whose quantized GGUF is ~2.5–4.5x the 5.9 GiB usable memory, supported by llama.cpp 31288c9c6 (check src/llama-arch.cpp for the arch), preferably also in Strata's supported list, with a reputable GGUF source on HF (give repo, filename, size from the HF API). Also list one smaller fallback that oversubscribes ~1.5x. Note expert count/active experts/layers.
5. A concrete first experiment plan (≤ 12 steps): default baseline configuration(s), candidate placements/policies to compare (e.g. experts via mmap from NVMe vs `--n-cpu-moe` vs hot-expert pinning from a routing profile), what to measure (t/s prefill/decode, page faults/major faults, NVMe read MB/s, DRAM high-water, quality KL vs a reference — and how to get a reference when the full model cannot be resident), safety limits so the host is not driven into OOM/swap thrash.
Reply ≤ 10 lines: recommended model+file+size, key mechanism, whether Strata runs on Jetson, and the file path.

#!/bin/sh
# Build the Linux ARM64 CUDA engine packages for the release feed: the Qwen engine package and the separate DeepSeek engine package
# for the NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121).
#
#   COMMIT=<40 hex> packaging/build_cuda_linux_aarch64.sh
#
# Run it on the Spark (arm64 Linux, CUDA 13.0 toolkit, a Python 3 venv with requirements.txt and requirements-build.txt, cmake and
# ninja on PATH; PYTHON=<that python>).  It runs spark/build_engine.sh, then makes two packages in $OUT (default ./out-engine-cuda13-aarch64):
#   <ver>-linux-aarch64-cuda-cuda13/       strata, libstrata_kq.so, strata-vision, strata-dsv41 and the CUDA libraries  (feed member "engine")
#   dsv41/<ver>-linux-aarch64-cuda-cuda13/ strata-dsv41 and the CUDA libraries                                         (feed member "dsv41")
# Nothing is signed or uploaded: sign with packaging/feed_tool.py (sign-package, then pack-engine; --prefix strata-dsv41 for the second).
#
# PKGVER is the package version (default: the version in CMakeLists.txt); COMMIT names the source commit in the build id and is required
# for a tree copy without .git.  The packages need glibc 2.39 or newer (Ubuntu 24.04, DGX OS 7): they are built on the Spark itself; there
# is no older arm64 chroot to build in.
set -eu
repo=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd -P)
py=${PYTHON:-python3}
out=${OUT:-$repo/out-engine-cuda13-aarch64}
mindriver=580.65
case "$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" in
  Linux-aarch64|Linux-arm64) ;;
  *) echo "build_cuda_linux_aarch64.sh: this builds on arm64 Linux (the DGX Spark)" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
cd "$repo"
ver=${PKGVER:-$(sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*project([^)]*VERSION[[:space:]]*\([0-9][0-9.]*\).*/\1/p' CMakeLists.txt | head -1)}
commit=${COMMIT:-$(git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || true)}
[ -n "$commit" ] || { echo "build_cuda_linux_aarch64.sh: set COMMIT=<hex> (no .git here)" >&2; exit 2; }
export COMMIT=$commit
stage=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/strata-engine-stage.XXXXXX")

# One long document, many questions (0.1.40.2, opt-in)

Read a long document once, then ask many different questions without reading it again. All numbers: Tesla P100 16 GB,
IQ2_XS, `--kv int8 --kv-resident 32768`, MTP on, greedy, the 0.1.40 engine unless a row says "pin".

## What the engine already did (0.1.40)

The conversation cache keeps small checkpoints (the GDN and indexer state, about 118 MiB each); the K/V of the document
stays in the session, so a question that starts from a checkpoint reads only what lies past it.

| 262K document (258,655 tokens) | time to first token |
|---|---|
| first question (cold read) | 904 s (286 tok/s) |
| questions 2-20, engine with a turn boundary at the document's end | 0.53 s median (0.44-0.72) |
| the same through the server's chat API (no turn boundary at the document's end) | 55.5 s each (15 measured): the engine re-reads up to `--prompt-cache-every` (16,384) tokens from the last periodic checkpoint |
| `parallel` 2 through the server | the first two questions 918 s and 979 s; the next pair read the document again from token 0 |

Checkpoint RAM: +804 MiB resident after the first read (6 checkpoints); each later question adds at most 10 MiB. The
K/V of 262K takes 3.06 GiB of pinned RAM, once per session (`--batch` slots each take their own).
Identity (greedy, 64 tokens): questions 1 and 12 on a fresh engine give the same tokens as in the 20-question run.

Back to the 6 [README](../README.md#how-does-it-work). 7 8 ## Who does what 9 10

11 12 - **The model is a team of 24,576 small specialists ("experts"),** and each word it writes needs only 10 of them. 13 So it doesn't have to have all of them on the graphics card at once. 14 - **Your graphics card** does the part of the work needed for every word, and keeps the few thousand experts that 15 are asked most often. It keeps learning which ones those are while you use it. 16 - **Your RAM** holds every expert. When a word needs one the card doesn't have, **your processor** works on it - 17 at the same time as the graphics card, so neither waits for the other. 18 - **Your SSD** holds a big lookup table; the model only reads a few small rows of it per word. 19 20 The same in technical terms: 21 22 - **GPU (VRAM):** attention and DeltaNet mixers, the gated-residual weights, routers, shared experts, output head, the 23 MTP draft layer, the KV cache (from 64K: only its most-read part, the rest streams from RAM), and an **expert 24 cache** that fills the rest of VRAM with the most-used experts (it adapts to the conversation while you chat). 25 More VRAM matters more than a faster GPU: every extra GB holds ~700 more experts, and every expert on the GPU is one 26 the CPU does not have to compute. 27 - **RAM:** all 24,576 experts, pinned. The CPU computes the experts that are not on the GPU **in place**, at the same 28 time as the GPU works on the cached ones (AVX-512 / AVX2 kernels, ggml's for the i-quants). On a PC with little RAM 29 and a big card, the [low-RAM mode](MODELS.md#a-big-graphics-card-and-little-ram) keeps in RAM only what the GPU does 30 not hold. 31 - **SSD:** the 28.8 GB n-gram table, read a few rows per token through the OS cache. 32 33 This works the same on NVIDIA (CUDA) and AMD (HIP) cards: the same engine, compiled for each. 34 35 ## Guess, then check 36 37

38 39 - **Guess, then check.** A small, fast helper built into the model guesses the next few words, and the big model 40 checks all the guesses in one go. 1	# Avoid duplicate expert slots across helper and primary GPUs
     2	
     3	## Why this helps
     4	
     5	On a PC with two small GPUs, helper experts start out separate from the primary
     6	cache. Later, the adaptive primary cache can promote an expert that the helper
     7	already holds. Both cards then spend memory on the same expert.
     8	
     9	We observed about 1,900-2,000 duplicate slots during sustained requests.
    10	This opt-in change keeps helper-owned experts out of primary promotion candidates,
    11	in both the server and command-line generation paths.
    12	
    13	## Use
    14	
    15	Set `STRATA_DISJOINT_ADAPT=1` before starting the engine. It is off by default.
    16	It leaves the existing peer-tier check and expert arithmetic unchanged.
    17	The check is live: each promotion candidate is asked of the helper's own cache (`RemoteExperts::holds`), so an expert
    18	the helper's tier swaps in or out later is followed (a mask copied at load would go stale). Needs the helper-share
    19	change (#854) for `holds`.
    20	
    21	## Validation environment
    22	
    23	- Two modified RTX 3080 20 GB cards; CUDA SM86, CUDA 13.1, Linux.
    24	- Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 (18 cores / 36 threads), about 94 GiB usable RAM.
    25	- PCIe 3.0, no GPU peer-to-peer access; 17 expert-pool workers.
    26	- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_S, 131,072-token context, INT8 KV,
    27	  32,768 resident KV cells.
    28	- Medium thinking: 2,048-token reasoning cap, 8,192-token output cap.
    29	- Physical GPU power limits stayed at 250 W and 280 W. No power increase.
    30	- Historical performance tests used an isolated engine based on official
    31	  v0.1.38 plus reviewed architectds/Strata changes (best, 05c0f36).
    32	  This PR contains only our change, ported to official main (99f3dbd).
    33	  The historical timings are NOT a measured speedup of this pure-upstream port.
    34	
    35	## Historical benefit
    36	
    37	Same binary and helper capacity, six complete JSON tasks per arm:
    38	
    39	| 32K cached request | Original | Ownership guard |
    40	| --- | ---: | ---: |
    41	| Generation | 81.5 tokens/s | 94.1 tokens/s |
    42	| Complete request | 12.997 s | 11.417 s |
    43	
    44	Generation improved by 15.5%; request time fell by 12.2%.
    45	The tasks returned complete 100-record arrays and correct source facts.
    46	All 18 checks passed across the original, guarded, and larger-cache arms.
    47	The larger-helper arm is not included in the comparison above.
    48	These repetitive tasks do not represent all agent workloads.
    49	
    50	## Validation and remaining work
    51	
    52	- Standalone ownership test passes, including disabled, empty, unowned,
    53	  owned, and out-of-range entries, plus candidate filtering.
    54	- Linux compile/link against pure official main (99f3dbd) passed. No engine

     1	# Strata on the NVIDIA DGX Spark (Linux, ARM64)
     2	
     3	The DGX Spark is a small desktop box with a GB10 chip: a Blackwell GPU (compute capability 12.1, 48 SMs) and 20 Arm CPU cores that share
     4	128 GB of memory. Strata 0.2.7.1 runs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on it. This page says what works, how to install it, what
     5	the Spark does with its memory, and how the speeds were measured. It was tested on one Spark (Ubuntu 24.04, driver 580.173, CUDA 13.0).
     6	Nothing here is known to work on another ARM machine.
     7	
     8	## What works, and what does not
     9	
    10	- **Works:** Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_S and the NVFP4 GPTQ pack (64K context, every expert in the GPU's cache), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 2.00 bpw
    11	  (a short chat), the Terminal (`strata launch`, `strata update`, `strata serve`) and the engine packages of the signed feed.
    12	- **Not built for ARM:** the desktop app (no AppImage; use the Terminal), the HIP, SYCL and CPU-only engines, and the Q2_0 and Gyro packs,
    13	  whose CPU kernels are x86-only (the engine refuses them at start). Picture reading is compiled in and was not tried on the Spark.
    14	- **Not tested:** contexts above 128K, more than eight chat slots (four and eight were measured: "Several chats at once" below), a long soak. `strata doctor --live` lists the GB10 with no memory
    15	  figure, because `nvidia-smi` reports none for it.
    16	
    17	## Install with the Terminal
    18	
    19	```sh
    20	curl -fsSL https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/releases/latest/download/install.sh -o install.sh && sh install.sh
    21	strata launch
    22	```
    23	
    24	`install.sh` unpacks the Terminal into `~/.local/share/strata` (no administrator rights) and checks the release's signed feed. `strata launch`
    25	fetches the `linux-aarch64` engine package, shows what each model needs, downloads the one you choose and starts it. Pick Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
    26	IQ3_S (84 GB download) or the NVFP4 pack, or DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 2.00 bpw (257 GB). The engine package needs glibc 2.39 or newer
    27	(Ubuntu 24.04, DGX OS 7) and NVIDIA driver 580.65 or newer.
    28	
    29	## Install from a source checkout
    30	
    31	```sh
    32	./setup.sh --setup --family qwen --model IQ3_S --context 65536 --vision no --yes --no-start --data-dir ~/Strata-data
    33	./setup.sh --setup --family nvfp4 --model NVFP4 --context 65536 --vision no --yes --no-start --data-dir ~/Strata-data
    34	```
    35	
    36	`--data-dir` must be a folder you can write (the default, next to the checkout, may be under `/home`, which a normal user cannot create).
    37	Setup finds the GB10, calls it unified memory, takes the engine from the feed (or compiles it with `spark/build_engine.sh` when the release
    38	has none) and writes the run config with the settings measured on this part:
    39	
    40	| Setting | Why |
    41	|---|---|
    42	| `--mmap-experts` | the experts are read from the model files in place, so the GPU's cache holds all 24,576 of them instead of a second copy in RAM |
    43	| `--prefill auto:32768` | a 32,768-token prompt chunk; the automatic 8,192 measured 2 to 6% slower here |
    44	| `--mtp-q4 all` | the draft layer as 4-bit copies: +3.5% decode, the answers do not change because the target checks every draft |
    45	| `--mtp-hnorm stream` | one norm per hyper-connection stream in the draft layer: draft acceptance 0.60 to 0.63, +4.3% decode |
    46	
    47	Setup prints `--draft-vocab en` as a tip and does not set it: it measured +3.1% decode on English prompts, and it would cut the Chinese,
    48	Japanese and Korean drafts.
    49	
    50	Start a model with its run script (`./run-iq3_s.sh`) or `./setup.sh`.
    51	
    52	## Build the engine yourself
    53	
    54	You need the CUDA 13.0 toolkit (`/usr/local/cuda`; DGX OS has it), cmake, ninja and Python 3.10 or newer.
    55	
    56	```sh
    57	python3 -m venv .venv-build
    58	.venv-build/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-build.txt
    59	PATH="$PWD/.venv-build/bin:/usr/local/cuda/bin:$PATH" PYTHON="$PWD/.venv-build/bin/python" JOBS=16 sh spark/build_engine.sh
    60	cp -r out-spark/engine ./engine
    61	```
    62	
    63	About 3 minutes for the Qwen engine and 6 with the DeepSeek engine and the picture reader (the first run also fetches llama.cpp at the
    64	pinned commit). `out-spark/engine/` holds `strata`, `strata-dsv41`, `strata-vision`, `libstrata_kq.so`, the CUDA libraries and a `BUILD.json`.
    65	`BUILD_VISION=0` and `BUILD_DSV41=0` leave a part out. `packaging/build_cuda_linux_aarch64.sh` runs this build and makes the engine packages
    66	for the feed ([packaging/README.md](../packaging/README.md)). A model on a Q2_0 pack cannot run: its CPU kernels need AVX-512.

    68	## What the Spark does with its memory
    69	
    70	The GPU's memory and the CPU's are the same 121.6 GB, so a model's experts are held once. With `--mmap-experts` there is one copy: the model
    71	file's pages, which the GPU cache uses.
    72	
    73	| | IQ3_S | NVFP4 GPTQ |
    74	|---|---|---|
    75	| Expert bytes | 50.3 GB | 68.0 GB |
    76	| Expert cache | 24,576 of 24,576 slots, 46.84 GiB | 24,576 of 24,576 slots, 63.29 GiB |
    77	| n-gram table | 28.8 GB, locked in RAM (`--ple-io ram`) | 51.2 GB, read from the SSD |
    78	| Context | 64K, 8-bit KV, 32,768 cells streamed | same |
    79	| Free memory at start | about 1 GiB | about 1.2 GiB |

1	# Resident expert exchange buffer rotation
     2	
     3	When the resident RAM complement exchanges an expert with the GPU cache, the
     4	evicted expert lands in a temporary host buffer. The existing path then copies
     5	those bytes into the promoted expert's old RAM slot. Rotation removes that last
     6	host copy: the temporary buffer becomes resident, and the old RAM slot becomes
     7	the next temporary buffer.
     8	
     9	## Enable
    10	
    11	Rotation is **off by default**. Set `STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE=1` before starting the
    12	engine with your existing arguments:
    13	
    14	```bash
    15	export STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE=1
    16	```
    17	
    18	```powershell
    19	$env:STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE = '1'
    20	```
    21	
    22	Only the exact value `1` opts in. Set it to `0` or remove it to restore the copy
    23	path. This setting does not select resident RAM mode or change any preset.
    24	It applies only when the resident complement is fully pinned and GPU-mapped
    25	and the exchange buffers can also be pinned and mapped. Other layouts keep the
    26	copy path and log why rotation could not be enabled. Configurations without a
    27	resident complement do not use it. Layers may differ in expert block size (a
    28	GGUF with mixed quantizations per layer): see
    29	[Layers of different block sizes](#layers-of-different-block-sizes).
    30	
    31	The startup diagnostic confirms activation:
    32	
    33	```text
    34	FileExpertSource: exchange buffer rotation enabled: ...; no host commit memcpy
    35	```
    36	
    37	Serving diagnostics report the cumulative rotated block count and avoided
    38	`memcpy` payload bytes. This counts the copied payload once, not read plus write
    39	traffic, and does not include the GPU transfers, which still occur.
    40	
    41	## Ownership and synchronization
    42	
    43	The original allocations own their memory until `FileExpertSource::close()`.
    44	Rotation updates slot ownership and keeps each host pointer paired with its GPU
    45	alias. Atomic slot IDs let background residency queries observe those immutable
    46	pairs. Compute readers and GPU transfers must still finish before the existing
    47	serialized commit; rotation adds no overlapping compute or new synchronization
    48	policy. Reserve the maximum exchange capacity before rotation starts: growing a
    49	live exchange arena is rejected because it can now hold resident experts.
    50	
    51	## Layers of different block sizes
    52	
    53	A swap exchanges two experts of the same layer, so the RAM slot the promoted
    54	expert leaves has exactly the size of the block the evicted one needs. Rotation
    55	therefore keeps its spare buffers per block size: an exchange of a layer takes
    56	a spare of that layer's size and hands back one of the same size, and every
    57	size keeps its number of spares for good. The first version required one size
    58	for all layers and fell back to the copy path on any other pack; Swift 1.5
    59	IQ3_S has seven sizes (1,510,400 to 2,662,400 bytes) and IQ3_XXS has nine
    60	too, so neither could rotate.
    61	
    62	The exchange allocation holds one spare of every size per swap of a round:
    63	`--adapt-swaps` (at most 96) times the sum of the distinct sizes. With
    64	`--adapt-async 1` the second half of the buffers only stages copies and is
    65	kept in the largest size alone. On IQ3_S with `--adapt-swaps 80` that is
    66	1.06 GiB of page-locked RAM (1.26 GiB with `--adapt-async 1`), against 0.20
    67	and 0.40 GiB for the copy path's buffers. The startup line says how many sizes
    68	and how much:
    69	
    70	```text
    71	FileExpertSource: exchange buffer rotation enabled: 80 buffers in 7 block sizes (largest 2662400 bytes, 1.06 GiB page-locked); no host commit memcpy
    72	```
    73	
    74	With `--adapt-async 1` a rotated round also ends one verify window sooner:
    75	there are no bytes for the background job to move, so the ownership flip runs
    76	in the tick that sees the copies in.
    77	
    78	`tests/core/exchange_storage_test.cpp` covers it without CUDA (three sizes,
    79	6,144 exchanges: bytes, aliases, a spare of another size or an expert of
    80	another layer refused, overlapping resident blocks refused).

     1	# Overlap streamed KV uploads with prefill computation
     2	
     3	## Why this helps
     4	
     5	When long-context KV lives partly in system RAM, prefill uploads each attention
     6	layer's cached prefix. Waiting for every upload on the compute stream leaves
     7	the GPU idle.
     8	
     9	This opt-in change starts the next attention layer's upload on a separate stream
    10	while the current layer continues computing. It reuses the existing staging
    11	pool; it does not allocate another KV buffer.
    12	
    13	## Use and ordering
    14	
    15	Set `STRATA_KV_PREFETCH=1` before starting the engine. It is off by default.
    16	A release event protects the staging pool's last reader; a ready event orders
    17	the next attention consumer. Early returns drain pending copies before the caller
    18	can refill borrowed expert slots. Relayout and destruction also drain the stream.
    19

"""The auto-tuner: find the fastest settings for this PC, for this model, for what the user asked for.

What it does (TUNING-SPEC.md sections 5-6, measured on five machines):

1. **Starts from the user's own configuration** (the "base") and changes one knob at a time (`tune_knobs`). It never starts
   a candidate at "the first value of every dimension".
2. Measures with the real worker over HTTP, on the engine's own clock (`tune_session`), the same fixed request set every
   time. Restart knobs are tried as **interleaved rounds**: every round runs the base and each candidate once, in a
   rotating order, so machine drift cannot favour one of them. Per-request knobs need no restart and are tried first, in
   one engine.
3. Accepts a candidate only if the **median of its per-round ratios** to the base beats the noise: at least +3%, and twice
   the drift and twice the A/A gap measured on the base runs, in every round (quick) or at least 4 of 5 (thorough
   confirm), without losing more than 2% elsewhere (prompt speed). A gain the noise can explain is not a gain: the result
   is then "your current settings are already the fastest" and nothing changes.
4. Guards before every start: free RAM, free graphics memory, other engines running, the CPU busy with something else.
   A candidate that does not fit is skipped, never started. A candidate must not use more memory than the base the user
   asked for (so "leave 20% for my work" is respected). The first crash stops the stage.
5. Only knobs whose answers are byte-identical (class exact) are chosen on their own; the others need the user's tick.

Progress and time left are reported through a callback; a cancel stops at the next run and keeps nothing half-measured.
"""

     5	is `0`, retaining the existing per-expert copies. The normal kernel-copy mode
     6	is unchanged. This is an experiment to reduce host submission overhead, not a
     7	demonstrated increase in model tokens per second.
     8	
     9	`STRATA_DMA_BATCH=2` also sets CUDA 13.4's
    10	`cudaMemcpyFlagPreferOverlapWithCompute`. It is a scheduling hint, not a
    11	guarantee of overlap. On CUDA 13.0–13.3 this mode behaves like `1`. Older CUDA
    12	builds and HIP retain individual copies. A single upload or a group larger than
    13	128 also uses individual copies.
    14	
    15	The sources must be immutable pinned host blobs, and destinations must be
    16	disjoint. `expert_source.cpp` already restricts the DMA group to pinned experts.
    17	The helper resolves device-visible aliases for registered host allocations;
    18	Windows registered host pointers need not equal their GPU aliases. No extra
    19	VRAM or weight conversion is introduced. All copies remain on the existing
    20	stream, before the callback that signals flag B. A submission error fails the
    21	engine rather than signalling readiness for stale weights.
    22	
    23	## Tests
    24	
    25	With the normal CUDA build and `STRATA_BUILD_TESTS=ON`:
    26	
    27	```sh
    28	cmake --build build --target dma_batch_parity
    29	ctest --test-dir build -R dma_batch --output-on-failure
    30	```

    32	The test checks bytes and cross-stream event ordering for 0, 1, 4, 17, 64, 128,
    33	and 129 uploads, at 37 bytes, 4 KiB and 2 MiB per upload, in all three modes.
    34	Windows also runs the same cases with `VirtualAlloc` plus `cudaHostRegister`.
    35	It prints interleaved diagnostic timings separately for submission and total
    36	transfer time. These times overlap; they must not be added. On Windows it also
    37	reports submitting-thread cycles using `QueryThreadCycleTime`. Cycle counts
    38	are neither whole-process CPU utilization nor an energy measurement.
    39	
    40	The 63-case matrix passed with both host allocation methods on CUDA 13.4 and
    41	13.0, and with the individual-copy fallback on CUDA 12.6, all using the same
    42	RTX 4070 Laptop and driver 616.56. This checks the older-toolkit fallback;
    43	it is not a HIP runtime test.

    45	## Initial measurement

    47	RTX 4070 Laptop 8 GB, Ryzen 9 7940HS, 64 GB DDR5-5600, Windows, CUDA 13.4:
    48	16 independent registered-host uploads of 2 MiB each, five measured repetitions
    49	after warmup, alternating mode order:
    50	
    51	| Path | Median host submission | Median total transfer |
    52	| --- | ---: | ---: |
    53	| Individual copies | 0.0936 ms | 2.5589 ms |
    54	| Batch | 0.0162 ms | 2.5248 ms |
    55	| Batch with overlap hint | 0.0155 ms | 2.5206 ms |

    57	Batch submission latency fell 82.7%; total transfer latency fell only 1.3%.
    58	Submission latency is measured wall time around the API calls, not whole-process
    59	CPU utilization or energy consumption. The initial full-model screen on Swift
    60	1.5 IQ3_XXS at 64K allocated context did not establish a generation-speed gain:
    61	one coding request measured 30.3 tokens/s with individual DMA and 30.0 with
    62	batching. Its generated lengths differed, so total task times cannot isolate
    63	the transfer change. This evidence does not justify changing the default.
    64	
    65	A separate CUDA 13.4 repetition with submitting-thread cycle measurements gave
    66	449,824 cycles for individual copies and 67,939 for the batch, about 84.9% fewer.

    68	2.5584 vs 2.5309 ms (about 1.1% lower). These are separate runs from the initial

# Config snapshot

For every **machine class x model set x entry point** this records what the engine would be started with, and a test fails on any difference.

Nothing real is used: no GPU, no model file (the model files are empty), no engine (a text stub), no download (the drafter fetch is a recorder), no network,
no real user folder (every run has its own scratch HOME, data folder and install folder, removed afterwards).

## Run it

```
python -m pytest tests/snapshot -q -p no:cacheprovider      # the gate: about a minute; needs Python 3.11+ and Node 24
STRATA_SNAPSHOT_UPDATE=1 python -m pytest tests/snapshot     # after an intended change: rewrites golden/, then review the git diff of golden/
python -m tests.snapshot.generate --out DIR                  # write the snapshot of this tree somewhere else (to compare two branches)
python -m tests.snapshot.report --golden DIR_A --against DIR_B   # Markdown: where the entry points differ, what changed between A and B
```

`STRATA_SNAPSHOT_SKIP_APP=1` skips the two app entry points by name when Node is not installed (the test prints what it skipped).
The same command works on Windows, Linux and macOS; the golden files hold no path, user name or time of the machine that made them.

## What is simulated

* **machine classes** (`matrix.py`): NVIDIA all-resident (RTX PRO 5000 72 GB), NVIDIA 12 GB streaming (RTX 3060), DGX Spark (linux-aarch64, GB10),
  Strix Halo Windows (gfx1151), Radeon R9700 (gfx1201, Linux), Intel Arc A750 (SYCL), Mac M-series small (16 GB) and large (128 GB).
  A class sets the engine family, the card architecture, the card memory, the platform and the hardware report the Terminal's catalog and the app's host read.
* **model sets**: IQ3_S, UD-Q4_K_XL, UD-IQ4_XS-v31, DeepSeek (IST-DAS-2.00bpw).
* **entry points**: `setup`, `launch`, `app_plain`, `app_models`.

## What the Spark does with its memory

The GPU's memory and the CPU's are the same 121.6 GB, so a model's experts are held once. With `--mmap-experts` there is one copy: the model
file's pages, which the GPU cache uses.

| | IQ3_S | NVFP4 GPTQ |
|---|---|---|
| Expert bytes | 50.3 GB | 68.0 GB |
| Expert cache | 24,576 of 24,576 slots, 46.84 GiB | 24,576 of 24,576 slots, 63.29 GiB |
| n-gram table | 28.8 GB, locked in RAM (`--ple-io ram`) | 51.2 GB, read from the SSD |
| Context | 64K, 8-bit KV, 32,768 cells streamed | same |
| Free memory at start | about 1 GiB | about 1.2 GiB |

The NVFP4 table does not fit in RAM beside the page cache the 68 GB expert file needs. Locking it measured 137 tok/s on a 4K prompt and 26 tok/s
decode, against 1,252 and 39 without. Leave it on the SSD (setup does).

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 2.00 bpw places 12,163 of its 15,744 experts in the GPU's share and runs the rest on the CPU lane from the model's files.
The engine sizes that from the memory Linux can still give back (`MemAvailable` less 6 GiB, `DS4_UMA_HEADROOM_GIB`), because the model files' page
cache is most of the memory `cudaMemGetInfo` calls used.

## Qwen3.6-35B-A3B

A smaller model from the same maker: [Qwen3.6-35B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) (35 billion
parameters, 3 billion active per token, 256 experts, Apache 2.0). Strata runs
[Unsloth's GGUFs with the MTP draft layer](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-GGUF) on its own engine
path, chosen by the file. It is in the app's model list and in setup (`--family qwen36`). It runs on NVIDIA and AMD
cards; the Intel Arc engine and the Mac engine do not run it. It reads pictures and serves several requests at once.

| Size | File | RAM setup plans for | In plain words |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| **UD-Q4_K_XL** | 22.9 GB | 32 GB | 4-bit (Unsloth Dynamic), the smallest |
| **UD-Q6_K_XL** | 32.6 GB | 44 GB | 6-bit, closer to the full model |
| **Q8_0** | 37.8 GB | 52 GB | 8-bit, the closest to the full model |

The picture reader file adds 0.9 GB. The engine keeps every expert it can on the graphics card and computes the rest on
the CPU.

| Hardware | Decode |

| Radeon AI PRO R9700 (32 GB) | 117.8 tokens/s |

## Adding or switching models

- **In the app:** the Models page lists every model with its size and whether it fits your computer. Pick one and press the install button.
- **In the Terminal:** `strata launch` has a Model step with the same list and "Use model files I already have".
  `strata models list` shows what is installed. `strata models import <folder or .gguf> --plan` shows what a set of
  files you already have would become, without changing anything.
- **From a source checkout only:** `SETUP.bat` or `./setup.sh --setup` adds another model ([SOURCE_INSTALL.md](SOURCE_INSTALL.md)).

"""tools/make_profile.py - the expert-cache profile (`data/expert-profile.bin`): every (layer, expert) pair, ranked.

`--expert-cache auto` fills the VRAM slots it can afford with the profile's pairs in order, so the ranking decides
which experts start resident (the adaptive tier then swaps in what a conversation routes most).  A profile that
ranks fewer pairs than a card can hold caps the cache (issue #46: a 32 GB card stopped at 8,000 slots); this tool
writes one that ranks all 24,576.

The order: the base profile's ranking (default: the shipped data/expert-profile.bin), then the pairs your routing
traces used, most frequent first, then every pair still missing, interleaved across the layers.  The base is only
*appended to*, never reordered - and the shipped profile already ranks all 24,576 pairs, so with it a trace is a
no-op.  `--reorder` ranks the traces first and lets the base fill the rest, which is how a workload's trace decides
the top; `--no-base` drops the base entirely.

WATCH THE BASE: `take()` skips a pair it has already ranked, and the shipped base ranks all 24,576, so a plain
`--base` run cannot be moved by any trace - the output is the base again.  `--reorder` (traces first) or
`--no-base` is what makes a trace decide the top.  Which ordering is in use is not cosmetic: the layer-split cost
model reads this RANKING as if it were a frequency curve, and the coverage curve in src/program/generate.cpp
carries the measured hit rates that say how far off that goes (94.9% claimed against 69.2% measured at 5,805 pairs
held, on the IQ3_S 4-way rig).

    python tools/make_profile.py [TRACE ...] [--base data/expert-profile.bin | --no-base] [--reorder] [--out PATH]
                                 [--n-expert 256]      (a pruned model: GSQ-RCO Coder keeps 256 of 512)

A routing trace comes from a one-shot engine run with `--dump-routing FILE` (a prompt typical of your use; the
routed experts of every layer and position are written).  Point the model config's `--expert-profile` at the result.
"""
import argparse
import struct
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
N_LAYER, N_EXPERT = 48, 512
MAGIC, VERSION = b"STRP", 1


def read_profile(path, n_expert=N_EXPERT):
    blob = Path(path).read_bytes()
    if blob[:4] != MAGIC:
        raise SystemExit(f"{path}: not a Strata profile")
    ver, nl, ne, slots, n = struct.unpack_from("<5I", blob, 4)
    if (nl, ne) != (N_LAYER, n_expert):
        raise SystemExit(f"{path}: {nl}x{ne}, not {N_LAYER}x{n_expert}")
    return [struct.unpack_from("<HH", blob, 24 + 4 * i) for i in range(n)]


def read_trace(path, n_expert=N_EXPERT):
    """(layer, k, k expert ids, k weights) records, as `--dump-routing` writes them."""
    blob = Path(path).read_bytes()
    off, freq = 0, defaultdict(int)
    while off + 8 <= len(blob):
        layer, k = struct.unpack_from("<ii", blob, off)
        off += 8
        for e in struct.unpack_from("<%di" % k, blob, off):
            if 0 <= layer < N_LAYER and 0 <= e < n_expert:
                freq[(layer, e)] += 1
        off += 8 * k                                    # the ids and the weights
    return freq

"""tools/collect_profile_traces.py - routing traces of a varied set of prompts, for tools/make_profile_mix.py.

For every prompt of a corpus (default bench/profile_corpus.json: 45 chat, code, maths, reasoning, writing, science, tool
use and six-language prompts) it runs the engine once (greedy, --max-new tokens) and keeps the routed experts of the
generated text:

    python tools/collect_profile_traces.py CONFIG.json OUTDIR [--corpus FILE] [--max-new 250] [--mode usage|routing]

CONFIG.json is a run config setup wrote (strata-*.json: "exe", "args", "env", "tokenizer", "cwd").  The engine is run as
`exe args... --tokens-file F --max-new N --greedy` (--serve and --batch are dropped).  `--mode usage` (default) is the
SYCL engine's STRATA_USAGE_DUMP=PATH, which counts on the device and works with STRATA_VERIFY_NO_HOST; `--mode routing`
adds `--dump-routing PATH` (the CUDA/HIP engines and the SYCL host path).  Then, for example:

    python tools/make_profile_mix.py OUTDIR/c*.trace:1 --out data/expert-profile-new.bin

A prompt takes a start-up of the engine (20-60 s) and ~10 s of decoding; 45 prompts are ~30 minutes.  The traces are the
generated text's routing only (decode windows); the prompt's own routing is not counted.
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent))
import strata_tokenizer as ST  # noqa: E402


def load_tokenizer(tdir):
    tdir = Path(tdir)
    vocab = json.loads((tdir / "vocab.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    toks = [None] * len(vocab)
    for t, i in vocab.items():
        toks[i] = t
    return ST.Tokenizer(toks, (tdir / "merges.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8").split("\n"),
                        json.loads((tdir / "token_type.json").read_text()))


def drop(args, flag, with_value=False):
    args = list(args)
    while flag in args:
        i = args.index(flag)
        del args[i:i + (2 if with_value else 1)]
    return args

"""tools/bench_eviction.py - replay a `--dump-routing` trace against candidate ExpertCache eviction policies.

`ExpertCache::admit` never evicts: eviction policy is the measured question (R4.1's LFU-decay vs LRU sweep,
`include/strata/core/expert_cache.hpp`), and a placeholder policy would set the hit rate that everything
downstream is sized against.  This tool is the harness for that measurement, without a GPU: a policy's hit
rate depends only on the ORDER the run routed (layer, expert) pairs, and `--dump-routing` records exactly
that order.  Replay the trace through a simulated slot pool per policy and the rates are comparable with
the engine's own `h`, at any slot count, on any machine.

    python tools/bench_eviction.py TRACE... [--slots 4105,8000] [--per-layer] [--windows 4]
                                 [--policies fill-only,lru,lfu-decay,oracle] [--decay-window 65536]
                                 [--prefill data/expert-profile.bin] [--n-expert 512] [--csv out.csv]

Policies (`--policies`, default all four):

  fill-only   the engine's current admission: compulsory miss, never evict.  The baseline a policy has
              to beat, and the answer for any run whose trace never exceeds the slot count.
  lru         evict the least-recently-used resident.
  lfu-decay   frequency counts halved every --decay-window lookups, so a hot-once expert fades and the
              cache can follow a topic shift; evict the lowest count, the oldest on a tie.  (Halving the
              table is O(slots) per window; this instead DOUBLES new increments at each window boundary,
              which scales every past access by the same 1/2 and leaves the table untouched.  Comparisons
              stay exact: counts are sums of powers of two, below 2^53 for any realistic trace.)
  oracle      Belady's MIN: evict the resident whose next use is furthest in the future.  Not
              implementable online - it reads the trace ahead - but it is the upper bound any policy can
              reach on this trace, so it says how much headroom a real policy is leaving.

Scope mirrors `ExpertCache`: global (one shared pool, the engine's default) or `--per-layer` (R4.2g:
layer `l` owns slots `[l*q, (l+1)*q)`, `q = slots // n_layers`, the last layer taking the remainder, and
eviction stays inside the layer's own range - `layer_slot_range` in `src/core/expert_cache.cpp`).

`--prefill` starts the run with the profile's top pairs resident (rank 0 counts as most-recently-used),
which is how the engine actually starts with `--expert-profile`; without it the run starts cold.

AGENTS.md: a number needs what it was measured on.  The tool prints the trace files and the lookup and
distinct-pair counts it ran over; quote those with any rate you take from it.  The trace itself comes
from a one-shot engine run (`--dump-routing FILE` on a prompt typical of the workload) - the model,
quant and prompt are the environment, and they belong in any report of these rates.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

"""tools/make_profile_mix.py - an expert-cache profile from several routing traces, each trace counting the same.

`make_profile.py` adds the traces' raw counts, so the longest trace decides the ranking.  A cache profile should
rank the experts by how often a USER's tokens need them, across the kinds of text that user writes, so here every
trace is first turned into a distribution (its counts / its total) and multiplied by its weight; the ranking is the
weighted sum.  Weights are per trace, so a kind of text with more traces counts more - give a group of N traces the
weight 1/N each to make the group count once.

    python tools/make_profile_mix.py TRACE[:WEIGHT] [TRACE[:WEIGHT] ...] [--out PATH] [--n-expert 512]

A trace is a `--dump-routing` file, or a `STRATA_USAGE_DUMP` file of the SYCL engine (same record format).  The output
is a profile for `--expert-profile`; the pairs no trace uses are appended in make_profile.py's fill order.

Measured on an Arc Pro B70 (IQ3_S, 11.5k cached experts, decode of 250-300 tokens): the shipped profile holds 60% of the
experts 45 chat/code/language prompts route and 85% of those a document summary routes; a profile from the 45 chat prompts
and the 8 summaries (weight 1 : 2 per prompt), tested on prompts left out of it, holds 71% and 84%.

Verdicts: ADOPT = use as is, PORT = port a narrow piece, PATTERN = copy the idea only, REJECT.

## 0. What Strata is (context for every verdict)
Product-level inference engine (own C++/CUDA/HIP/SYCL/Metal runtime in `src/`, Python server in `serve/`, CLI in `strata_cli/` + `strata_control/`, Tauri/Node desktop app). It runs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (48 layers x 512 experts = 24,576 experts) and DeepSeek V4.1-Flash (15,744 experts) with a GPU expert cache + all experts in pinned RAM + CPU experts (`docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md`). It is NOT llama.cpp-based at the top level (only the vendored `third_party/strata-ggml` for IQ-quant kernels). So engine code does not transfer to us; the tooling and methods do.

## 1. Tools / profiling / observability

Replay simulates cache policies (LFU-decay, LRU, adaptive swap) with no GPU; hit rate depends only on routing ORDER. ## 2. Methodology comparison (from `docs/BENCHMARK_PROTOCOL.md`, `COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS.md`, `DGX_SPARK_LINUX.md`, `autotune.py`)
Strata rules worth noting:
- Frozen fixtures with committed `MANIFEST.sha256`; corpus sha is `protocol.corpus_sha256`; `.gitattributes -text` so line endings never change bytes; runner refuses on one byte difference; rebuilds byte-for-byte via `tools/build_standard_corpus.py`.
- Any change to prompts/order/caps/scoring requires a NEW protocol ID; schema changes use a separate version. Draft protocol is labelled "draft" until a two-hardware pilot.
- Two tracks never merged: `default` (setup-generated) vs `custom`; "claimed improvement requires a separate same-machine baseline".
- Metrics defined by engine counters only (`read_tokens/prompt_s`, `decode_tokens/decode_s`); cached tokens never in numerator; client clocks only for TTFT/total; never divide output tokens by wall time and call it decode speed; keep API token count and engine count separately and explain mismatch.
- Unexpected prompt-cache reuse check: `cached_tokens <= max_shared_prefix_tokens + 8` else exclude from speed summary, mark run nonconforming; restart engine between runs.
- null with a JSON-Pointer `missing` reason for every unavailable value; no 0/"N/A"/NaN. Status `complete|partial|nonconforming`. Medians/min/max/n per case, never pooled across sizes/quants; exclusions listed with reasons; "never hide early EOS, failures, slow samples"; partial keeps real n.
- Capped outputs counted (`Capped` column): 35/36 long requests hit the cap while still reasoning, so decode TPS is "to-cap" time.
- Sanity checks are exact-match / strict-JSON with no LLM judge; quality never merged with speed.
- Hardware record: unified memory flagged `memory_kind: shared`, power limit null with reason, `background_workloads` listed, loopback only, remote = nonconforming.
- DGX doc: ABBA block order, 4 samples/cell, medians, "figures move a few percent between sessions"; `STRATA_SM121_PERF=0` A/B switch to isolate a table; identical-logits check to prove a diff is the switch, not noise.
- Autotune: gain must beat 2x A/A gap and 2x drift; early drop after 1 round at -5%; "a gain the noise can explain is not a gain".
- What Strata does NOT do (we do): no clock/governor capture ("no clock capture" is admitted in COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS L58), no formal A/A run, no ub=1 KL gating (its KL uses decode windows and a fixed config), no per-sample first-iteration-ramp exclusion.

Concrete rules for us to add:
1. Record `protocol_id` + corpus sha256 in every result; any change to prompts/caps/seeds/order = new id; `-text` gitattribute on fixtures.
2. Result schema: unavailable = null + pointer-keyed reason; status `complete|partial|nonconforming`; `n` kept honest.
3. Prompt-cache-reuse assertion (`cached_tokens` vs allowed shared prefix) on every serve-style run; restart between runs.
4. Report "capped / early-EOS" counts next to every decode rate; forbid pooling across context depths.
5. Adopt Strata's accept rule in `perf_summary`: median of per-round ratios >= +3% and > 2x A/A gap and > 2x drift, in all rounds (>=4 of 5 in confirm), plus <=2% regression on the other phase (pp when tuning tg).
6. Classify every optimisation as `exact` (byte-identical greedy output) / `numerically different` / `lossy`; only `exact` auto-accepted (our D027 "identical outputs" is that class).
7. Tag runs with the machine "noise state": record A/A gap and drift beside each A/B (we have A/A; make it a stored field).
8. Keep default vs custom tracks and a same-machine baseline for any claim.
9. Add a cell grid (prompt length x cached fraction x gen) and ABBA ordering for depth sweeps, which also addresses our Jetson first-sample clock-ramp artefact (J-E002).
10. For unified memory, adopt `memory_kind: shared` + the "pinned RAM costs 2x in a shared pool" kind of measured constant (`strata_control/uma_pool.py`: pool demand = fixed + cache slots x slot size + 2 x RAM-held experts; measured on 128 GB Strix Halo, hang with 41 s silent exit when overcommitted). Test whether our Jetson mmap/pinned path doubles residency (J-E003 saw +2.5 vs +1.8 GB cached).

- Toolchain: `flake.nix` pins nixpkgs-unstable (flake.lock), CUDA 13.0 (`cudaPackages_13_0`) because 13.2.0/13.2.1 miscompile sm_120; x86_64-linux only; cmake/ninja from nix, not pip. `spark/build_engine.sh` warns on those toolkit versions. - CMake: `CMakePresets.json` v5 (new since ffa80d73): `cpu-check` (no GPU/no network), `cpu-check-native`, `cuda-compile` (`CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES "86-real;89-real;89-virtual"`), `hip-compile`; same flags as the release scripts so CI compile-only builds equal release builds. - Packaging: per-platform build scripts, `package_engine.py`, signed feed with `min_driver`, `collect_libs.py`/`binary_deps.py` bundle CUDA libs.
- aarch64/Jetson/sm_87: aarch64 YES but only DGX Spark: `packaging/build_cuda_linux_aarch64.sh` + `spark/build_engine.sh` (default `ARCHS=121`, CUDA 13.0, glibc >= 2.39, driver >= 580.65, built on the device itself, "no older arm64 chroot"). `grep` for sm_87/Jetson/Orin in the repo (excluding third_party) finds no hit; sm_87 is not a target, CPU kernels for Q2_0/Gyro are x86-only. `CMakePresets` omit aarch64.
- Fit to our two targets: (a) reproducible pip-style pins + per-platform lock files are ADOPT for Python helpers (`cc/`, `lab/`); (b) CMake preset names `*-compile` = what our Build CC `cuda_compile_check` does, copy the "same flags as release" discipline; (c) nix flake is PATTERN only: x86 only and JetPack 6.2 cannot be nix-built (L4T driver stack), so for the Jetson keep host-native build + ccache; for amd64 CUDA 12.8 sm_120 a flake could pin nvcc/gcc, but our Docker/Buildx digest pinning already gives the same and works on both targets, so do not add nix; (d) record toolkit-version blacklist (miscompile warning) in the Build CC.

## 5. Gaps neither project covers (goal: MoE ~4x device memory, unified memory + SSD, acceptable quality and t/s)
Strata does not either: its largest case (DeepSeek V4.1 2-bit) is 257 GB on a 128 GB Spark and still keeps experts in RAM/mmap plus CPU lane; the 4x oversubscription with SSD in the expert path is only touched via the n-gram table on SSD (NVFP4 locked-in-RAM measured 26 vs 39 tok/s decode). Gaps:
1. SSD expert streaming with prefetch/readahead and a cache hierarchy (VRAM/pinned/pagecache/SSD) on unified memory: no I/O model (queue depth, O_DIRECT vs mmap, NVMe bandwidth on Orin/Spark), no cold-start vs steady-state split. Strata has `tests/platform/direct_file_async.cpp`, `io_priority_test.cpp` and `serve/cache_drop.py` (page-cache give-back) only as small hooks.
2. Router-aware prefetch (predict next-layer experts from the current routing) and its accuracy measurement on traces; replay tools here only cover reactive eviction.
3. Quality under on-demand quantization/mixed precision and under expert skipping/substitution (Strata has `STRATA_ROUTE_TAIL_SKIP`, KVA approximations, but no joint t/s vs KL Pareto per memory budget); our `cc/memory_pareto` is the nearest.
4. A trace corpus for a LARGE real MoE (routing skew at 256-512 experts, top-8+); we only have Granite 1B/400M-active (mild skew, D017). Strata's skew claims come from its own model.
5. Memory-limited execution test: hard enforcement of a device-memory cap on shared DRAM (our `gpu_budget` shim is untested on Jetson; Strata sizes from `MemAvailable - 6 GiB` heuristics, `DS4_UMA_HEADROOM_GIB`).
6. Thermal/clock/power state as a first-class covariate (neither records governor + clocks per sample; ours has nvpmodel/devfreq in summary but not per-sample).
7. Cost model that predicts t/s for (hit rate, miss cost, SSD bandwidth, overlap) validated end-to-end; our D019 says the overlap bound is not supported.
8. Crash/soak behaviour of a swap-heavy run (OOM killer / zram / page-cache thrash cliffs, our D015) with an automated guard that aborts before the host stalls.
