# Paper Claim Register (upstream claims, NOT local facts)

Read date: 2026-11-09. Every claim below is what a paper says under ITS conditions. Nothing here has been tested on our proxy
(RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB + 48 GB RAM + NVMe, granite-3.1-1b-a400m, 24 layers x 32 experts, top-8, llama.cpp). Status of every claim: source-supported.

How read: arXiv abs page (version/date from listing) + PDF text extracted locally with pdftotext from the arXiv PDF of the stated version.
Section/figure numbers are taken from the extracted text; where I could not pin a number I say "location approximate".
Papers were read selectively (grep + targeted passages), not cover-to-cover.

Target = unified memory, ~500 GB weights -> 128 GB + 4 TB SSD, single/low-batch interactive decode.
Verdicts: reproduce | adapt mechanism | inspiration only | not applicable.

Key framing caveat: nearly all offloading papers below assume DISCRETE memory (PCIe is the bottleneck). On unified memory there is
no CPU->GPU copy; the tiers are RAM (high BW) and SSD (low BW). Latency numbers do not transfer; hit-rate / accuracy / predictability
properties (model properties) can transfer.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## P01 Fiddler - CPU compute vs weight transfer for missed experts
- Paper: Fiddler: CPU-GPU Orchestration for Fast Inference of MoE Models, arXiv 2402.07033, read v3 (1 May 2025; ICLR 2025). https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07033
- Location: Sec 1 / Sec 3.1-3.3 (latency model, Algorithm 1), Appendix A + Fig 7 (microbenchmark), Sec 4.2 Fig 4 (result).
- Claim: Expert-layer CPU latency grows ~linearly with number of input tokens; GPU latency ~constant but needs weight transfer when expert not resident;
  transfer time "independent of the batch size". For small inputs it is faster to run a missed expert on the CPU than copy its weights. Activation copy is <1% of latency.
  Result: 1.26x avg speedup over best baseline (llama.cpp) in single-request end-to-end tok/s; 1.30x on long prefill (TTFT); 11.57x beam search (abstract numbers).
- Conditions: Mixtral-8x7B 16-bit (>90 GB); Env1 Quadro RTX 6000 24 GB + Xeon 6126 48c, PCIe3 x16 (32 GB/s), 56/256 experts on GPU; Env2 RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB + Xeon 8480+ 112c, PCIe4 (64 GB/s), 125/256 on GPU.
  ShareGPT, input 32-256, output 64-512, SINGLE request (batch 1; beam widths 4-16 for the 11.57x). Baselines DeepSpeed-MII, Mixtral-Offloading, llama.cpp b2956. 16-bit weights in host DRAM (no SSD).
- Applicability: target = inspiration only (unified memory has no transfer; "CPU vs GPU for a miss" becomes "compute from RAM vs stream from SSD", where SSD read-then-compute vs partial compute is a different tradeoff).
  Proxy = adapt mechanism (we can measure CPU-expert vs PCIe-copy crossover; granite experts are tiny).
- Hypothesis: For one decode token on granite, computing a non-resident expert on the CPU (from RAM) is faster than PCIe-copying it to the GPU and computing there, for all experts sizes in this model.
- Experiment: microbench per-expert CPU matvec (llama.cpp CPU backend, Q4_K) vs cudaMemcpy of one expert tensor slice + GPU matvec, token count 1,8,64. Refuted if copy+GPU <= CPU latency at 1 token.
  Transfer to unified target: ratio does NOT transfer (no copy); only the batch-dependence shape (CPU linear, GPU flat) is portable.
- Status: source-supported.

## P02 MoE-Infinity - skew is per-request, vanishes across requests (batch 1)
- Paper: MoE-Infinity: Efficient MoE Inference on Personal Machines with Sparsity-Aware Expert Cache, arXiv 2401.14361, read v3 (12 Mar 2025). https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.14361
- Location: Sec 1 Contribution 1; Sec 4 (Fig 2 expert reuse counts; text "Analyzing over 1000 sequences"); Table 2 / Fig 3-4 (K-means groups, Markov chain).
- Claim (quote): "With a batch size of one ... memory available on a consumer-grade GPU is often sufficient to store the most frequently used experts during decoding";
  "experts exhibit skewed reuse patterns when continuously decoding tokens within a single request... However, this reuse pattern is only present at the request level;
  after processing multiple requests, the skew disappears, and all experts tend to be activated uniformly." Hence global-frequency caching fails; per-request activation traces (EAMs) are needed.
- Conditions: DeepSeek-V2-Lite and others (Mixtral, Switch, NLLB, Arctic); traces from BigBench/FLAN/MMLU; batch size 1; no GPU/SSD numbers for this specific claim (analysis).
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism (the property is model/workload-level, memory-tier independent; reuse within a request is exactly what a 128 GB cache + SSD needs). Proxy = reproduce on granite traces.
- Hypothesis: On our granite traces, per-request frequency (or recency) residency achieves a higher hit rate than a single global static top-k set chosen from pooled traces at equal budget (16/32), and the global distribution is closer to uniform than per-request.
- Experiment (offline, no GPU): replay existing routing traces; compute per-layer expert-usage entropy pooled vs per-request; hit rate of (a) global static top-16 (b) per-request LFU/LRU (c) random static (expected 50%). Refuted if (a) >= (b) within noise or pooled entropy ~ per-request entropy.
  Transfers to unified target: qualitatively yes IF the large model's routing resembles granite (fine-grained experts); magnitude is model specific.
- Status: source-supported.

## P03 MoE-Infinity - trace-guided cache+prefetch latency
- Paper: same as P02 (v3). Location: Table 1 (p1), Fig 7 (Sec 5.1), Fig 9 (EAMC capacity), Table 3 (workload shift).
- Claim: DeepSeek-V2-Lite TPOT (time per output token) on one A5000 24 GB: MoE-Infinity 155 ms vs vLLM 485, DeepSpeed 737, Mixtral-Offloading 1250, Ollama (llama.cpp) 2590 ms (avg TPOT) = 3.1x-16.7x.
  Small trace store suffices (EAMC capacity ~3% of requests; Fig 9). Mixtral is their worst case (836 ms). Long context shrinks GPU buffer for experts: latency degrades as context grows 2^12 -> 2^17 (Fig 8).
- Conditions: single RTX A5000 24 GB, PCIe4 (24 GB/s measured, "32 GB/s" nominal), FULL MODEL RESIDENT IN HOST DRAM (32 GB host for DeepSeek, 128 GB Mixtral, 1 TB Arctic); no SSD tier in the main experiments; batch size 1; LongBench/BigBench/FLAN/MMLU.
  Baselines were run in offload configurations; the 16.7x is against Ollama/llama.cpp (CPU compute for offloaded layers).
- Applicability: target = inspiration only (their win is hiding PCIe fetch; our tiers differ and their SSD path is not evaluated). Proxy = adapt mechanism (the cache policy; latency numbers not comparable).
- Hypothesis: Trace-based prefetch+replacement raises hit rate above plain LRU by >=5 points on granite at 16/32 residency.
- Experiment: extend the P02 replay with an EAM-like predictor (match current request prefix to stored traces) vs LRU/LFU. Refuted if gain <5 points or only on one domain.
  Transfer: hit-rate delta transfers weakly; tok/s does not.
- Status: source-supported.

## P04 FlexGen - SSD tier is viable only for throughput; latency-insensitive batched
- Paper: FlexGen: High-Throughput Generative Inference of LLMs with a Single GPU, arXiv 2303.06865, read v2 (12 Jun 2023). https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06865
- Location: Sec 1 bullets; Fig 1 (latency-throughput); Table 1 (hardware); Sec 6.1 Table 2; Appendix A.4 (Table 24 SSD speeds).
- Claim: OPT-175B on one 16 GB T4 reaches 1 tok/s with effective batch size 144 (4608 tokens generated) at ~4000 s block latency (4-bit, weights held in CPU RAM, no disk);
  without compression 69x over baselines at batch up to 256 / 12000 s latency. "The batch size of 1 did not result in a noticeably better latency" (Appx) - i.e. batch-1 latency is poor.
- Conditions: T4 16 GB, 208 GB DRAM, 1.5 TB cloud NVMe SSD (read ~2 GB/s), OPT-30B/175B, prompt 512, output 32, THROUGHPUT/batched, dense model, latency-insensitive.
  Authors state unified-memory architectures "could be more friendly to our approach" (Appx, no experiment).
- Applicability: target = not applicable for the throughput result (we need single-request tok/s). Inspiration only for the lesson: when weights spill to SSD, decode rate is bounded by SSD BW / bytes touched per token unless batch amortizes. Proxy = inspiration only.
- Hypothesis: In the SSD-bound regime, single-request decode tok/s is approximately SSD_BW / (bytes of non-resident experts touched per token), within 30%.
- Experiment: container memory-limit run (known collapse regime) logging read bytes/token via iostat/perf vs measured tok/s; fio sequential and 4k-random expert-sized read BW. Refuted if model error >30% (page-cache readahead/granularity dominates).
  Transfer: the bandwidth-bound form transfers (constants change: target SSD BW, expert size).
- Status: source-supported.

## P05 FlexGen - 4-bit group-wise quantization of weights+KV to avoid disk
- Paper: same as P04 (v2). Location: Sec 5 (group-wise quantization), Table 5 (accuracy), Sec 6.1 (effective batch 144 + compression fits CPU memory).
- Claim: Group-wise 4-bit weights and KV cache, no retraining/calibration: OPT-175B Lambada acc 0.758 (FP16) -> 0.756 (4-bit); WikiText ppl 10.82 -> 10.94; OPT-30B ppl 12.72 -> 12.90.
  Compression's throughput benefit comes mainly from fitting in CPU memory and avoiding SSD swapping (112x vs baselines with compression at prompt 512).
- Conditions: dense OPT models (not MoE), group-wise asymmetric min/max (not k-quants), perplexity + Lambada only (no instruction-following or KLD), batch throughput setting.
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism (reducing bytes moved is the lever when below working-set RAM). Proxy = reproduce the principle (we already measured Q4 vs mixed precision quality; the untested part is tok/s vs bytes under SSD/page-cache pressure).
- Hypothesis: At fixed (insufficient) RAM, decode tok/s scales with 1/(expert bytes): Q4 experts give >=1.5x tok/s over Q8 experts in the page-cache-collapse regime.
- Experiment: same container limit, run Q8 vs Q4 vs Q3 expert GGUFs, record tok/s and read MB/token. Refuted if speedup <1.3x or does not track bytes ratio.
  Transfer: yes in direction; magnitude depends on the target SSD vs RAM ratio and cache hit rates.
- Status: source-supported.

## P06 PowerInfer - hot/cold split from power-law activation
- Paper: PowerInfer: Fast LLM Serving with a Consumer-grade GPU, arXiv 2312.12456, read v2 (12 Dec 2024; SOSP 2024). https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.12456
- Location: Sec 3.1 Insight-1 / Fig 4 (CDF), footnote 3; Table 1 (sparsity); Sec 8.2, Fig 10 / Fig 14 (batch scaling).
- Claim: Neuron activation follows a power law: a minority of "hot" neurons carries ~80% of activations (OPT-30B ~26% of neurons; LLaMA2-70B ReGLU ~43%; SwiGLU-70B ~69% per Sec 3.1 and footnote 3; figures partially garbled in extraction, check Fig 4 before citing).
  Preloading hot neurons on GPU and computing cold on CPU: avg 8.32 tok/s, up to 16.06 tok/s, up to 11.69x over llama.cpp on RTX 4090 (24 GB); GPU handles ~70% of neuron load (vs 20% llama.cpp). Speedup shrinks as batch grows (Fig 14); input-heavy/short-output cases only 1.07x-4x.
- Conditions: ReLU-family sparse models (OPT, Falcon-ReLU-40B, ReGLU LLaMA2-70B); RTX 4090 24GB (PC-High) and 2080Ti 11GB (PC-Low); batch size 1 default; Alpaca/ChatGPT prompts 8-128 tokens; FP16 and INT4; trained activation predictors; best gains need high-sparsity ReLU models.
- Applicability: target = inspiration only (neuron-level sparsity of dense models, not expert routing; SwiGLU models gain much less). Proxy = inspiration only; the analog is expert-level skew (see P12 which suggests modern fine-grained MoEs are flatter).
- Hypothesis: The top 25% of granite experts per layer account for >50% of routed token-expert assignments in our traces (i.e. a real power law exists at expert granularity).
- Experiment: compute per-layer expert usage CDF from existing traces (also per domain). Refuted if top-8/32 experts cover <40% (near-uniform = 25%).
  Transfer: skew property is model-specific; the target model's own router stats must be measured.
- Status: source-supported.

## P07 vLLM / PagedAttention - KV cache fragmentation
- Paper: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention, arXiv 2309.06180, read v1 (12 Sep 2023; SOSP 2023). https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180
- Location: Sec 3 / Fig 2 ("only 20.4%-38.2% of the KV cache memory is used to store actual token states" in existing systems); Sec 6 Fig 12-14 (throughput).
- Claim: Existing systems waste 62-80% of KV memory through reservation/fragmentation; PagedAttention (block-table paging) gets near-zero waste, enabling larger batches: 2-4x throughput at same latency vs FasterTransformer/Orca (more at longer sequences, larger models, complex sampling).
- Conditions: A100 40GB (OPT-13B), 4xA100 (66B), 8xA100-80GB (175B); ShareGPT/Alpaca; many concurrent requests (batch-serving throughput); dense OPT/LLaMA.
- Applicability: target = not applicable for the 2-4x (we are single-request, no KV fragmentation problem). Inspiration only for the paging abstraction and for budgeting: KV competes with experts for fast memory (see P03 Fig 8). Proxy = not applicable.
- Hypothesis: At our intended context lengths, KV cache for the target model is <10% of the 128 GB budget, so KV management is not a first-order lever.
- Experiment: compute KV bytes = 2*layers*kv_heads*head_dim*ctx*bytes for target config (needs target model config - unknown to me) and measure granite KV size/tok/s vs ctx 2k/8k/32k. Refuted if KV >10% at the target context.
  Transfer: arithmetic transfers once target config is known; granite measurement does not.
- Status: source-supported.

## P08 MxMoE - bits by block sensitivity x expert frequency; linear-block granularity
- Paper: MxMoE: Mixed-precision Quantization for MoE with Accuracy and Performance Co-Design, arXiv 2505.05799, read v1 (9 May 2025; ICML 2025 format). https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05799
- Location: Sec 3.1 + Fig 1a/1b (sensitivity and activation-frequency heterogeneity, DeepSeekV2-Lite layer 11); Sec 5.4 Table 3 (granularity); Sec 4.2 Eq 7 (ILP).
- Claim: Sensitivity varies across experts and across linear blocks inside an expert (e.g. Down proj of Expert 40 needs more bits than Gate proj); expert activation frequencies within one MoE block vary by >10x (Fig 1b).
  Allocating bitwidth per linear block beats per-expert allocation at 5-bit w-a: DeepSeek-V2-Lite PPL 6.11 vs 6.32, avg acc 69.01 vs 67.88; Qwen1.5-MoE PPL 6.95 vs 6.98 (Table 3; the gain is small on some models).
- Conditions: DeepSeek-V2-Lite (29.3 GB), Qwen1.5-MoE (26.7), Qwen2-MoE (106.9), Mixtral-8x7B (92.9); RTX 4090; calibration-based sensitivity statistics; WikiText2 PPL + 7 zero-shot tasks (not KLD, no long-form generation); GPU-resident kernels (no offload).
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism (accuracy-per-byte allocation is hardware independent; frequency-weighting also tells which experts deserve precision vs residency). Proxy = adapt (stock llama.cpp quantizes per-tensor and each layer's experts are one 3D tensor, so per-expert precision is not available without a custom quantizer; per-layer and per-matrix-type (gate/up/down) precision IS available).
- Hypothesis: At equal total bytes, giving ffn_down (and/or high-frequency layers) more bits than gate/up lowers KLD vs uniform Q4 on granite.
- Experiment: llama-quantize with tensor-type overrides (down at Q6/Q5, gate/up at Q3/Q4, matched bytes) vs uniform Q4_K_M and our 4/8 mix; measure KLD vs bf16. Refuted if KLD not lower than the existing mixed result (0.040) at equal GB.
  Transfer: accuracy conclusions likely transfer to larger MoEs only partly (sensitivity patterns are model-specific); speed claims (kernel) do not.
- Status: source-supported.

## P09 MxMoE - very low bit (2.25-bit) MoE accuracy vs GPTQ
- Paper: same as P08 (v1). Location: Sec 5.2 Table 1; abstract.
- Claim: At 2.25 average bits (weight-only, group 128 asym + Hadamard): WikiText2 PPL MxMoE vs GPTQ*: DeepSeekV2-Lite 7.01 vs 8.49 (fp16 5.92); Qwen1.5-MoE 8.79 vs 11.19 (fp16 6.79; gap 2.40 = the abstract's "2.4 lower"); Qwen2-MoE 7.57 vs 7.98 (fp16 5.84); Mixtral 5.63 vs 5.69 (fp16 3.88).
  At 3.25-bit: MxMoE better than GPTQ except Qwen2-MoE (6.18 vs 6.11). Abstract also: up to 3.4x speedup over FP16 and up to 29.4% over uniform quant at equal accuracy (5-bit w-a; kernel throughput, Fig 5).
- Conditions: GPU-resident, RTX 4090, PPL gap numbers are for weight-only; the 3.4x and 29.4% are batched MoE-block kernel throughput (512 tokens memory-bound; 8192 compute-bound), not end-to-end single-token decode.
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism for depth: indicates ~2-3 bit experts are feasible with allocation but degrade (PPL +1.7 to +2.0 on DeepSeek-Lite even with best method). Proxy = adapt (llama.cpp IQ2/IQ3 + imatrix is the closest available).
- Hypothesis: On granite, expert tensors at IQ3_XXS/IQ2_S with imatrix and Q8 attention remain within KLD ~2x of the Q4 mixed configuration while cutting expert bytes by 25-40%.
- Experiment: quantize expert tensors at Q3_K/IQ3/IQ2 with imatrix, keep attention Q8; measure KLD and size. Refuted if KLD >4x the Q4-mixed result at <=30% byte saving.

- Status: source-supported.

## P10 HOBBIT - substitute low-precision experts on cache miss
- Paper: HOBBIT: A Mixed Precision Expert Offloading System for Fast MoE Inference, arXiv 2411.01433, read v2 (6 Nov 2024). https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.01433
- Location: Sec 2.2 / Fig 3b (replace vs skip), Sec 3.2 (Expert Scorer, token-level), Table 3 (accuracy), Sec 5.2 Fig 14 (speed).
- Claim: Replacing a required-but-missing, low-importance expert with a low-precision copy (importance from gate score x magnitude per token) preserves accuracy: "when fewer than 20% of experts are quantized, performance declines by no more than 1%";
  fp16->int4 loading is up to 4x faster. Table 3 (Mixtral-8x7B GSM8K): FP16 0.52, FP16+Int4 mix 0.51, Int8 0.52, Int8+Int2 mix 0.51; Phi-MoE 0.83 / 0.82 / 0.83 / 0.83.
  Speed (decode, batch 1): vs MoE-Infinity 3.64x (Mixtral) and 9.93x (Phi-MoE) on Jetson AGX Orin; 13.0x / 18.9x vs llama.cpp on Jetson ("up to 9.93x" in abstract is vs SOTA offloading).
- Conditions: Mixtral-8x7B (45B, 87 GB, top-2 of 8) and Phi-MoE (42B, top-2 of 16); RTX 4090 24 GB + 256 GB DRAM (PCIe 32 GB/s, FP16) and Jetson AGX Orin 32 GB UNIFIED memory with SSD ~3 GB/s (INT8 base, INT4/INT2 variants); batch 1; accuracy only GSM8K + TruthfulQA, on one 2-model set. Built on llama.cpp.
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism - closest paper to the target (unified memory, SSD, batch 1, llama.cpp). Caveat: top-2 experts means each expert is individually important; granite is top-8 of 32 (less per-expert importance, possibly MORE tolerant). Proxy = adapt.
- Hypothesis: On granite, replacing the lowest-gate-weight 20% of selected experts per token with a Q2/Q3 copy raises KLD by less than half the gap between uniform Q4 and Q8-experts.
- Experiment: offline emulation with two GGUF variants of experts (needs per-expert switching in a patched path, or simulate in PyTorch/HF by swapping dequantized weights for the lowest-scoring experts) and measure KLD/task accuracy. Refuted if KLD rise exceeds that threshold or if gate-score is a poor importance proxy (rank-correlation with per-expert output-norm < 0.5).
  Transfer to unified target: accuracy side yes; speed benefit depends on how often misses go to SSD (4x smaller transfer = ~4x faster miss).
- Status: source-supported.

## P11 HOBBIT - next-layer expert prediction from current hidden state; page-fault collapse on unified memory
- Paper: same as P10 (v2). Location: Sec 3.3 / Fig 7 (cosine similarity, prediction accuracy), Sec 5.2 (Jetson discussion).
- Claim: Feeding layer i's gate input to layers i+1... gates predicts next-layer experts with 96% average accuracy (accuracy decays for 2-3 layers ahead; adaptive prefetch depth); high prediction accuracy lets prefetch overlap load with compute.
  Observed on unified-memory Jetson: llama.cpp mmap "can result in severe page faults when there is insufficient CPU memory to store the model weights"; MoE-Infinity also struggled there due to slow SSD reads.
- Conditions: Mixtral-8x7B (top-2 of 8, 32 layers) and Phi-MoE; batch 1; accuracy definition = predicted set matches actual (random baseline for top-2/8 is 25%).
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism (lookahead is hardware-independent; essential for hiding SSD latency). Proxy = reproduce: granite has 24 layers, top-8/32 (random baseline 25%).
- Hypothesis: Applying layer i+1's router to layer i's input hidden state recovers >=80% of the true top-8 set at i+1 on granite, and >=60% two layers ahead.
- Experiment: forward-hook run on a few hundred tokens (HF transformers, small model); compute recall@8 for lookahead 1,2,3 vs actual routing, by domain. Refuted if recall@8 < 60% at lookahead 1.
  Transfer: recall property depends on depth/width/residual structure; measure again on target. Prefetch benefit also depends on SSD latency vs per-layer compute time (target layers are much heavier -> more time to hide).
- Status: source-supported.

## P12 ProMoE - modern decoder-only MoEs have near-uniform expert access, LRU caching is weak
- Paper: ProMoE: Fast MoE-based LLM Serving using Proactive Caching, arXiv 2410.22134, read v3 (1 Sep 2025). https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.22134
- Location: Sec 3 (motivation), Fig 1 and Fig 4 (blocking time vs cache rate), Fig 5 (cumulative expert access frequency and LRU hit rate).
- Claim: Switch-Transformer and NLLB (encoder-decoder) show power-law expert access, giving high LRU/static hit rates; "modern decoder-only MoE models exhibit a more uniform access pattern" so caching is much less effective.
  DS-1 (DeepSeek-V2-Lite): caching 50% of experts leaves 60.4% of decode time blocked on missing experts (82.7% in prefill; llama.cpp 79.0% decode); fetching experts takes 58.1 ms = 85.6% of a decode step at 23 GB/s (2.67 GiB experts/token FP16).
- Conditions: RTX 4090 24 GB, i9-14900K, 128 GB DRAM, PCIe4 32 GB/s; DS-1/DS-2/QW-1 FP16, QW-2/Mixtral INT4; ShareGPT; batch 1 default (also 1-4); hit rates from LRU on ShareGPT.
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism (decides whether residency policies can work at all; QUALIFIES the "70% hit rate at 50% residency" local result). Proxy = reproduce (we have traces).
- Hypothesis: Our measured ~70% hit rate at 16/32 is materially above the random-static baseline (50%), and this advantage shrinks (<10 points) when traces from many unrelated prompts are mixed (domain dilution).
- Experiment: from existing traces compute random-static, global-LFU, and LRU hit rate at 16/32 for single-domain vs mixed-domain streams; also cold-start vs warm. Refuted if LRU/LFU advantage over random >=15 points even on mixed streams.
  Transfer: tells us whether to expect residency to work; target model's routing must be measured (the 500 GB model is likely closer to DeepSeek-class fine-grained routing, which ProMoE says is flat).
- Status: source-supported.

## P13 ProMoE - learned predictor + chunked/priority prefetch
- Paper: same as P12 (v3). Location: Sec 4 (GoodPred = Accuracy x FetchRate, Fig 8), Sec 5 (prefetcher, Algorithm 1-2), Sec 7.2 Fig 10-11.
- Claim: A small learned predictor on intermediate hidden states with stride prefetching achieves avg 84.7% accuracy (token-based predictor 58.3%; skip-based predictor as low as 66.9% on QW-2). Chunked, preemptible prefetch with reordered execution gives avg 2.20x (up to 3.21x) prefill and 2.07x (up to 5.02x) decode vs existing offloading
  (vs static and LRU baselines decode avg 1.47x and 1.31x in transformers; llama.cpp codebase decode 1.34x avg per intro).
- Conditions: as P12; DRAM-resident offload (no SSD); PCIe-bound; predictors trained offline on traces per model.
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism (learned predictor + chunk-level scheduling are what hides SSD latency). Proxy = adapt (compare to P11's training-free predictor).
- Hypothesis: A small learned linear predictor trained on granite traces beats the training-free lookahead of P11 by >=10 points recall@8.
- Experiment: same hooks as P11; fit logistic regression on (hidden state at layer i -> experts at i+k) with a train/test split by prompt. Refuted if gain over training-free lookahead <5 points or fails to generalize across domains.
  Transfer: training cost and generalization for the large target are unknown; it needs traces from the target.
- Status: source-supported.

## P14 Pre-gated MoE - router lookahead built into the model (requires retraining)
- Paper: Pre-gated MoE: An Algorithm-System Co-Design for Fast and Scalable MoE Inference, arXiv 2308.12066, read v3 (27 Apr 2024; ISCA 2024 format). https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12066
- Location: Sec 1 (contribution bullets and results sentence), Sec 4 (pre-gate function, Fig 5-6), Sec 6 Fig 10-12 (latency, throughput, memory).
- Claim: Pre-gate in block N selects experts for block N+1, removing the select-then-execute dependency so CPU->GPU migration overlaps compute; only +23% latency over an oracle GPU-only baseline and 4.2x lower peak GPU memory, while matching model quality (ROUGE/ExactMatch after fine-tuning).
- Conditions: Switch-Transformer (encoder-decoder, top-1, 64/128/256 experts; Switch-Large 128 experts), A100 80GB, PCIe4, host DRAM / SSD described as tiers; pre-gate functions are trained during task fine-tuning (model modified, not a drop-in); batch-1 oriented but dated model family.
- Applicability: target = not applicable as-is (we cannot retrain a 500 GB model; changes architecture). Inspiration only: shows the ceiling for lookahead accuracy when training is allowed. Proxy = not applicable.
- Hypothesis: Retrofit pre-gating is unnecessary: training-free lookahead (P11) recall is within 10 points of what a trained predictor (P13) achieves on granite.
- Experiment: reuse P11/P13 results; no extra run. Refuted by P13 gain >10 points.
  Transfer: same as P11/P13.
- Status: source-supported (numbers from intro text and abstract; Fig 10-12 not examined).

## P15 MoE-Lightning - roofline policy for batch offload; CPU attention
- Paper: MoE-Lightning: High-Throughput MoE Inference on Memory-constrained GPUs, arXiv 2411.11217, read v1 (18 Nov 2024). https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11217
- Location: Abstract; Sec 3.2 Hierarchical Roofline Model (Fig 3-5); Sec 6 Table 4 (HELM), Fig 7.
- Claim: A hierarchical roofline model (GPU / CPU / PCIe levels) predicts whether an operator is memory-bound at which tier, and finds batch/micro-batch/offload policies; with CGOPipe pipelining and CPU attention it reaches up to 10.3x higher throughput than FlexGen-class systems for Mixtral 8x7B on one T4 and hits the memory-bound ceiling with 2-3x less CPU memory.
- Conditions: BATCH THROUGHPUT (large effective batches, MTBench/HELM/synthetic), T4 16 GB / L4 24 GB, 192 GB CPU RAM, Mixtral 8x7B/8x22B/DBRX, int4 and fp16; not single-request latency.
- Applicability: target = inspiration only (the roofline method is reusable, numbers are not); single-request decode sits at the bottom-left of their roofline (memory-bound at every tier). Proxy = adapt the method.
- Hypothesis: Single-token decode on our proxy is memory-bound at each tier, so measured tok/s matches min over tiers of (tier BW / bytes touched) within 25%.
- Experiment: build a 3-parameter roofline (VRAM BW, RAM/PCIe BW, SSD BW) from microbenchmarks and compare to measured decode in GPU-resident, CPU-offload, and page-cache-limited runs. Refuted if error >25% in any regime.
  Transfer: the method transfers directly; constants change (unified memory bandwidth, SSD).
- Status: source-supported.

Weights, when present, must be aligned, finite and nonnegative; they do not
weight cache accesses. The simple form is also supported:
`{"tok":0,"layer":0,"experts":[0,1],"phase":"decode"}`.
`request` is an optional integer alias for `seq`; absent request IDs mean one

hardcoded or inferred from observed maxima. Conflicting metadata/flags and

# hybrid_expert / `hybrid_moe_bench` (agent-facing)

A focused harness, not an engine change. It executes the **batch-1 Granite MoE expert FFN** with **expert-granular placement**.
Hits run on the GPU and misses run on the CPU, concurrently. It uses real weights and real routing, and is numerically checked.
It exists to confirm or refute the D014 prediction (expert-granular GPU-hit/CPU-miss dispatch with a linear 33.3 us/miss cost) on real kernels.
Results: `RESULTS.md`. Raw samples: `results.json` (24 layers) and `results_L12_single_layer.json`.

## What it does
- **Weights.** Real `blk.N.ffn_{gate,up,down}_exps` (Q4_K, [1024,512,32] / [512,1024,32], 0.844 MiB per expert) are read via the gguf API from
  `granite-3.1-1b-a400m-instruct-mixE4K.gguf`. Each layer has three copies:
  - a pinned host copy, used as the H2D source;
  - a CPU compute copy in `CPU_REPACK`, which is what llama.cpp uses for `--n-cpu-moe` experts (see below; `--cpu-repack 0` uses the plain copy);
  - a full GPU copy, used by the reference path.
- **Routing.** Top-8 ids and weights are replayed from `artifacts/traces/out/{prose,code,chat}.jsonl`. The timed stream is the decode tokens of all three traces
  concatenated: 352 positions per layer. The static slot profile is taken from the **prefill** tokens only, so the decode tokens are never used to choose slots.

  Graphs are prebuilt per (backend, n experts = 1..8) with `ggml_gallocr`.
- **Paths, per layer.**
  - `gpu_ref`: all 32 experts on the GPU.
  - `cpu_all`: all experts on the CPU.

`possible_truncated_tail`. A valid final JSON object needs no newline. The
parser reports tokens with incomplete layer coverage separately; it cannot
detect an entirely missing token or a file truncated exactly at a record
boundary. Capture success and expected token counts remain external checks.
No valid records, inconsistent token phases, missing dimensions, invalid
configuration and I/O failures return nonzero. A successful replay with
reported errors is a partial-data result, not proof of a complete capture.

## Replay conventions

Records are ordered by `(seq, position, layer)` and expert accesses follow array
rank order, sequentially, including within a token. This deliberately differs
from routing_trace's atomic token-entry scoring. All policies start cold and
keep state across phases and requests. `--warmup N` replays the first N test
tokens without scoring them. It does not warm from the training partition.
Tokens include all their available layers; rates aggregate expert requests,
not averages of layer rates. Missing rates are JSON null. Per-layer metrics
use tokens observed at that layer; overall metrics count each token once.

`--capacity-experts C` is a global number of `(layer,expert)` slots.
`--per-layer-capacity` instead assigns **C slots to each layer** (up to L*C
total), rather than dividing C among layers. Zero capacity is supported.

* `lru`: evict least recently accessed resident.
* `lfu`: resident-only access counts, reset on eviction; LRU breaks ties.
* `lfu-decay:H`: same counts with continuous exponential decay, half-life H
  global expert lookups. Counts are evaluated lazily at eviction, avoiding
  growing exponentials. LRU breaks ties. This differs from periodic halving.
* `static-profile:PATH`: pin the top C ranked pairs globally or C per layer.
  Selected pairs enter on first demand; other misses bypass. No free preload
  hits or profile updates. Profiles must match dimensions.
* `belady`: **reads-the-future upper bound**, not deployable online. Evict the
  resident or bypass the incoming pair according to furthest next use. Allowing
  bypass lets the oracle bound pinned static caching as well as admitting
  policies under the same cold-start and capacity conventions.

Belady sees the replay partition, including warmup, not training records.
All traces are held in memory. LFU/Belady victim selection scans resident slots;
this is a correctness-oriented reference simulator, not a runtime cache.

## Training and profiles

`--split train:test` gives nonnegative training and positive test weights;
`4:1` selects the first floor(4/5 * token_count) whole tokens for training.
Token order is the normalized `(seq,pos)` order, so sequence IDs should reflect
the desired request order. Simulate/sweep only replay the test suffix. Profile
uses only the training prefix when split is supplied, otherwise all records.
No splitting inside a token, test-based ranking, or training-state warming.

Profiles rank all L*E pairs by score, then `(layer,expert)` for ties, including
zero-score pairs. `raw` counts expert accesses. `per-request` divides each
request's counts by its total expert accesses so every request has unit mass;
provide distinct `seq`/`request` IDs for distinct requests. The weighting and
scores are stored explicitly. Strata's make_profile uses raw counts and can
preserve an existing base ranking; make_profile_mix normalizes per input file
and applies file weights. This implementation has no base ranking and
normalizes by request, not file.

Profiles retain SHA-256 fingerprints of normalized training records. Split
replay rejects profiles without provenance or with any test-record overlap,
including warmup records. This catches accidental reuse of a full-trace
profile; it is not an authentication mechanism or proof of independence
between semantically equivalent traces with changed IDs. Without `--split`,
the caller owns train/test separation.

## Bytes and prediction

A miss moves `--expert-bytes B` bytes (default 0). Optional
`--per-layer-bytes B0,B1,...` overrides it with exactly L nonnegative integer
sizes. No cache writeback, prefetch, overlap, compression or fixed overhead is
modeled. JSON reports overall, per-layer and decode-only hit rate, misses per
token and bytes per token. Decode predictions use decode-only moved bytes:

`prediction seconds/token = compute_ms/1000 + decode_bytes_per_token/(bw_gbs*1e9)`

`--bw-gbs` is decimal GB/s (default 1); `--compute-ms` defaults to 0.
The prediction is null if no scored decode tokens exist. Sweep writes one CSV
row per capacity with overall metrics, decode hit rate, decode prediction and
malformed/truncation counts. Full line diagnostics remain on stderr.

# Memory, quality and speed report

Run from any working directory (Python standard library only):

```sh
python /home/muk/projects/siminfeng/campaign/cc/memory_pareto/pareto.py
python cc/memory_pareto/pareto.py experiments/memory/configs.csv --budget-mib 700
```

The script prints a Markdown table sorted by ascending GPU MiB (unknown memory last), followed by a terminal ASCII scatter of GPU MiB versus KLD. It writes `pareto.md` and `pareto.json` beside the script by default. `--output-dir artifacts/codexI` selects another assignment-permitted destination. Reports are overwritten on reruns. Nothing is written to the input paths. No network, Docker, or third-party runtime packages are used.

## Inputs

The primary input is `experiments/memory/configs.csv`, resolved relative to the campaign root, with these required headers:

```csv
config,desc,class,gpu_mib,host_mib,tg_ts,pp_ts,kld,top1_pct,ppl_ratio,notes
```

`class` must be `transferable`, `discrete-only`, or `mixed`. Supply the orchestrator's classifications; the script does not validate scientific transferability. Memory is MiB; TG and PP are tokens per second. KLD is smaller-is-better. Top1 is a percentage; PPL ratio is supplied relative to the experiment's stated reference. Neither is converted into KLD. Empty cells, NA, N/A, null, none, NaN and nonfinite numbers become unavailable, never zero. Invalid numbers, negative values, invalid classes, and percentages above 100 are errors. Zero is valid. # Engine handoff receipt tool

`engine_handoff.py` inspects delivery bytes and requester requirements offline.
It never imports an image or launches a workload. Python 3 and PyYAML are
required; pytest is used for tests. Optional GGUF header inspection uses the
bundled gguf-py and its existing NumPy dependency, without loading model tensors.
No network or Docker is used.

## Archive observations

`observe_archive(path)` returns `image_config_id`, `platform`, `layer_count`, and
`executables` (absolute `/app/...` names mapped to SHA-256). It supports classic
Docker `manifest.json` archives and OCI `index.json`/`blobs/sha256` archives,
including nested OCI indexes and Docker attestation descriptors. It admits one
runnable image; ambiguous multi-image deliveries are rejected.

# resource_observe (J-T2)
Stdlib-only Python 3.10 sampler emitting JSONL under one contract, with platform backends.

## Usage
    resource_observe.py capabilities
    resource_observe.py sample --backends auto|tegrastats,proc,sysfs_tegra,nvml [--interval-ms 500] [--duration-s N] [--pid P] [--cgroup PATH] [--nvpmodel-mode STR] --out F.jsonl
    resource_observe.py summarize F.jsonl [--interval-ms 500]   # per-metric min/max/mean/high_water + coverage (expected vs received, gaps > 2x interval)
Tests: `python3 -m pytest` (no GPU/root; fixtures in `fixtures/`, paths injectable).

## Record
`{"schema":"resource-observe/0","ts","mono_s","host_id","backend","seq","metrics":[{name,value,unit,scope,source}],"unavailable":[{name,backend,reason}],"parse_errors":[...]}`
Missing data is listed in `unavailable` with a reason, never as 0. Malformed tegrastats lines yield a record with `parse_errors` carrying `line_sha256_16` (no crash). Units: MiB, MHz, percent, mW, celsius, load.
`tegrastats` emits one record per line it produces (the interval is set on the child); other backends emit one per tick.

## Attribution scopes (do NOT sum across scopes)
- `system-shared-dram` (tegrastats RAM): whole-system DRAM shared by CPU and GPU on Jetson.
- `system` (/proc/meminfo): same physical pages viewed system-wide; `process` (VmRSS/VmHWM) and `cgroup` (memory.current/peak/max) are subsets of the same pages. Adding them to tegrastats RAM double counts.
- cgroup metrics carry `accounting_note`: cgroup v2 may not include nvmap/driver GPU allocations on Tegra, so it can under-report GPU memory. Unlimited `memory.max` is reported unavailable. memory.peak may be missing on older kernels (unavailable). T
- `device-discrete` (nvml): dedicated VRAM, x86 only. On Orin nvidia-smi exists but returns [N/A]; backend reports unavailable.
- sysfs_tegra: GPU devfreq (MHz), thermal zones (celsius, unreadable zones listed unavailable), nvpmodel mode (`nvpmodel -q`, query only, or `--nvpmodel-mode`).

## Known gaps
No NvMap fields on this kernel's meminfo (reported unavailable); no iomem/debugfs nvmap per-client attribution (needs root); tegrastats gets its own interval, summarize infers interval from median spacing if not given; nvml parsed from CSV fixtures o

    python3 resource_observe.py sample --backends io --path ~/models/campaign --duration-s 5 --out io.jsonl
    python3 resource_observe.py sample --backends io --device nvme0n1 --pid 123 --cgroup /sys/fs/cgroup/example --out io.jsonl
    python3 resource_observe.py sample --backends io --pid-from-cgroup /sys/fs/cgroup/example --out io.jsonl
    python3 resource_observe.py watchdog --min-available-mib 900 --max-swap-used-mib 512 --max-swap-rate-mibs 20 --interval-ms 250 --kill-pid 123 --out events.jsonl
"""Linux I/O telemetry and an explicitly targeted memory watchdog (stdlib only)."""
import os
import shlex
import signal
import subprocess
import time

MIB = 1048576
VM_KEYS = ('pgmajfault', 'pgfault', 'pgpgin', 'pgpgout', 'pswpin', 'pswpout', 'workingset_refault_file')
MEM_KEYS = ('anon', 'file', 'file_mapped', 'active_file', 'inactive_file', 'workingset_refault_file', 'pgmajfault')


def read(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return f.read()


def pairs(text):
    return {p[0].rstrip(':'): int(p[1]) for line in text.splitlines()
            if len(p := line.split()) == 2 and p[1].isdigit()}


def resolve_device(path, sysroot='/sys', stat=os.stat):
    dev = stat(os.path.expanduser(path)).st_dev
    link = os.path.join(sysroot, 'dev/block', '%s:%s' % (os.major(dev), os.minor(dev)))
    if not os.path.exists(link):
        raise OSError('no sysfs block device for %s (filesystem may be overlay/network)' % link)
    node = os.path.realpath(link)
    while os.path.exists(os.path.join(node, 'partition')):
        node = os.path.dirname(node)
    name = os.path.basename(node)
    if not os.path.isfile(os.path.join(sysroot, 'block', name, 'stat')):
        raise OSError('parent disk stat unavailable: ' + name)
    return name


def proc_stat(text):
    # comm can contain spaces and closing parentheses; fields after the last ')' are fixed.
    fields = text[text.rindex(')') + 2:].split()
    return int(fields[7]), int(fields[9]), fields[19], fields[0]  # minflt, majflt, starttime, state

results:
The search turned up several recent arXiv papers on SSD-backed MoE expert offloading, with Jetson hardware in some of them.

- **Bevy (arXiv 2611.04794, Nov 2026):** This paper proposes a runahead scheduling method for offloading-based MoE inference. It evaluates on two unified-memory machines, an Apple Mac mini M6 and an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor with a PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSD. The paper's main finding is that prefetching can hurt performance when an expert cache already sits in GPU memory. An Apple Mac mini with the M6 chip, 24 GB of unified memory, and a 512 GB SSD, and an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Developer Kit with 128 GB of unified memory are the test platforms.

- **Edge0 (arXiv 2609.18063, Sep 2026):** This work serves MoE expert weights from SSD instead of keeping the full model in RAM. It predicts routing for the next token so SSD reads overlap with computation, and it reports serving 35B MoEs this way. It was submitted 17 Sep 2026.

- **FlashMoE (arXiv 2601.17063):** This paper targets SSD I/O bottlenecks with ML-based cache replacement for edge devices. It reports a cache hit rate up to 51% higher than LRU and LFU, and up to 2.6x speedup over existing systems on a desktop setup. It also argues that DRAM-based offloading systems become impractical as models reach hundreds of gigabytes.

- **ZipMoE (arXiv 2601.21198):** This paper targets on-device MoE serving with lossless compression and cache-affinity scheduling. It evaluates on Jetson AGX Orin 64GB and 32GB, and notes that the design is meant to apply to any shared-memory platform.

- **VisMMOE (arXiv 2605.05899):** This paper covers visual-language MoE offloading. On Jetson Orin, it relied on Linux swap to extend memory onto SSD, because no mature framework-level SSD offloading path was available for those models.

Bevy and Edge0 look like the closest matches to your query. FlashMoE and ZipMoE are also relevant. I only ran one search, so I did not check whether the Edge0 and Bevy results are peer-reviewed or still preprints.

## 3. cc/gpu_budget on Jetson (cooperative cap?)
- Covered: cudaMalloc, MallocManaged, MallocAsync, Free/FreeAsync (adds a stream sync), MallocPitch, Malloc3D (synthesized), cudaMemGetInfo, cuMemAlloc_v2, cuMemAllocAsync, cuMemFree_v2/FreeAsync, cuMemGetInfo_v2. Single process-wide counter, JSONL log, hard denial returns cudaErrorMemoryAllocation, env `GPU_BUDGET_MIB/RESERVE/COUNT_MANAGED/LOG`.
- Missing: cudaMallocHost / cudaHostAlloc / cuMemAllocHost / cuMemHostAlloc (ggml pinned host buffers, ggml-cuda.cu:1324; on Tegra this is also DRAM), cudaHostRegister (`GGML_CUDA_REGISTER_HOST`), cuMemAllocManaged, cuMemAllocPitch, VMM (`cuMemCreate`/`cuMemAddressReserve`, ggml-cuda.cu:627), `cudaMallocFromPoolAsync`/mem pools, cudaMallocArray. No obvious compile bug (`-std=c99 -Werror` build.sh passed on x86); weak points: dlsym on every call, one global mutex held across the real allocation, thread-local `nesting` only guards re-entry.
- Decisive Jetson problem: cudaMemGetInfo virtualization is bypassed by llama.cpp. `ggml_backend_cuda_device_get_memory` (ggml-cuda.cu:5429-5460) calls cudaMemGetInfo, then if `prop.integrated` (Orin) OVERWRITES `*free` with `/proc/meminfo` MemAvailable (`ggml_backend_cuda_get_available_uma_memory`, 5352). So the shim's virtual free never reaches auto-fit or `--fit` (D023's n_ctx 45568 would recur); only `total` is faked. A second path (`ggml_backend_cuda_get_device_memory`, 5283) does use the faked value. The only effective part is hard denial of device cudaMalloc, which does not constrain mmap'd CPU-resident experts or page cache. Net: usable as a hard cap on GPU-resident bytes (weights/KV/compute buffers) if cudart is dynamically linked (static cudart bypasses LD_PRELOAD; verify with `ldd /app/llama-*`), NOT as a steer for autofit or a limit on host-pinned/page-cache DRAM. For the over-memory experiment the physical limit is the budget; pin `-c`, `-ngl`/`-ncmoe` explicitly instead.

- P06 PowerInfer hot/cold ("minority carries ~80% of activations") and P08 MxMoE ("expert frequency varies >10x"): same trace; per-layer 256-bin histogram, coverage curve, entropy.
- P11 HOBBIT / P13 ProMoE (next-layer expert predictability): partial proxy only: adjacent-layer expert-set overlap from the same trace; true predictor claims need hidden states (not cheap).
- P04 FlexGen / P15 MoE-Lightning roofline: SSD-bound token rate = NVMe B/s / fetched B per token; check with io_watchdog counters (rbytes, majflt) vs measured tg at cmoe.
- P01 Fiddler (CPU compute vs weight movement): on Jetson re-ask as CPU-expert vs GPU-expert decode with all weights page-cache-resident (no transfer exists); 1-hour test using `-ncmoe` sweep with a small model first.

4. Refresh routing_trace README (stale "not compile-linked") and move trace_replay constants to CLI flags or deprecate in favour of expert_replay.

tool_response.result:
**Summary of the forum thread**

- **Question:** The poster profiled a model on a Jetson Orin Nano (8 GB) for a memory-bandwidth study. Using Nsight Systems' `ga10b-gfxt` GPU metrics set, the DRAM throughput counters (CPU-L3, GPU, and SoC peripheral reads and writes) returned zeros, while other GPU metrics in the same capture had non-zero values.
- **Questions asked:** (1) Is the GA10B expected to support the `mcc__dram_throughput_*` counters through nsys periodic sampling? (2) Are there settings to expose them on JetPack 6.2.2? (3) Is there a newer nsys or patched config? (4) Are `dram__read_throughput` and `dram__write_throughput` available on GA10B through nsys or ncu?
- **Answer:** No resolution. NVIDIA staff suggested adding `--cuda-memory-usage=true` and `--gpu-metrics-devices=all`, which did not help. Staff then asked for a stats report, a minimal memcpy reproduction, and an Nsight Compute cross-check. The poster supplied these, but the thread has no reply with a diagnosis. The last staff post pointed to a different thread, and its image was not readable.

**Versions reported**

- Nsight Systems: 2024.5.4
- Nsight Compute: 2024.3.1.0
- JetPack 6.2.2 (L4T R36.5.0), CUDA 12.6

**Is GPU metric sampling supported on Orin Nano?**

The thread does not confirm this. The DRAM counters returned zeros in the `ga10b-gfxt` set, and the config for GA10B lacks the DRAM counters found in the `ga10x` config. Whether this is a hardware limitation, a tool gap, or a configuration problem remains unresolved. The poster's fallback options were ncu for per-kernel DRAM bandwidth and `tegrastats` EMC utilization for system-wide measurements.

The search doesn't support the "Jetson Linux 38" part of your query. Sources consistently say JetPack 7.2 ships with Jetson Linux 39.2, not 38.

- **Jetson Linux version:** Jetson Linux 39.2 is the latest Jetson Linux release that supports NVIDIA JetPack 7.2. NVIDIA's archive page lists the release as Jetson Linux 39.2 (6/02/2026). The Jetson Linux 38 line appears only as a source for the Crosstool-NG toolchain on that page, not as the JetPack 7.2 baseline.
- **CUDA 13 on Orin:** JetPack 7.2 adds Orin to the JetPack 7 stack. JetPack 7.2 supported components include Jetson Linux 39.2, CUDA 13.2.1, cuDNN 9.20.0, and TensorRT 10.16.2. One source describes it as a common software foundation built on Ubuntu 24.04, Linux Kernel 6.8, and CUDA 13.
- **Orin Nano specifics:** There is no SD card image for Jetson Orin Nano Developer Kit in this release. Use the unified ISO image to flash the developer kit using a USB stick. Super Mode is part of the Orin Nano story. Just like the Orin Nano offering a Super mode, NVIDIA introduces the Jetson AGX Orin 32GB Super.
- **Migration:** Rebuild CUDA applications and do not reuse JetPack 6.x binaries without validation.
- **Release notes:** The full details are in the Jetson Linux 39.2 release notes, which NVIDIA hosts at docs.nvidia.com's r39.2 archive.
- **Later point release:** JetPack 7.2.1 uses Jetson Linux 39.2.1. Its highlights include ISO now flashes the Jetson Orin Nano Developer Kit with Super Mode flashing configuration by default.

# External survey: MoE larger-than-memory inference, Jetson/x86 tooling (2026-11-10)

Method note: GitHub REST API (repos, search/issues, pulls) queried 2026-11-10; WebSearch (extended/standard);
WebFetch of NGC / NVIDIA forum pages; local probes on this Jetson (R36, kernel 5.15.199-tegra).
Verification levels: [V] = fetched/API-confirmed today, [S] = search-snippet only (verify before relying).
Our pin 31288c9c6 is 519 commits behind master (3b4d6ab3f, 2026-11-10) per compare API.
No version below is recommended unless >= 2 weeks old (cutoff 2026-10-27); newer items are marked "watch".

## A. Engines / forks

### A1. llama.cpp upstream, post-31288c9c6 (MIT, all platforms incl. CUDA aarch64)
Found by: `GET search/issues?q=repo:ggml-org/llama.cpp+<kw>+is:pr+created:>2026-10-01` for kw in
moe offload / moe-cache / cuda graph moe / expert cache ssd / jetson orin / unified memory mmap / lazy-mode;
then `GET pulls/<n>` for bodies; `compare/31288c9c6...master` for ahead_by.
- #29887 `--moe-cache-mib N` GPU LRU cache of host-resident experts (merged 2026-10-07; port of Tether qvac-fabric
  MoE cache; only <=32-token batches; suggests cache ~10% of expert size). Already in or near our pin: verify with
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor`. Verdict: ADOPT (it is the core mechanism for our goal).
- #30966 moe-cache: run missed experts on CPU (`--moe-cache-cpu-share`) + tuning script (merged 2026-11-07).
  Useless where CPU == same DRAM bus as GPU? On Orin (unified LPDDR5) CPU read of expert may beat H2D copy: STUDY/benchmark.
- #31233 LRFU/MQ-like ClassLRU replaces SLRU (merged 2026-11-06): +6-7% decode warm cache, 8% fewer uploads. ADOPT w/ rebase.
- #31888 CPU part no longer waits on cached-expert matmuls (merged 2026-11-08): +7-9% TG on Gemma 4 -cmoe. ADOPT.
- #31286 cpu-share auto controller: closed unmerged ("fixed 0.95 works just as well"). Reject; use fixed value.
- #31850 (open) separate CUDA stream for expert H2D (`GGML_CUDA_UPLOAD_STREAM=1`, `GGML_SCHED_COPIES=N`). WATCH; on UMA
  H2D is a memcpy within DRAM so gain may be nil on Orin, real on 5070 Ti.
- #31469 (open) out-of-core MoE streaming, VRAM slot pool + RAM victim cache, `--moe-direct-io` (NVMe regime beyond RAM).
  The closest upstream analogue to our "model >> memory" goal. STUDY now (read diff, test branch on x86), WATCH merge.
- #31775 (open) sched: start new split at incompatible weight (fixes #31675 with -nkvo hybrids). WATCH.
- #31957 (open, 2026-11-09) "apply the iGPU lazy-mode fallback only when mmap is off": directly about the
  `-lm auto` iGPU behavior we hit. STUDY/test on Orin; likely ADOPT as local patch.
- #27969 (merged 2026-08-29) renamed `--tensor-read-lazy` to `--lazy-mode`/`-lzm`; #30772 (closed) `-lzm direct` pread
  of PLE rows (idea reusable for expert rows). #24156 (open) reclaim mmap pages after CPU_REPACK. STUDY.
- #31268 (open) "CUDA: optimize Orin single-column MMVQ"; #30858 (merged) small_k MMVQ on Orin bs=1; #28285 (merged)
  MMVQ->MMQ crossover for SM87. All Orin-specific decode-kernel work. ADOPT (cherry-pick); #31268 STUDY.
- #29142 (closed) hardcoded 32GB VMM pool cuMemAddressReserve fails on Jetson iGPU; #29499 (open) server hang on Orin NX
  L4T 36.4.7. Check whether our pin has the #29142 fix. Reference for known Tegra bugs.
- #29949 (open FR) GPU-resident LRU where cache decisions run on GPU (CUDA-graph friendly). WATCH.
- #31288 `cuda : add top-k MoE fusion for 384 experts`, #31084 deterministic radix Top-K (merged): MoE routing fusion
  inside graphs. Low relevance to Orin bf16/Q4_K gate/up slowness; WATCH.
- #31452 (open RFC) deterministic layer & MoE streaming, "70B/141B on 16GB RAM". Low maturity; WATCH.
- #31419 (merged) ggml-backend: do not upload unread inputs. Cheap win; ADOPT with rebase.
- Issue #15034 (Gemma 3n broken on Orin Nano CUDA, closed 2025-08) and #28160 (closed; lazy-mode auto halves pp512 on Vulkan
  iGPU) are the two refs in our source; both closed, read their linked fixes.
CUDA-graph note: no MoE-specific CUDA-graph PR surfaced in the window; the search `cuda graph moe is:merged` returned only
top-k fusion PRs (#31288, #31615 Metal). Gap: nobody upstream seems to be graph-capturing expert-cache lookups.

### A2. ik_llama.cpp  https://github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp  [V]
MIT, last push 2026-11-09, 3.4k stars, no GitHub releases. llama.cpp fork with extra quants (IQK), fused MoE ops, better
CPU/hybrid MoE. Platform: ARM NEON supported but issue #308 shows arm64 build breakage; CUDA sm_87/sm_120 unverified.
Use: source of fused-MoE and quant ideas (compare to our slow gate/up fused kernels). Verdict: STUDY (read, do not adopt; fork drift).
Found by: GitHub API repo lookup from memory of well-known forks; confirmed active via `repos/` endpoint.

### A3. KTransformers  https://github.com/kvcache-ai/ktransformers  [V]
Apache-2.0, v0.7.2 (2026-10-15), 19.7k stars. CPU-GPU heterogeneous MoE (hot experts GPU, cold CPU; AMX/AVX512/AVX2 kernels;
expert scheduling doc 2026-01). Also has a jetson-containers package (`packages/llm/ktransformers`). x86-CPU-centric: kernels
target x86 AVX/AMX, so Orin (ARM) benefit is doubtful. Use: x86 5070 Ti hybrid baseline for expert placement ideas.
Verdict: STUDY (x86), REJECT for Orin. Found by: README via contents API; jetson-containers `packages/llm` directory listing.

### A4. PowerInfer / PowerInfer-2 / SmallThinker  https://github.com/Tiiny-AI/PowerInfer  [V]
MIT, last push 2026-05-11, 9.9k stars (old SJTU-IPADS URL 301-redirects). Activation-locality neuron-level sparse
offload; PowerInfer-2 (2024, smartphone, NVMe-streamed, arXiv 2406.06282 [S from memory, verify]) plus SmallThinker-21B-A3B
models designed for on-device/SSD. Models (HF PowerInfer/SmallThinker-21BA3B-Instruct) are useful MoE test targets. Code
is a fork of llama.cpp (older base). Verdict: STUDY paper; use SmallThinker as workload; REJECT engine.
Found by: `repos/SJTU-IPADS/PowerInfer` returned "Moved Permanently" -> followed to Tiiny-AI.

### A5. MoE-Infinity  https://github.com/EfficientMoE/MoE-Infinity  [V]
Apache-2.0, v0.2.2 (2026-09-30), 382 stars, active. Sequence-level expert activation tracing + prefetch/cache for
offloaded MoE; PyTorch (not GGUF). aarch64/Jetson unverified. Verdict: STUDY (prefetch policy ideas; trace methodology).
Found by: GitHub repo API from known name.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# om_run.sh — guarded over-memory engine run on jetson-arm.
# usage: om_run.sh OUTDIR IMAGE "ENV_FLAGS" TOOL ARGS...
#   e.g. om_run.sh experiments/jetson/OM/b1-r1 campaign/llamacpp:jetson-c1-p03 "" llama-bench -m /om/model.gguf -lm mmap -ngl 99 -cmoe -p 64 -n 32 -r 2
# Model dir ~/models/campaign/qwen36-35b-a3b is mounted read-only at /om. Watchdog kills ONLY this container
# when MemAvailable < OM_MIN_AVAIL_MIB (default 700) or zram swap used > OM_MAX_SWAP_MIB (default 1536).
set -u
OUT=$1; IMG=$2; ENVF=$3; TOOL=$4; shift 4
R=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.." && pwd); mkdir -p "$OUT"
NAME="om-$(date +%s)-$$"
MODELDIR=${OM_MODELDIR:-$HOME/models/campaign/qwen36-35b-a3b}
DATADIR=$HOME/models/campaign/data/wikitext/wikitext-2-raw
DP=${DOCKER_CMD_PREFIX:-}
dk(){ if [ -n "$DP" ]; then $DP "docker $*"; else docker "$@"; fi; }
printf '%s\n' "$IMG" "$ENVF" "$TOOL $*" > "$OUT/cmd.txt"
dk run -d --name "$NAME" --runtime nvidia --network none --label campaign=c1 --label om=1 $ENVF \
   -v "$MODELDIR":/om:ro -v "$DATADIR":/d:ro "$IMG" /app/$TOOL "$@" > "$OUT/container.id" || { echo "START_FAIL" > "$OUT/status"; exit 2; }
python3 "$R/cc/resource_observe/resource_observe.py" watchdog --min-available-mib ${OM_MIN_AVAIL_MIB:-700} \
   --max-swap-used-mib ${OM_MAX_SWAP_MIB:-1536} --interval-ms 250 --kill-cmd "${DP:+$DP }docker kill $NAME" --out "$OUT/watchdog.jsonl" & WD=$!
python3 "$R/cc/resource_observe/resource_observe.py" sample --backends io,proc,tegrastats --path "$MODELDIR" --interval-ms 500 \
   --duration-s ${OM_MAX_S:-1800} --out "$OUT/telemetry.jsonl" >/dev/null 2>&1 & SM=$!
T0=$(date +%s.%N)
RC=$(dk wait "$NAME"); T1=$(date +%s.%N)
kill $WD $SM 2>/dev/null; wait $WD 2>/dev/null; WDRC=$?
dk logs "$NAME" > "$OUT/stdout.txt" 2> "$OUT/stderr.txt"
OOM=$(dk inspect "$NAME" --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}')
dk rm "$NAME" > /dev/null
TRIP=$(grep -c watchdog_trip "$OUT/watchdog.jsonl" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
python3 - "$OUT" "$RC" "$T0" "$T1" "$OOM" "$TRIP" <<'PY'
import json,sys
o,rc,t0,t1,oom,trip=sys.argv[1:]
json.dump(dict(exit_code=int(rc.strip() or -1),wall_s=round(float(t1)-float(t0),2),oom_killed=oom.strip()=="true",watchdog_trips=int(trip),
  status="watchdog_killed" if int(trip) else ("ok" if rc.strip()=="0" else "failed")),open(o+"/result.json","w"),indent=1)
print(open(o+"/result.json").read())
PY
EOF

# MoE cache

When the experts of MoE layers stay in host memory (`-cmoe`, `-ncmoe`, `-ot`), the MoE cache keeps the most used ones in device memory for small batches (decode, speculative decoding). Large batches still upload the experts they use.

| Argument | |
|---|---|
| `--moe-cache-mib N` | cache size in MiB, split among the GPUs like the layers (default: 0, disabled) |
| `--moe-cache-cpu-share F` | share of the cache misses computed on the CPU from the host experts instead of uploaded, once the cache is full (default: 0) |

The cache hits run on the device. With `--moe-cache-cpu-share F` the CPU computes a share `F` of the misses while the device computes the hits and uploads the other misses into the cache. This is faster when the CPU reads the host experts faster than the device can upload them, for example with fast RAM, a PCIe 4 link or experts that are not in pinned memory. The host experts are pinned with `-lm none`, `-lm mlock` and `-lm dio`, unless `--no-host`, but not when they are mmap'd (the default). The device uploads pinned experts at the full speed of the link, so the CPU share often does not help then. Until the cache is full every miss is uploaded, so the cache fills as fast as without the CPU share. The best share depends on the machine, the model and the cache size.

## Picking the arguments

Put the script in front of your server command:

```bash
python3 scripts/moe-cache-tune.py -- build/bin/llama-server -m model.gguf -cmoe -t 8 -c 32768
```

It starts the server 6 times, at two cache sizes × shares 0, 0.5 and 0.95, and times the generation of a few thousand tokens. That takes a few minutes, mostly model loading.

From these runs it fits the upload and CPU speeds of the machine, then replays the routing of all the runs through a copy of the cache logic for other sizes and shares. It prints the measured speeds, the predicted t/s and the recommended arguments: the lowest share within 5% of the fastest.

- **Server command:** keep your own arguments (`-t`, `-c`, expert placement, load mode); the speeds and the free device memory depend on them.
- **`--max-mib N`:** tunes a smaller cache than what fits on the device. The runs in `--out` are reused while the command stays the same, so trying another value is instant.
- **`--markdown`:** prints Markdown tables to paste in a PR.

PYTHONPATH=<llama.cpp>/gguf-py python3 gguf_layout.py MODEL.gguf [--json OUT]"""
import sys, json, re, collections
from gguf import GGUFReader
p = sys.argv[1]; r = GGUFReader(p)
arch = r.fields['general.architecture'].contents()
kv = {k: r.fields[k].contents() for k in r.fields if k.startswith(arch + '.') and not isinstance(r.fields[k].contents(), list)}
rows = []; moe = collections.defaultdict(lambda: collections.defaultdict(int)); resident = 0
for t in r.tensors:
    b = int(t.n_bytes); rows.append(dict(name=t.name, type=t.tensor_type.name, shape=[int(x) for x in t.shape], bytes=b, offset=int(t.data_offset)))
    m = re.match(r'blk\.(\d+)\.(ffn_(gate|up|down|gate_up)_exps)\.weight', t.name)
    if m: moe[int(m[1])][m[2] + ':' + t.tensor_type.name] += b
    else: resident += b
n_exp = kv.get(f'{arch}.expert_count'); used = kv.get(f'{arch}.expert_used_count')
per_layer = {l: sum(d.values()) for l, d in moe.items()}
exp_total = sum(per_layer.values())
out = dict(file=p, arch=arch, n_tensors=len(rows), total_bytes=sum(x['bytes'] for x in rows), expert_bytes=exp_total, non_expert_bytes=resident,
           expert_count=n_exp, expert_used=used, layers_with_experts=len(moe),
           bytes_per_expert_by_layer={l: (v // n_exp if n_exp else None) for l, v in sorted(per_layer.items())},
           expert_types_by_layer={l: dict(d) for l, d in sorted(moe.items())}, kv=kv)
if n_exp and used and moe:
    bpe = exp_total / (n_exp * len(moe)); out['avg_bytes_per_expert'] = bpe
    out['routed_expert_bytes_per_token'] = bpe * used * len(moe)
if '--json' in sys.argv: json.dump(dict(out, tensors=rows), open(sys.argv[sys.argv.index('--json') + 1], 'w'), indent=1, default=str)
print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in out.items() if k not in ('expert_types_by_layer', 'bytes_per_expert_by_layer', 'kv')}, indent=1, default=str))
print('types layer0:', dict(list(out['expert_types_by_layer'].items())[0][1]) if moe else None)
EOF

# Upstream MoE-cache study (read-only; pinned 31288c9c6 vs up1108 cf34d3113 vs PR #31469 fc4a5a77a)

Paths: P = ref/llama.cpp, U = ref/llama.cpp-up1108, R = ref/llama.cpp-pr31469. All refs file:line.

## 1. Pinned vs upstream moe-cache

Common skeleton (both trees; P file 639 lines, U 916):
- Eligibility: a layer is cached only if ALL its expert tensors (gate_up|gate,up,down) are WEIGHTS usage in a host buffer
  (`ggml_backend_buffer_is_host`) - U llama-moe-cache.cpp:312-316, 422-444 (P: same helper at ~150-160). Device type GPU or IGPU
  accepted (U:405) so Orin Nano qualifies. mmap'd CPU buffers count as host.
- Granularity: one slot = one whole expert across all its tensors (bank per tensor, `bank ne[2] = n_slots(+n_zero+1)`; U:553-558).
  Slot size = sum of `t->nb[2]` (gate+up+down or gate_up+down) -> for Q4_K_XL ~ 1.3-1.6 MiB/expert/layer.
- Budget: ONE global budget `--moe-cache-mib` (per device, split by free mem/tensor-split, U:462-483). Within a device, layers with identical
  tensor layout form a `group` that shares ONE bank set and ONE LRU across all layers (U:332-343, 503-519), i.e. a global pool across layers,
  not per-layer. `n_slots` = largest N with padded alloc <= budget (U:508). Must be >= n_expert_used else "not cached" (U:511).
  Hybrid layouts (e.g. different quant per layer) become separate groups, each getting budget proportional to host bytes.
- Slot map: per-layer I32[n_expert] in host memory (U:569). Graph does `get_rows(slot_map, ids)` -> `mul_mat_id(bank_view, cur, slots)`
  (llama-graph.cpp U:2664-2713, 1765). Scheduler copy callback `llama_moe_cache::copy` (U:761-856) fires when the slot-map split is
  copied: D2H-reads selected ids (U:799-800, SYNCHRONIZES the backend each layer), runs `plan()`, uploads misses, uploads slot map (U:853).
  Hook: llama-context.cpp:2991 (copy cb), 3044 (large-batch `copy_experts`, device->device copy of cached experts into the scratch).
- Used only for ubatch <= `max_batch`=32 tokens and when unique experts fit (U:368, 694); bigger batches bypass (read-only reuse via copy_experts).
- Upload path: `ggml_backend_tensor_set_async` -> `cudaMemcpyAsync(H2D)` straight from `w->data + e*nb[2]` (U:840; ggml-cuda.cu:2894-2901).
  Source is the model tensor in place: pageable mmap pages unless weights were loaded pinned. NO staging buffer of its own; consecutive
  expert+slot pairs are merged into one memcpy (U:835-843). Sorted miss order gives mergeable runs (U:270).

Policy:
- P: plain LRU (single doubly-linked list; `plan` P:74-109): hits touched to tail, misses sorted, victim = head, no admission control, no
  frequency. Slot-map sentinel -1.
- U (#30637 SLRU -> #31233 ClassLRU): "ClassLRU" U:20-287. Per-expert CRF = decayed use count, half-life 128 tokens (U:27), retained across
  evictions (U:46); class = floor(log2 CRF) in 0..7 (U:116); 8 LRU lists; victim = per-class LRU candidate with max age/2^class (U:152-175);
  experts selected by the current plan are protected (U:132-150). No hard admission filter other than CPU-share rule below. Slot map sentinel =
  n_slots ("empty"), slots >= n_slots point at zero slots (CPU-computed).
- #30966 CPU share (U docs/moe-cache.md; U:187-266, 450-452, 801-827, graph 2599-2603, 2664-2713): only AFTER cache is full (`n_filled==n_slots`, U:807),
  a fraction `--moe-cache-cpu-share F` of misses (lowest CRF first; fractional carry `cpu_acc` U:808-812) are NOT uploaded: the device reads
  zero-slot rows (n_zero = min(n_expert_used,64) extra zero experts, U:452) and a second `mul_mat_id(host_expert_tensor, cpu_ids)` computes
  those experts; result `ggml_add`ed (graph U:2603). `cpu_map` (host I32, -1 = skip) selects them. Runs on the ggml CPU backend via the
  scheduler (threads = `-t`/ggml threadpool; no private pool), as its own split. Overlap with GPU is only what async launch gives: GPU kernels
  of the hit part are queued, CPU split runs, then add. Disabled if `ggml_backend_offload_op` says the GPU would take such small op
  (U:701-719), not with LoRA / weight_before_ffn / Hadamard-rotated experts (graph U:2423). #31888 (cf34d3113, +3 lines graph) just forces
  `ggml_build_forward_expand(gf, cur)` before the lookup so the CPU part's input is ready (does not wait on cache upload).
- #31497 not separately studied (unknown content; not in the moe-cache files).
- Stats: `impl::stats` {hits,misses,cpu,bytes} for ubatch<=8 (decode) and >8, plus `stats_copy` (U:361-374, 846-850). Printed once at
  destructor via `LLAMA_LOG_INFO` (U:858-872): `llama_moe_cache: ubatch <= 8: hits=.., misses=.. (.. on the CPU), hit rate=..%, uploaded=.. MiB`.
  Init log U:626-634 prints size, slots per group, "tokens worth". P prints same minus CPU column (P:585-597). Nothing per-layer.
- Flags (U common/arg.cpp:2747-2766; P arg.cpp:2780): `--moe-cache-mib N` (env LLAMA_ARG_MOE_CACHE_MIB, default 0=off), `--moe-cache-cpu-share F`
  (env LLAMA_ARG_MOE_CACHE_CPU_SHARE, default 0). Env `LLAMA_MOE_CACHE_TRACE=<file>` (U:494, format U:642-678) dumps routing ids
  (binary "MCT1": per-lookup layer + ids) - this IS a ready routing-trace producer on the real model.
- Tuning script `U scripts/moe-cache-tune.py` (630 lines): input = a `llama-server` command (after `--`), options `--max-mib`, `--out` dir
  (cached runs), `--markdown`. Runs server 6x (2 sizes x shares 0,0.5,0.95; N_FIRST 2048/N_CALIB 512 tokens, fixed prompt; py:21-27),
  sets LLAMA_MOE_CACHE_TRACE, reads timings via HTTP, fits upload and CPU speeds, replays trace through a Python copy of the cache logic
  and prints predicted t/s per (size, share) + recommended args (lowest share within 5% of best). Server-only; many minutes at 20 GiB load.
  Replay model assumes bytes/upload-speed; on UMA both speeds are DRAM-bound so fit will be poor. The replay is reusable as simulator.

## 2. UMA behaviour (Orin Nano, integrated=1)

- Bank allocated with the device's own buft (`llama_memory_bufs::alloc_buf(.., d.buft, ..)` U:591) = plain cudaMalloc buffer. On Tegra that
  is a second allocation in the same DRAM. Each upload = CPU-driven pageable cudaMemcpyAsync (cuda stages through its own pinned bounce
  buffer, so for pageable mmap memory it effectively synchronizes the host thread) -> double residency of every cached expert
  (host page + bank), and the host copy is page-cache-backed, i.e. droppable only if mmap. Net: cache of X MiB costs X MiB extra DRAM
  while the full 20.8 GiB model is still referenced; with 8 GB RAM the model can never be fully resident anyway.
- No zero-copy path anywhere in the cache. `ggml-cuda.cu:352 (P)/338 (U)` forces `info.devices[id].integrated=false` ("corrupted output #15034"),
  which feeds only `supports_buft` for cuda_host (U:6381), a debug assert (U:4888-5062), and graph-compute placement; cache device-type test
  uses `prop.integrated` directly (U:5858) so it is unaffected. `cudaHostRegister` exists as `ggml_backend_cuda_register_host_buffer`
  (U:5680-5700; flags Portable|ReadOnly) but is gated by env `GGML_CUDA_REGISTER_HOST` (U:167) and NOTHING in src/ calls it
  (grep: header only) - mmap region never registered. Model-loader pinned host buffers: `-lm none/mlock/dio` use CUDA_Host buft
  (cpu buft list, llama-model.cpp:1245-1258, `--no-host` disables) -> cudaMallocHost; those are device-visible zero-copy on Tegra,
  `docs/moe-cache.md` says mmap (default) is NOT pinned. On UMA a pinned host expert can be consumed by kernels directly (mul_mat_id
  reading host pointer is not done by ggml: host-buffer weights run on CPU backend unless offloaded op, so no GPU read of host weights).
- Implication: on Jetson the cache converts "CPU computes experts from RAM at DRAM BW" into "CPU memcpy + GPU computes". The memcpy
  costs the same DRAM traffic as the CPU compute reading it once, so a cache only wins on re-use (hits), not on cold misses; cpu-share
  is likely good (the doc's own caveat: CPU share wins when upload is not faster than CPU reading host experts - true on UMA).

## 3. Pre-warm / pin from a routing profile

Not supported. No pinning, no warmup; cache starts empty (`slots[e]=empty` U:606; `key_of=-1` U:36,63). P likewise.
Minimal patch `--moe-cache-profile <file>` (text lines "layer expert [score]" ranked, top-N taken in file order):
1. common/common.h:600 add `std::string moe_cache_profile; int moe_cache_pin=0`; common/arg.cpp:2747 new opt (+env); common/common.cpp:1761 copy
   to cparams; include/llama.h:400 + llama-cparams.h + llama-context.cpp:394/4276 (default) plumb; llama-context.cpp:616 pass to ctor.
2. `llama_moe_cache::llama_moe_cache` / `impl::impl` signature (h:17, cpp:401): add profile path + n_pin.
3. After `g.lru.init(...)` (U:516) compute `n_pin = min(profile size for layers of g, n_slots - n_expert_used*max_batch margin)`.
   Pin to the high slot range: keep `g.n_slots` for bank/alloc and add `lru.n_slots = n_slots - n_pin` (use `n_lru` for init U:56-80, victim lists,
   `n_filled==n_slots` test U:807, `slot < n_slots` hit tests U:216,739,743). Slots [n_lru, n_slots) are never in any list so can never be
   victims; "empty" sentinel must move to `n_slots` (>= n_slots) and hit test become `slot < n_slots` unchanged. zero slots stay after n_slots.
4. After `buf_host` is cleared (U:599-609): for each pinned (il,e): `slot_map[il][e]=slot`, `key_of`-equivalent not needed (not in lists),
   then upload once with synchronous `ggml_backend_tensor_set(bank, w->data + e*nb2, slot*nb2, nb2)` for each tensor `ip` (like U:840).
   Also set CRF so the class logic is consistent (optional). Pinned experts then hit via normal path; `plan` `uniq.size()>n_slots` check
   (U:205) must use n_lru-aware count only for misses. `copy_experts` (U:739) works unchanged.
5. In P (plain LRU) the same: init lru over `n_slots - n_pin`, pre-set `slot_map`, touch nothing. Also needs stats line `pinned=N`.
Do on U (policy + CPU share); P gets no CPU share. Patch size ~100 lines. Pre-warm without pin is the same minus step 3 (call plan once with the profile ids).

## 4. PR #31469 (R, "Demand-paged MoE", Codex-assisted)

- Base 8345f3339 (Oct 5), +293 commits, 61 files, +9012/-86 vs base; tested envelope only: Linux x86-64, RTX 3060 12 GB sm_86, 16 GB RAM,
  `qwen4exp` (48 layers x 512 experts, IQ2_XS, custom arch) (R docs/moe-direct-io.md:5-13). Not general.
- Design: `--moe-direct-io` (R common/arg.cpp, env LLAMA_ARG_MOE_DIRECT_IO) forces ffn_*_exps to CPU buffer (mmap) and builds a global VRAM
  slot pool (`--moe-slots N`, default 4096, shared across layers; llama-context.cpp:1413-1437 scales a built-in per-layer table),
  per-layer hot seeding from a baked table `src/moe_hot_profile.h` (top-72 per layer for qwen4exp only; `--moe-profile PATH` can override;
  `data/profile-universal.bin`), GPU "doorbell" kernel (moe_doorbell.cu, 735 lines) resolves expert->slot inside the stream without D2H sync,
  user-space pager `moe_pager.cpp` (1049 lines): io_uring reads (buffered by default despite the flag name; O_DIRECT at pager.cpp:625/660),
  expert pack `experts.bin` (tools/moe_pack.py, +33 GiB for the tested model, one contiguous read per expert), pinned staging ring
  (cudaHostAlloc), `cudaMemcpyAsync` H2D (pager.cpp:870,902,974), "victim cache": anonymous host mmap registered with `cudaHostRegister`
  (pager.cpp:462-480) default 8 GiB, `MOE_CACHE_MIB`, plus a learned router predictor (`moe_predictor.cu`) / prefetch (MOE_PRED,
  MOE_HOT_K, MOE_PREKICK, MOE_RA_*), `--cache-warmup/--auto-warm` (runs a generation to warm).
- Flags: --moe-direct-io, --moe-slots, --moe-profile, --moe-pack-dir, --moe-chunk-max (8), --auto-warm, --cache-warmup N, --cache-warmup-prompt,
  --rs-seq; ~40 MOE_* env vars (llama-context.cpp). Diagnostics MOE_DIAG=1 MOE_IO_DIAG=1 (hit/IO bytes).
- UMA: assumes discrete VRAM + separate system RAM (RAM victim cache sits between NVMe and VRAM; docs envelope 12 GiB cgroup). On Orin
  everything is one DRAM, so VRAM pool + victim cache + page cache all compete (triple copy). Needs liburing, sm_86 kernels, cudaHostRegister
  of anonymous memory (works on Tegra but cudaHostRegister read-only flag etc. unverified). Only qwen4exp graph path is wired
  (src/models/qwen4exp.cpp, llama-graph.cpp:2220-2330); qwen35moe not hooked -> would need porting. Benefit on UMA: the NVMe->RAM
  pager design (expert-aligned reads from a pack, io_uring readahead, predictor) is the relevant idea for 20.8 GiB > 8 GB RAM; VRAM pool
  is not. Reuse as ideas, not code.
- Conflicts vs U: `git diff 8345f333 cf34d3113 -- src/llama-context.cpp src/llama-graph.cpp` = 1557+/552- (graph refactors, ClassLRU,
  hdmd); R rewrites llama-context.cpp by +2860 and llama-graph.cpp by +211 -> heavy, near-certain conflicts; R also edits ggml.h/ggml.c
  (+32/+77), ggml-cuda.cu(+159), ggml-cpu ops. Merge R onto U is a port, not a rebase. R is also orthogonal to moe-cache (does not use it).

## 5. Experiment matrix (Jetson; mem 8 GB, model 20.8 GiB, qwen35moe 40L x 256E)

Fixed: `-m Q4_K_XL.gguf -ngl 99 -ncmoe 40 (or -cmoe) -c 2048 -t 6 -ub 8? -b 8? -fa on -n 256 --temp 0 --seed 1`, fixed prompt (use tune script's PROMPT).
Tool: llama-bench has NO --moe-cache-mib / --moe-cache-cpu-share / -lm? (bench takes -ncmoe/-cmoe/-ot but not cache flags; verify with
`llama-bench -h`) -> use llama-cli/llama-completion/llama-server with `--perf` timings (prompt eval + eval t/s); trace via env var.
Trees: P (pinned, 3 variants), U (up1108), R not run (needs qwen4exp/NVMe pack).
 A0 baseline P/U: `-lm mmap` no cache (the 1 t/s figure; control); A1 `-lm none` / `-lm mlock` with `-cmoe` if RAM allows (it does not: 20.8 GiB
   > 8 GiB -> will thrash/OOM; use only mmap).
 A2 cache sweep (U): `--moe-cache-mib` 512, 1024, 1536, 2048, 3072 (RAM headroom: 8 GB - OS - KV - non-expert weights) with share 0.
 A3 cpu-share sweep (U): MiB best of A2 x `--moe-cache-cpu-share` 0, 0.5, 0.8, 0.95 (is CPU read faster than cudaMemcpy of pageable mmap? On UMA likely yes).
 A4 P vs U same size (LRU vs ClassLRU hit rate), run twice (cold page cache via `echo 3 > drop_caches`, then warm).
 A5 `-lm dio`/pinned host (`--no-host` on/off) once to see pinned zero-copy upload effect on UMA.
 A6 patched U with `--moe-cache-profile` pinned top-N (from LLAMA_MOE_CACHE_TRACE profile) vs unpinned, same total MiB.
 Each: 2 runs, tg 256, report median; also decode with n_batch 1 (spec off).
Counters to log: exit-time `llama_moe_cache:` lines (hit rate, misses, cpu misses, uploaded MiB per ubatch<=8), init line (slots, tokens worth),
 llama_perf (pp/tg t/s), `/proc/meminfo` MemAvailable + Cached + Mapped, `cat /proc/pressure/memory`, `vmstat 1` (bi, si/so),
 `iostat -x` NVMe read MB/s, tegrastats RAM/GR3D/EMC, majflt/minflt of the process (`/proc/PID/stat`), and the MCT1 trace for offline replay.
 Add per-layer hits and wall time inside `copy()` (U:761) in a follow-up patch (sync D2H at U:800 costs per-layer latency; log ns/layer).

## Caveats / unverified
- #31497 content not identified in these files; P line numbers approximate (structure identical to U before ClassLRU/CPU-share).
- Overlap claim for CPU share is inferred from scheduler design, not measured. llama-bench flag set not checked in this pass.

# D030 — Over-memory baselines on Jetson; upstream moe-cache is a net loss on UMA (2026-11-10, jetson-arm)
Model Qwen3.6-35B-A3B UD-Q4_K_XL 20.8 GiB on 7.4 GiB shared DRAM (D029). All runs via cc/om_run/om_run.sh (watchdog + io/proc/tegrastats telemetry). Category: runtime-placement / cache-policy observations (no code change of ours yet).
## Baselines, pinned engine (jetson-c1-p03, env unset; llama-bench -p 128 -n 64 -r 2) — experiments/jetson/OM/base-20261110-0448
| config | pp t/s | tg t/s | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| -lm mmap -ngl 99 -ncmoe 40 (all experts via mmap/NVMe, rest GPU) | 4.49 | 1.30 | ok |
| -lm mmap -ngl 99 -ncmoe 38 (2 layers' experts on GPU) | 4.67 | 1.21 | ok (no gain) |
| -lm mmap -ngl 0 (CPU only) | 4.09 | 1.09 | ok |
| -lm none -ngl 99 -ncmoe 40 | — | — | watchdog: MemAvailable 401 MiB at 11 s |
| **default (-lm auto) -ngl 99 -ncmoe 40** | — | — | **watchdog: MemAvailable 321 MiB at 7 s** — default cannot run a >RAM model on Orin (auto disables mmap on iGPU) |
| repeat of row 1 | — | — | watchdog tripped on zram swap-rate burst 286 MiB/s with 3.5 GiB available (false positive → swap-rate limit raised to 1000 MiB/s; rerun queued in cmp sweep) |
Earlier 6 attempts failed on llama-bench flags (-c unsupported) — recorded.
## Upstream cf34d311 moe-cache (llama-completion, 800-char wiki prompt, -n 64, -lm mmap -ngl 99 -cmoe) — up-20261110-0436 (clean) + upv-20261110-0519 (with -lv 4 counters; TIMING CONTAMINATED: a CPU-heavy replay simulation ran at nice 0 for part of it)
| config | decode t/s (clean / upv) | decode hit rate | uploaded |
|---|---|---|---|
| no cache | 1.18, 1.19 / 1.21, 1.16 | — | — |
| cache 512 MiB | – / 0.98 | 37.7% | 23.0 GB |
| cache 1024 MiB | 0.91 / – | – | – |
| cache 2048 MiB | 0.98 / 0.98 | **64.0%** | 13.8 GB |
| 2048 + cpu-share 0.5 | 1.13 / – | – | – |
| 2048 + cpu-share 1.0 | – / 0.87 | 36.2% | 2.0 GB |
| 1024 + cpu-share 0.5 | – / 1.02 | 54.7% | 8.9 GB |
Interpretation: the cache achieves real hit rates (64% at 2 GiB ≈ 10% of experts — consistent with replay-sim LRU locality) yet decode is 17–23% slower than no cache. On UMA every miss still page-faults from NVMe AND is then copied into a separate device bank (~215 MB/token of copies at 2 GiB) while the bank's DRAM is subtracted from the page cache that serves misses. On discrete GPUs the upload buys PCIe-free GPU compute; on unified memory it is pure overhead + double residency. CPU-share (misses computed on CPU in place) recovers most of the loss but not more.
## Design consequence (hypothesis to test)
For unified-memory targets: do not copy experts into a separate cache. Campaign c1 · jetson-arm lane · branch jetson/c1
