State at 2026-11-10 05:40 UTC · Orin Nano 8 GB (sm_87, L4T R36.5.2) · llama.cpp pin 31288c9c6, upstream cf34d311 · evidence in campaign/decisions/D021–D030, experiments/jetson/

What real inference-improvement work on a small unified-memory board taught us to build, reuse, change or avoid. Every number below comes from a recorded run; anything pending or contaminated is marked.

+19.3%bf16 decode, MoE gate/up routed to tensor-core kernelD025 · 50.3 → 60.1 t/s · KLD 2.7e-4

Major findings

FindingEvidenceClass
Decode on Orin is GPU-kernel bound, not launch bound. CUDA graphs are already on; bf16 matvec is 81% of GPU time.J-P001profile
The fused MoE gate/up kernel is the slow one: ≈40 GB/s against ≈68 GB/s for the unfused down projection on the same weights.J-P001profile
Whether to fuse depends on weight type × platform: unfusing helps bf16 (+19%) and Q4_K (+24%) but hurts Q8_0 (−6%) on Orin. A global switch is wrong both ways.D027code gain
Q4_K experts were no faster than Q8_0 despite half the bytes: the fused Q4_K kernel ran at ≈18 GB/s (dequant/compute bound). After the fix the smaller model is also the faster one.J-P003, D027profile + gain
Over memory, decode is bound by NVMe access pattern and hit rate: 52 GiB read for 96 tokens, ≈20 KB per read, refault storms, zram swapping.D029observation
Upstream's expert cache reaches a 64% hit rate at 2 GiB yet makes decode 17–23% slower on unified memory: misses still fault from NVMe, then get copied, and the cache's DRAM is taken from the page cache.D030placement
Routing has strong temporal locality: LRU over ~12% of experts serves ≈54% of decode requests in replay.replay sweepsimulation
Upstream (Nov 8) decodes ≈9% faster than the pin on the over-memory model with the same tool and flags. Preliminary: half of the counterbalanced runs, simulator running at low priority.cmp sweepengine version
A container memory cap does not bound CUDA allocations on Tegra: 1.5 GiB allocated under a 1 GiB cap in 5/5 runs, cgroup counted ≈0.6 GiB.D028isolation
llama.cpp sizes context from free device memory; on Tegra that is free system DRAM, so a 24-token test took a 45k context and ~5 GB.D023memory fit
Build CC binaries are not bit-reproducible across attempts (embedded paths); identical behaviour (ppl 7.5479 both). ccache fix made rebuilds 22× faster.D026build

Measurement

  • Same image, environment switch per arm: isolates the code path from build noise.

Methodologies that held up

Measurement

  • Same image, environment switch per arm: isolates the code path from build noise.
  • Counterbalanced ABBA, two or more runs per arm, drop the first sample (GPU clock ramp), report steady mean.
  • A/A before trusting a delta: spread was ≤0.3 t/s at 50–100 t/s, so +10 t/s effects are unambiguous.
  • Keep compiles, simulators and downloads out of timing windows; mark contaminated runs instead of dropping them.

Quality

  • Decode-only kernel changes need -ub 1 perplexity and KL against saved base logits.
  • Scale every KL against a known reference (Q8_0 vs bf16: 3.4e-3).
  • Distinguish byte-identical (quantized unfuse) from small rounding change (bf16 MMF).

Platform hygiene

  • On shared memory, pin every free-memory-derived default (-c, load mode).
  • A fair over-memory baseline is what a competent user runs (-lm mmap, -ncmoe), with the default's failure reported separately.
  • Per-component applicability tables: weight type × compute capability × batch.

Process

  • Profile → cheap screen with an existing switch → targeted patch → counterbalanced A/B → KL → independent review → kernel inventory.
  • Search upstream before building: the moe-cache series landed days before we needed it.
  • Never stage a directory a running job writes to (a 1.4 GB archive nearly reached GitHub, D024).

What predicts, what correlates

Good predictors

  • Effective GB/s per kernel (weight bytes ÷ nsys time) pointed at every gain we found.
  • Bytes moved per token ÷ achieved read bandwidth predicts over-memory decode within ~10%.
  • Replay-simulated LRU hit rate landed close to the engine's own counter.
  • A/A spread sets the smallest effect worth chasing.
  • Byte-identical outputs predict a safe, computation-preserving change.

Poor or misleading predictors

  • Cache hit rate does not predict speed on unified memory.
  • Bytes per weight fails once kernels are dequant or compute bound.
  • Batch-512 perplexity is blind to decode-only kernel changes.
  • Single-layer or microbenchmark speedups are hypotheses until end-to-end.
  • Free-memory readings, container limits and binary hashes: each looked like a measure of budget or identity and wasn't.
  • Raw t/s across hosts: never comparable; only local A/B ratios are.

Structure and flexibility

Where structure paid off

  • Recorded commands and attempt IDs caught false successes: an exit code masked by a pipe, a watchdog that couldn't kill, a run that crashed after logging success.
  • Fixed identities (model hash, commit, patch hash, image digest) made cross-run comparisons trustworthy.
  • Per-host evidence folders, admission records and claim classes kept findings from being promoted without evidence.

Where flexibility paid off

  • Most progress came from fast throwaway screens: an existing env switch found the +14% before any patch.
  • Designs turned out model × hardware specific, so fixed recipes would have been wrong; env-gated components with applicability tables worked.
  • Swapping in upstream code beat building our own cache.

The working balance: rigid at the boundaries (identity, recording, admission, safety, quality gates), loose in the middle (which experiment to run next, which tool to try). About half the defects found tonight were in our own tooling, all caught because the boundaries were strict.

Methodologies that held up

Measurement

  • Same image, environment switch per arm: isolates the code path from build noise.

What predicts, what correlates

Good predictors

  • Effective GB/s per kernel (weight bytes ÷ nsys time) pointed at every gain we found.
  • Bytes moved per token ÷ achieved read bandwidth predicts over-memory decode within ~10%.
  • Replay-simulated LRU hit rate landed close to the engine's own counter.
  • A/A spread sets the smallest effect worth chasing.
  • Byte-identical outputs predict a safe, computation-preserving change.

Poor or misleading predictors

  • Cache hit rate does not predict speed on unified memory.
  • Bytes per weight fails once kernels are dequant or compute bound.
  • Batch-512 perplexity is blind to decode-only kernel changes.
  • Single-layer or microbenchmark speedups are hypotheses until end-to-end.
  • Free-memory readings, container limits and binary hashes: each looked like a measure of budget or identity and wasn't.
  • Raw t/s across hosts: never comparable; only local A/B ratios are.

Structure and flexibility

Where structure paid off

  • Recorded commands and attempt IDs caught false successes: an exit code masked by a pipe, a watchdog that couldn't kill, a run that crashed after logging success.
  • Fixed identities (model hash, commit, patch hash, image digest) made cross-run comparisons trustworthy.
  • Per-host evidence folders, admission records and claim classes kept findings from being promoted without evidence.

Where flexibility paid off

  • Most progress came from fast throwaway screens: an existing env switch found the +14% before any patch.
  • Designs turned out model × hardware specific, so fixed recipes would have been wrong; env-gated components with applicability tables worked.
  • Swapping in upstream code beat building our own cache.

The working balance: rigid at the boundaries (identity, recording, admission, safety, quality gates), loose in the middle (which experiment to run next, which tool to try). About half the defects found tonight were in our own tooling, all caught because the boundaries were strict.

# D031 — Upstream llama.cpp +7% over-memory decode; NVMe is a 570 MiB/s budget drive; first-order decode model (2026-11-10, jetson-arm)
## Engine version (dependency update, not our code) — experiments/jetson/OM/cmp-20261110-0534
llama-bench -p 128 -n 64 -r 2 -lm mmap -ngl 99 -ncmoe 40, Qwen3.6-35B UD-Q4_K_XL, order pin,up,up,pin:
- decode: pin 1.255 / 1.284 (mean 1.27), upstream cf34d311 1.365 / 1.353 (mean 1.36) → **+7%**; prefill pin 4.52/4.24, up 4.77/4.75 → ≈+9%. Caveat: runs partly overlapped a nice-19 replay simulation; pin arms show larger spread. Category: engine-version change (upstream moe/mmq/graph work between Oct 18 and Nov 8), local to Jetson.
## NVMe ceiling (fio on the model file, O_DIRECT, read-only) — experiments/jetson/OM/fio
rand4k qd1 19.6 MiB/s (181 µs) · rand4k qd32 74 MiB/s · rand128k qd8 475 · rand576k qd1 416 · rand576k qd8 536 · rand2m qd4 543 · seq1m qd8 573 MiB/s · 576k psync×4 535.
PCIe link is Gen3 x4 (8 GT/s, x4 — /sys current_link_*), so the limit is the drive: "X15 Lite SSD 128GB" (budget, small capacity). max_hw_sectors 128 KiB, read_ahead 128 KiB. The 825 MiB/s peak seen in D029 telemetry is likely a sampling-interval artefact (to verify).
## First-order model (prediction tool, validated loosely)
decode_tps ≈ disk_BW / (routed_expert_bytes_per_token × miss_rate). With 615 MB/token (layout) and 570 MiB/s: miss_rate 1.0 → ~1.0 t/s; measured 1.27–1.36 → implied miss ≈ 0.70–0.75 (page cache acting as a ~30% hit cache). Replay LRU at 1300–2048 expert slots (2.5–3.9 GB): miss 0.38–0.27 → predicted 2.4–3.4 t/s if the cache holds bytes ONCE and misses read at full drive bandwidth. Our UMA components (dedupe / direct-fill) target exactly that gap. Belady bound at 2048: miss 0.12 → ~7.8 t/s (prefetch headroom).
## Consequences
- For the 128 GB unified + 4 TB SSD target, SSD read bandwidth and access granularity are first-order design inputs; record drive model + fio matrix in every host inventory (added to NEEDS-MAP).
- Page-fault reads (≈20 KB) vs expert-sized reads (576 KB qd8 = 536 MiB/s) matter less on this drive than on a fast NVMe (both near the ceiling); on fast drives large aligned reads should matter more — x86 to measure.
EOF
echo ok

# Router-informed expert mmap prefetch (J-OM7)

`patches/02-router-prefetch.patch` applies after `patches/01-mmap-advice-random.patch` to `ref/llama.cpp-up1108` at `cf34d3113`. The reference checkout is unchanged. This is a Linux-only, opt-in experiment; no build or GPU execution was performed for this assignment.

```bash
cat cc/mmap_advice/patches/01-mmap-advice-random.patch \
    cc/mmap_advice/patches/02-router-prefetch.patch > /tmp/om7-combined.patch
git -C ref/llama.cpp-up1108 apply --check /tmp/om7-combined.patch
```

## Mechanism

Set `LLAMA_EXPERT_PREFETCH=1`. The loader supplies the file ranges of `ffn_*_exps.weight` tensors as mmap advice exclusions, separately from the existing lazy-loading placement policy. These ranges receive `MADV_RANDOM` and are excluded from initial `WILLNEED` and `MAP_POPULATE`; non-expert ranges retain default sequential file advice and initial `WILLNEED`. Existing lazy ranges remain excluded. Expert mode takes precedence over `LLAMA_MMAP_ADVICE=random`, so that setting both does not make the entire file random. With expert mode off, patch 01 retains its original behavior. NUMA and other explicit loading policies still apply.

The scheduler's new CPU-only before-node callback observes the first `MUL_MAT_ID` that uses a layer's original expert weights. Its `src[2]` is the same `ffn_moe_topk-L` I32 tensor named in `src/llama-graph.cpp:2367`, or the scheduler's host copy of that tensor. CPU graph prefixes finish before observation. The callback reads `{K,T,1,1}` with the actual strides, validates IDs, and deduplicates all selected IDs across the ubatch. Before that expert matmul starts, it issues `madvise(MADV_WILLNEED)` for each ID's gate/up/down slice (also supports merged gate-up). Each slice uses `data + id * nb[2]`, length `nb[2]`, aligned outward to OS pages. Qwen's observed gate/up slices are 589,824 bytes and down slices 720,896 bytes; the implementation derives sizes from tensors, including exceptional layers.

Only contiguous three-dimensional expert tensors whose entire actual data span is inside a model-owned mmap are eligible. A host buffer alone is insufficient proof. Unsupported tensors or router layouts are skipped with a once-per-context log. Biases/scales, transformed router IDs, and MoE-cache slot IDs are not interpreted as original expert IDs. No model weights, router IDs, or floating-point operations are modified.

Each layer retains at most 32 advised IDs in an LRU, with a 32-token expiry measured in that layer's ubatch token count. Cache hits update recency without extending the last-advice timestamp. Failed advice is counted and does not suppress a later retry. A large ubatch is one deduplicated observation; expiry is evaluated at its end, not separately for each token. This is a syscall limiter, not a page-residency tracker.

`LLAMA_EXPERT_PREFETCH_NEXT=1` additionally advises the same union of IDs in layer L+1, subject to its expert bounds and the same LRU. It has no effect without the primary switch. When L+1 is observed in the same ubatch, each distinct prediction counts once in `total`, and membership in its actual selected union counts as a hit. This is prediction precision over ubatch unions, not per-token accuracy; large prompts can inflate it. Predictions whose next layer is never host-observed are excluded from the ratio and are cleared at the next ubatch. No last-layer wraparound occurs.

At context destruction, after synchronization, `LLAMA_LOG_INFO` reports attempted advice calls, attempted page-rounded bytes, syscall failures, and next-layer prediction hits/total plus percent. Bytes advised are hints, not measured disk bytes. Startup logs identify both mapping policy and the host-consumer hook; zero calls must not be treated as evidence of active prefetch.

## Applicability and synchronization

Works with mmap-backed CPU experts under CPU-only execution or any GPU/CPU layer split, including `-ngl 99 -cmoe`. `-cmoe` moves expert weights/operations to CPU; it does **not** force router computation to CPU. With GPU-offloaded layers, router top-k can be GPU-computed. The scheduler already copies these IDs to the CPU expert split and waits for that copy (including its existing asynchronous prefetch event). Observation occurs at this first host consumer, after those existing waits. It does not request another readback or synchronize a GPU backend. The added synchronization is CPU-only; the existing CPU backend's graph compute is already synchronous and its synchronize function is null.

The regular scheduler eval callback is preserved, including its existing synchronization behavior. Installing an ordinary eval callback just to read GPU top-k would introduce a synchronization; this patch avoids that path. On all-CPU execution it finishes the prefix containing the router before reading IDs. On GPU routing it deliberately defers observation from top-k production to the first CPU expert consumer. Device-only expert paths are skipped instead of creating a new device-to-host dependency. GPU-uploaded weights, non-mmap loads, unsupported layouts, and cached/remapped IDs receive no exact host prefetch. Non-Linux builds do not enable the feature.

## Risks

`WILLNEED` is a best-effort kernel hint and may start late, block briefly, or fail; it does not guarantee expert-sized physical IO. Page rounding can include neighboring weights. Predictions and stale LRU entries can waste IO or suppress useful rereads after eviction. Even exact advice may compete with current reads and evict useful cache pages. The CPU graph prefix boundary adds planning/threadpool overhead. Applying RANDOM to experts also changes initial model upload behavior for offloaded weights; measure startup separately. The feature has not been compiled or performance-validated. D033's speedup estimate is a hypothesis, not a result.

## A/B/C for the build/run owner (jetson-arm)

Use one executable containing 01+02 for all three arms and the same Qwen model, fixed prompt, seed, context, thread counts, ubatch size, and generation length. Reproduce D033 with `-lm mmap -ngl 99 -cmoe`, 64 generated tokens, and its recorded p1 prompt. Keep the existing telemetry collector running and quiesce unrelated NVMe work. Example arm invocations, after setting `BIN`, `MODEL`, and `PROMPT_FILE`:

```bash

# resource_observe (J-T2)
Stdlib-only Python 3.10 sampler emitting JSONL under one contract, with platform backends.

## Usage
    resource_observe.py capabilities
    resource_observe.py sample --backends auto|tegrastats,proc,sysfs_tegra,nvml [--interval-ms 500] [--duration-s N] [--pid P] [--cgroup PATH] [--nvpmodel-mode STR] --out F.jsonl
    resource_observe.py summarize F.jsonl [--interval-ms 500]   # per-metric min/max/mean/high_water + coverage (expected vs received, gaps > 2x interval)
Tests: `python3 -m pytest` (no GPU/root; fixtures in `fixtures/`, paths injectable).

## Record
`{"schema":"resource-observe/0","ts","mono_s","host_id","backend","seq","metrics":[{name,value,unit,scope,source}],"unavailable":[{name,backend,reason}],"parse_errors":[...]}`
Missing data is listed in `unavailable` with a reason, never as 0. Malformed tegrastats lines yield a record with `parse_errors` carrying `line_sha256_16` (no crash). Units: MiB, MHz, percent, mW, celsius, load.
`tegrastats` emits one record per line it produces (the interval is set on the child); other backends emit one per tick.

## Attribution scopes (do NOT sum across scopes)
- `system-shared-dram` (tegrastats RAM): whole-system DRAM shared by CPU and GPU on Jetson.
- `system` (/proc/meminfo): same physical pages viewed system-wide; `process` (VmRSS/VmHWM) and `cgroup` (memory.current/peak/max) are subsets of the same pages. Adding them to tegrastats RAM double counts.
- cgroup metrics carry `accounting_note`: cgroup v2 may not include nvmap/driver GPU allocations on Tegra, so it can under-report GPU memory. Unlimited `memory.max` is reported unavailable. memory.peak may be missing on older kernels (unavailable). This host's cgroup controllers file lists memory.
- `device-discrete` (nvml): dedicated VRAM, x86 only. On Orin nvidia-smi exists but returns [N/A]; backend reports unavailable.
- sysfs_tegra: GPU devfreq (MHz), thermal zones (celsius, unreadable zones listed unavailable), nvpmodel mode (`nvpmodel -q`, query only, or `--nvpmodel-mode`).

## Known gaps
No NvMap fields on this kernel's meminfo (reported unavailable); no iomem/debugfs nvmap per-client attribution (needs root); tegrastats gets its own interval, summarize infers interval from median spacing if not given; nvml parsed from CSV fixtures only on this host (no discrete GPU).

## I/O telemetry and watchdog (J-OM1)

    python3 resource_observe.py sample --backends io --path ~/models/campaign --duration-s 5 --out io.jsonl
    python3 resource_observe.py sample --backends io --device nvme0n1 --pid 123 --cgroup /sys/fs/cgroup/example --out io.jsonl
    python3 resource_observe.py sample --backends io --pid-from-cgroup /sys/fs/cgroup/example --out io.jsonl
    python3 resource_observe.py watchdog --min-available-mib 900 --max-swap-used-mib 512 --max-swap-rate-mibs 20 --interval-ms 250 --kill-pid 123 --out events.jsonl

`io` reports vmstat counters in `system`, whole-disk counters in `device`,
PID data in `process`, and cgroup v2 data in `cgroup`. Never add these scopes.
`--path` defaults to the current directory and resolves the filesystem device
through `/sys/dev/block/MAJ:MIN`, walking partitions to the parent disk.
`--device` explicitly selects a disk name (or `/dev/NAME`). Overlay/network
filesystems without a block-device mapping report unavailable with a reason.
Disk read sectors use the kernel's fixed 512-byte sector unit.

Cumulative counters have `_delta` and `_rate` companions. First observations,
resets, missing samples, and nonpositive time intervals have unavailable interval
values; counters resume from a fresh baseline. Units: faults/refaults/I/Os/events
are `count`, pgpgin/out are `KiB`, swap-in/out are `pages`, read data and memory
are `MiB`, disk io_ticks are `ms`; rates append `/s`. `device_util` is
`100 * delta(io_ticks) / interval_ms` in `percent`. Device utilization is the
kernel busy-time measure, not an estimate of parallel NVMe queue saturation.
`pid_read_bytes` retains the kernel field name but is converted to MiB.
PID fields include minflt/majflt, read_bytes, VmRSS, RssFile, RssAnon, VmSwap.
`--pid` and `--pid-from-cgroup` are mutually exclusive. The latter sums only
PIDs in that file; incomplete per-field process sums are suppressed, and PID
membership/start-time changes invalidate interval baselines. Cgroup `io.stat`
read bytes remain separate per major:minor device. Cgroup memory accounting
may omit Tegra driver allocations.

The watchdog samples MemAvailable and SwapTotal minus SwapFree, and calculates
combined swap-in/out MiB/s using the host page size and monotonic elapsed time.
A particular limit must be crossed on two consecutive samples (equal to the
limit is safe). It flushes `watchdog_sample`, `watchdog_trip`, and
`watchdog_action` JSONL events using the same schema envelope. Targets are
mutually exclusive: `--kill-pid`, `--kill-cgroup`, or `--kill-cmd`.

# D041 — Upstream `--moe-cache-mib` beats static offload on Qwen at 8 GB (INDICATIVE); ncu decode roofline

Status: **INDICATIVE**. The screen was unfrozen, with 2 alternating rounds and no pre-registered protocol. A frozen follow-up is required before the factory adopts this.
Date: 2026-11-10. Lane: x86-main.
Engine: release-1 (`run_ref sha256:5b8a6a22…`, pin 31288c9c6). That pin contains upstream PR #29887, `--moe-cache-mib`.
Script: `artifacts/mc-qwen/screen.sh`, op T-MCQ. Raw output is in `artifacts/mc-qwen/`.

## Why
D022 found that static `--n-cpu-moe` beats the engine LRU cache at every footprint. That test used **Granite**, whose experts are 0.84 MiB each.
External reports for the upstream cache show decode gains on 16–32 GB cards with large MoEs (R9700 11→27.6 t/s; 5060 Ti 16 GB 15→19 t/s). They also say a hit rate of about 75% is needed.
D031 had already flagged a proxy-scale bias, so the D022 conclusion needed retesting on Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M.

## Result
Settings: chat prompt, 128 tokens, greedy decoding, FA on, ctx 4096. Peak VRAM is from nvidia-smi polled every 0.5 s.

| Config | Peak MiB | Decode t/s (r1, r2) | Prompt eval ms | Text sha |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| static `--n-cpu-moe 30` | 8193 | 36.88, 37.33 | 757, 783 | 1189257b |
| all-CPU experts + `--moe-cache-mib 6000` | 7831 | **51.13, 51.44** | 1082, 1089 | bf80f280 |
| static `--n-cpu-moe 42` | 4105 | 27.93, 26.77 | 1000, 996 | 77a3045a |
| all-CPU experts + `--moe-cache-mib 2200` | 4029 | 18.00, 18.15 | 1088, 1088 | bf80f280 |

- **At about 8 GB, the cache gives +38% decode with 362 MiB less VRAM.**
  - TTFT is about 40% worse, 1085 ms against 770 ms. This matches the reported prompt-processing loss.
- At about 4 GB, the cache is −34%. The crossover lies between the two budgets, and the hit rate is the likely driver.
  - That fits T-QRT's coverage curves. Held-out decode coverage is 77% at the K=8-sized hot set, falling to 15% at K=42.
- Every placement produced different greedy text, including static K30 against K42. This is the usual numeric divergence between CPU and GPU, not evidence of a bug. Even so, it needs a **KLD/PPL check**, not text identity.
  - The two cache configs produce identical text, which is consistent with all expert math running on the GPU.
- The host was quiet: no compiles, load average 2.4.

## Consequences
1. The D022 scope is narrowed to "small experts / low coverage". The planner must not hard-reject the expert cache.
2. Planner: add the cache as a lever. Model the hit rate from routing-trace coverage curves (T-QRT), and price misses at PCIe upload cost. The decision rule becomes: cache when predicted coverage ≥ about 70%, otherwise static.
3. The report must show the TTFT cost. The factory should expose a "decode-optimised vs TTFT-optimised" choice.
4. Frozen follow-up: ABBA ×3 at budgets 4/6/8/10/12 GB, with the cache size swept to find the crossover. Add KLD against a reference and the hit rate from engine logs.

## ncu decode roofline (Granite Q8_0, release-1, all-GPU), op T-NCU1
Settings: `ncu --launch-skip 2000 --launch-count 600` on `llama-bench tg32`. Raw data is in `artifacts/ncu1/ncu.csv`.
Caveat: ncu serialises kernels and flushes caches, so small-kernel times are inflated against graph replay.

- The effective DRAM bandwidth over the profiled window is 222 GB/s. The 5070 Ti's peak is about 896 GB/s.
- The large expert `mul_mat_vec_q` reaches 578 GB/s (66% of peak DRAM).
- About 40% of kernel time goes to tiny 2–4 µs kernels at under 1% DRAM: `quantize_q8_1`, `rms_norm`, `add`, `scale`, `topk_moe`, `moe_weighted_reduction`.
  - On a model this small, decode is launch- and latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound.
  - **Fusion candidates:** rms_norm with quantize_q8_1, and scale with add.
- An unprofiled nsys timeline is needed to size the real gain. ncu's serialisation exaggerates small kernels.

- **Methodology rule:** every bandwidth probe must (a) use a working set of at least 8× the last-level cache and (b) pass a physical-ceiling plausibility guard. T-CAL2 adds both.

**Claim category:** runtime-placement trade-off. This uses existing upstream flags (`--moe-cache-mib`, `--moe-cache-cpu-share`) with the weights unchanged.

**Protocol (D043 E1, frozen):**
- Accept "cache beats static at B" only if both hold:

- Quality gate: mean KLD ≤ 0.01 and same-top ≥ 97% against S1 K18, on 8×512 wikitext chunks.

**A/A interference (A1):** S1-K30 chat measured 36.46 t/s with the download running against 36.53 paused (n=3 each), a 0.2% difference against the 2% limit. **No arm is contaminated.**

## Verdict against the frozen rule
- **Speed + VRAM rule:**
  - C3 against S2 **MEETS** it at 4 GB (+30 / +34%), 6 GB (+54 / +66%), 8 GB (+76 / +65%) and 10 GB (+64 / +48%), with VRAM 2.6–6.5% below static.
  - C1 and C2 meet it only at 8 and 10 GB (+42–71%). At 4 GB they FAIL (−22 to −35%), and at 6 GB they FAIL on the chat prompt (C1 −6%, C2 +3%).
- **Quality gate, applied literally:**
  - The frozen batch-2048 run gives C3-6000 same-top 96.72%, below 97% → **FAIL**.
  - Under A2's decode path, C1, C2 and C3-2005 pass, and C3-6000 fails by 0.09 points.
  - The **reference configuration fails against itself** (96.47%) when only the batch shape changes, and so does the static K42 offload the factory already ships (96.37%).
  - The gate threshold therefore sits inside batch-shape noise and cannot separate placements. **Gate verdict: inconclusive / miscalibrated, not a pass.**
- **Post-hoc equivalence** (labelled as such): every placement falls in KLD 0.0055–0.0063 and same-top 96.4–97.3%, while the reference's own batch-shape floor is 0.0058 / 96.5%. The cache arms drift no more than static offload.

## Interpretation
1. **CPU-share is the missing lever behind D041's 4 GB loss.**
   - When misses are computed where static offload would have computed them anyway (on the CPU), while hits come from VRAM, the cache wins even at a 50% hit rate.
   - An upload-only cache wins only above roughly 70–75% hit rate. That matches D041 and T-POL.
2. **CPU-share costs speed at high hit rates.** At 10 GB (92% hit), code decode is 64.2 against 71.1 for share 0, because computing a few misses on the CPU costs more than uploading them.
3. **Prompt processing does not use the cache.** The stats cover only ubatch ≤ 8, so the TTFT penalty grows as static gains GPU layers.
4. **T-POL's offline replay predicted the 2 GB cell** at 18.9 (upload) and 31.8 (CPU-share); measured 18.4 and 34.2. Replay plus calibration is good enough for the planner.

## Limits
- One host: discrete PCIe 4.0 GPU, Zen 2 AVX2, and DDR4 at about 30.8 GB/s (CAL2). One model, at batch-1 decode.
- Two prompts of 128 tokens. Only 2 rounds per arm, with a spread of 3–9%. Every effect here (≥ 30%) is far larger than that spread, but the 10 GB C2/C3 difference (−10% on code only) is near it.
- KLD covers only 8×512 wikitext chunks, and the reference is K18 at batch 2048, not bf16. No task-level eval was run.
- Hit rates come from a cold start within one request. Multi-turn and long-context behaviour is not measured (gap G3).

## Next
- Add the planner lever: cache with CPU-share by default, and lower the share as the predicted hit rate exceeds about 90% (sweep share 0.3/0.6 at 8–10 GB).
- Add a TTFT model and a "TTFT-optimised" option (static, or a hybrid of static GPU layers plus the cache).
- Re-gate quality against the reference's own batch-shape floor in the next protocol. Add a bf16-free task check.
- Run a frozen 3-round follow-up on the 10 GB share sweep.
- **Factory rules:**
  - On discrete GPUs, use the expert cache with CPU-share for decode at every budget tested (4–10 GB), with less VRAM than static.
  - Always report TTFT next to decode.
  - KLD for a placement must run on the decode path (`-ub 1`). At large batches, CPU-resident experts are computed on the GPU.
- **Method lesson:** an absolute quality threshold must first be checked against the reference configuration's own run-to-run and batch-shape floor. A gate that the reference fails cannot judge candidates.

# D045 — E2: n-gram self-speculation ACCEPTED on static K30 (2.3× / 3.0×, text identical) and STACKS with the cache (3.9× over static on repeat), but the cache arm FAILS text identity on chat. E3: REAP-15B is a domain trade-off (code PPL +8%, wikitext ×2.84) at 6.6× decode

**Claim category:**
- E2 is a runtime trade-off: `--spec-type ngram-mod` is an existing upstream feature, workload-gated, with no change to the weights.
- E3 is a representation trade-off: a pruned model.
- **Not claimed:** lossless REAP; a general-purpose spec speed-up (chat gains nothing); task-level code quality from PPL.

**Evidence:**
- Op T-NIGHT2 (chain2) for E2 and E3.
- T-NIGHT3 (wikitext PPL) and T-NIGHT3b (code PPL).
- `artifacts/night/results.jsonl` exp `e2`, `e3`, `e3ppl`, `e3codeppl`, and the logs in `artifacts/night/logs/`. Protocol D043 E2/E3.

**Conditions:**
- E2:
  - Engines: `llama-server` on release-1 (K30) and up1 (cache arm: `--n-cpu-moe 48 --moe-cache-mib 6093 --moe-cache-cpu-share 0.9`, the best 8 GB E1 arm from D044).
  - Generation: 256 tokens, greedy, ABBA × 2.
  - Prompts: rewrite (`/no_think`, rename a variable in 3 kB of code), repeat (a 60-item list), and chat.
  - One server per arm. All three prompts run in sequence on that server.
- E3:
  - Models: 12bitmisfit REAP-15B Q4_K_M (9.75 GB, sha256 checked against the HF oid) against full Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M.
  - Engine: release-1, `llama-completion`, 128 tokens, ABBA × 2.
  - PPL on 8×512 wikitext-2 test chunks and on 16×512 chunks of `llama-model.cpp` source, used as a code corpus (local, upstream 3b4d6ab).
- Every arm ran with the host quiet; a throttled download ran, as allowed by A1.

## E2 numbers
Median decode t/s, n=2. Each pair varies by ≤ 4%, except cache-none chat (54.9–59.1).

| Placement | Prompt | spec none | ngram-mod | × | draft_n | text identical |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| static K30 (8.47 GB) | rewrite | 35.9 | 83.4 | **2.32** | 225 | yes (8ae79ff5) |
| | repeat | 35.5 | 106.8 | **3.01** | 229 | yes (39d706f1) |
| | chat | 35.4 | 35.8 | +1.1% | 0 | yes (920a5220) |
| cache C3 (8.26 GB) | rewrite | 65.7 | 100.7 | **1.53** | 225 | yes (8ae79ff5) |
| | repeat | 81.8 | 137.7 | **1.68** | 229 | yes (39d706f1) |
| | chat | 57.0 | 65.8 | +15% | 0 | **no** (43c59811 vs 67923475) |

**Verdict against the frozen rule** (all three must hold: text identical, copy-heavy ≥ 1.5×, chat within −3%; draft_n > 0 on copy-heavy prompts):
- **Static K30: ACCEPTED.** All conditions hold.
- **Cache C3: REJECTED as frozen.** Speed holds on every prompt (1.53× and 1.68× on copy-heavy, chat +15%), but chat text differs.
  - Chat made 0 drafts, so speculation never ran on that prompt. The text difference does not come from verification.
  - The most likely cause is cache history. Each server runs rewrite → repeat → chat in sequence. Speculative verify batches leave different experts resident. With CPU-share, residency decides which misses are computed on the CPU and which on the GPU, so the arithmetic, and therefore the text, depends on what ran earlier.
  - The same config gave the same text in both rounds, so the outcome is deterministic given the history.
  - The +15% chat gain is probably a warmer cache, not speculation. This is unverified.
  - This is G11 again: when CPU-share is on, the output depends on the cache's history.

**Stacking result:**
- Cache + ngram reaches 137.7 t/s on repeat, against 35.5 for static without speculation: **3.9×** at about the same 8.3–8.5 GB. Rewrite is **2.8×**.
- Speculation gains less on the cache arm (1.5–1.7×) than on static (2.3–3.0×). Verify windows touch more distinct experts (T-SPECM: about 19 per layer for 4 drafts), and on the cache those extra experts are misses. On static offload the CPU-layer cost is shared across the window.

## E3 numbers

| Model / placement | Peak MiB | Decode chat / code t/s | Prompt ms chat / code | wikitext PPL (8×512) | code PPL (16×512) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| full K30 | 8193 | 36.7 / 35.2 | 769 / 3502 | 8.820 (K18 ref) | 2.534 ± 0.097 |
| full, cache C3 8 GB (D044) | 7931 | 64.3 / 56.8 | 1100 / 5228 | (same weights) | (same weights) |
| REAP K12 | 8069 | 72.2 / 68.3 | 366 / 1190 | — | — |
| REAP K0 (all GPU) | 10213 | **242.7 / 214.5** | 200 / 421 | **25.05 (×2.84)** | 2.736 ± 0.103 (+8.0%) |

**Verdict:** a trade-off, never lossless (D043).
- REAP gives 6.6× decode and 3–8× faster TTFT with everything on the GPU, using 10.2 GB.
- At about 8 GB it gives 2× over static and +12–20% over the best cache arm, with much better TTFT.
- The cost is a large loss on general text (wikitext PPL ×2.84) against a modest loss on code (+8%; the two runs overlap within about 1σ of each other's errors).
- This matches Strata's note that its REAP "Coder" model is weaker outside code.

## Limits
- One host and one model family. Two rounds per arm.
- The spec prompts are synthetic copy tasks. The rewrite prompt is a best case.
- The code PPL corpus is llama.cpp source, which may be in either model's pretraining data. PPL is not task accuracy: no SWE/HumanEval-style eval was run.
- The REAP greedy text was not inspected for coherence.
- The E2 chat text mismatch is not yet diagnosed (rerun with chat first, or one prompt per server).

## Next
- Diagnose the cache text drift: same arm, prompt order permuted, one prompt per server.
- Add a workload-gated spec lever to the planner: enable for copy-heavy workloads only, and give it a lower expected gain on cache placements.
- Add a REAP-style pruned variant as a "domain" lever, gated on a task-level eval (lm-eval-harness or a code benchmark) before the factory may offer it.
- E4 (MTP) once the Qwen3.6 download lands.

**Factory rules:**
- N-gram speculation is free on chat and gives 2–3× on copy-heavy text with static placement, or 1.5–1.7× on cache placement. It stacks with the cache.
- With CPU-share on, greedy output depends on cache history. Use KLD and agreement checks, not text identity, to gate anything that runs on top of it.
- Pruned models need a domain-matched quality check. Wikitext alone would reject REAP-15B, and code PPL alone would accept it.

**Method lesson:** a multi-prompt server shares state across prompts. Order and history are experimental variables.

| C2 ngram | df2e7b05 | 68.1, 67.7 |

# D046 — E4: MTP speculative decoding on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ACCEPTED for copy-heavy prompts (+23–42%, text identical); chat +11–14% but text differs → INCONCLUSIVE under the frozen rule

**Claim category:** runtime trade-off. This is an existing upstream `--spec-type draft-mtp`, run on the model's own MTP (nextn) layer, and it costs +0.8–0.9 GB of VRAM.
- **Not claimed:** lossless output on chat; results for any other model; that the MTP VRAM is better spent than on GPU layers (a predicted comparison, below).

**Evidence:**
- Op T-NIGHT4 (chain3 E4: rewrite/repeat/chat) and op T-E4CHAT (chat rerun, amendment A3).
- `artifacts/night/results.jsonl` exp `e4` and `e4chat`; server logs `artifacts/night/logs/e4*-server.log`.

**Conditions:**
- Model: unsloth Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP UD-Q4_K_M, 22,663,387,424 B, sha256 0b21525e…, matching the HF LFS oid.
  - Architecture `qwen35moe`: 41 blocks, 30 Gated-DeltaNet (ssm) layers + 11 full-attention layers, and one `nextn` MTP head.
  - 256 experts with top-8 routing, plus a shared expert. Experts are 1.81 MiB each (Q4_K gate/up, Q5_K down), against 2.72 MiB for Qwen3-30B.
- Engine: up1, `llama-server`, `-fa on -c 8192 -np 1`, 256 tokens, greedy, ABBA × 2. Every arm ran with the host quiet; the download finished before E4 started.
- **Amendment A3 (post-hoc, engagement):** the frozen chat arm sent the raw chat prompt to `/completion`. Qwen3.6 emitted EOS at token 1 (0 tokens, sha of the empty string), so the arm is invalid. It was rerun with a ChatML prompt plus an empty `<think></think>` block (op T-E4CHAT).

## Numbers
Median t/s, n=2. Pairs are within 3%. Text "=" means identical to spec-none.

| K (peak MiB none / mtp3) | Prompt | none | mtp n_max 2 | mtp n_max 3 | text | accepted / drafted (mtp2, mtp3) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| K18 (13189 / 14073) | rewrite | 63.9 | 86.8 (+36%) | **90.7 (+42%)** | = | drafted 170, 191 |
| | repeat | 64.9 | 81.2 (+25%) | **86.5 (+33%)** | = | drafted 170, 191 |
| | chat (A3) | 64.9 | 72.2 (+11%) | 72.7 (+12%) | **≠** | 148/212 (70%), 167/259 (64%) |
| K30 (7623 / 8505) | rewrite | 45.8 | 59.8 (+31%) | **64.1 (+40%)** | = | drafted 170, 191 |
| | repeat | 46.2 | 57.0 (+23%) | **58.6 (+27%)** | = | drafted 170, 191 |
| | chat (A3) | 46.2 | 51.3 (+11%) | 51.9 (+12%) | **≠** | 145/220 (66%), 169/258 (66%) |

- MTP VRAM cost: +820 MiB (n_max 2) and +882 MiB (n_max 3).
- The chat text is stable within each config across rounds, but differs between none, mtp2 and mtp3. It also differs between K18-none and K30-none, so placement alone changes it too.

**Verdict against the frozen rule** (text identical to spec-none at temp 0 AND decode ≥ +10%):
- rewrite and repeat: **ACCEPTED** at both K, for n_max 2 and 3. The text is identical and the gain is +23% to +42%.
- chat: the speed condition is met (+11% to +14%), but the text condition FAILS → **INCONCLUSIVE**.
  - A verify batch of 3–4 tokens runs different kernels than single-token decode. A2 (D044) showed batch shape alone moves outputs by as much as placement does, so this divergence is the expected class of numeric difference.
  - No logprob/KLD-level check was run for MTP, so equivalence is **unproven**.

## Interpretation
- **MTP helps every prompt type, unlike n-gram speculation** (D045: 0 drafts on chat).
  - About 65–70% of drafts are accepted on chat.
  - On copy-heavy text, n-gram speculation is stronger (2.3–3.0× on Qwen3 K30 against MTP's +27–40%).
  - The two could be combined; that is not tested.
- **Is the VRAM worth it? (Predicted, not measured.)** One CPU layer on Qwen3.6 costs about 464 MiB of VRAM ((13189 − 7623) / 12). The +882 MiB for MTP would therefore buy about 1.9 more GPU layers. On the K-curve, that is roughly +4–5% decode, against +12% (chat) and +27–40% (copy) for MTP. So MTP is the better use of about 0.9 GB here.
- **Qwen3.6 decodes faster than Qwen3-30B at similar VRAM** (46 t/s at 7.6 GB against 36 at 8.2 GB), despite having more parameters. Its experts are smaller (1.81 MiB against 2.72), so each token moves fewer bytes, and only 11 of its layers keep a KV cache.
- **G17 confirmed:** `inspect_model` reports the architecture but has no state/KV accounting for the 30 DeltaNet layers.

## Limits
- One host and one model. Two rounds per arm.
- Synthetic copy prompts, and one chat prompt.
- MTP acceptance on the copy prompts was not recorded: the server returned `draft_n` only on the first pass, and the accepted count came back null.
- No logprob-equivalence test was run for chat. The matched-VRAM comparison against more GPU layers is predicted, not measured.

## Next
- Equivalence test for speculation: per-token top-1/KLD between spec-none and MTP on the chat prompt, against the batch-shape floor (D044 A2).
- Combine MTP with n-gram, and MTP with the expert cache plus CPU-share.
- Measure the matched-VRAM comparison (K28 none vs K30 mtp3).
- Extend `inspect_model` to hybrid layers (ssm state bytes and the attention-layer count).

**Factory rules:**
- For models that ship MTP heads, MTP speculation is a lever worth +11–14% on chat and +23–42% on copy-heavy text, for about 0.9 GB of VRAM.
- Prefer n-gram speculation for copy-heavy workloads; prefer MTP for general chat.
- Gate it with distributional equivalence, not text identity.

**Method lesson:** prompts must be formatted for each model. A raw prompt that works on one model can end at token 1 on another, so engagement (n > 0) must be checked per arm.

- **Engagement lesson.** Run T-SPEC1 used prompts without `/no_think`. Qwen3 then began with free-form reasoning, so no drafts were made, and the probe looked like "no effect".

- **Result: lossless, and gated by workload.** The factory should enable `ngram-mod` for copy-heavy work (editing, RAG quoting, code refactors). It costs nothing on chat.
- **Why it suits offloaded MoE.** Verifying a batch of drafted tokens reads the CPU-resident experts once per batch instead of once per token. That cuts the dominant per-token CPU byte cost (see §3).

## 2. perf (host change: `perf_event_paranoid` 4→1, runtime only; system-wide counting runs through `sudo perf`)
- Zen 2 on kernel 6.8 exposes **no `amd_df` / UMC PMU**, so true DRAM bandwidth can't be counted.
- The proxy, L1 data-cache fills from DRAM × 64 B, gave 14.9 GB/s during Qwen all-CPU-expert decode (24.4 t/s).
  - It undercounts because it misses fills made only by the L2 prefetcher.
  - IPC was 0.58 across 16 threads.
- Conclusion: **CPU bandwidth must come from a microbenchmark** (T-CAL), not counters. perf remains useful for IPC and cycles.

## 3. bpftrace uprobes on the CPU backend (sudo; target `/proc/<container pid>/root/app/libggml-cpu.so`)
Settings: Qwen K=48, all experts on the CPU, 5 s window. Output: `artifacts/bpf1/bpf.txt`.
- 5626 calls to `ggml_graph_compute`, which is **48.9 per token at 23.1 t/s**. That is one CPU split per layer.
- CPU split time was **4.45 s of 5 s (89% of wall time)**, with a median per-split time of 0.5–1 ms (mean 0.79 ms).
  - This independently confirms D039's 0.757 ms per CPU layer.
  - The remaining 11% is GPU work, handoff and sampling.
- **Pitfalls:**
  - Use `docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}'`. `pgrep` matches the host docker client.
  - The CPU MoE matmul function is a templated static (`ggml_compute_forward_mul_mat_id_tiled_one_expert<…>`). Probe the C-exported `ggml_compute_forward_mul_mat_id_tiled` or `ggml_graph_compute` instead.
- This is a zero-rebuild, low-overhead per-layer timer, and it should become a CC (`bpf_split_timer`).

## Verdict against the frozen rule
- **Speed + VRAM rule:**
  - C3 against S2 **MEETS** it at 4 GB (+30 / +34%), 6 GB (+54 / +66%), 8 GB (+76 / +65%) and 10 GB (+64 / +48%), with VRAM 2.6–6.5% below static.
  - C1 and C2 meet it only at 8 and 10 GB (+42–71%). At 4 GB they FAIL (−22 to −35%), and at 6 GB they FAIL on the chat prompt (C1 −6%, C2 +3%).
- **Quality gate, applied literally:**
  - The frozen batch-2048 run gives C3-6000 same-top 96.72%, below 97% → **FAIL**.
  - Under A2's decode path, C1, C2 and C3-2005 pass, and C3-6000 fails by 0.09 points.
  - The **reference configuration fails against itself** (96.47%) when only the batch shape changes, and so does the static K42 offload the factory already ships (96.37%).
  - The gate threshold therefore sits inside batch-shape noise and cannot separate placements. **Gate verdict: inconclusive / miscalibrated, not a pass.**
- **Post-hoc equivalence** (labelled as such): every placement falls in KLD 0.0055–0.0063 and same-top 96.4–97.3%, while the reference's own batch-shape floor is 0.0058 / 96.5%. The cache arms drift no more than static offload.

## Interpretation
1. **CPU-share is the missing lever behind D041's 4 GB loss.**
   - When misses are computed where static offload would have computed them anyway (on the CPU), while hits come from VRAM, the cache wins even at a 50% hit rate.
   - An upload-only cache wins only above roughly 70–75% hit rate. That matches D041 and T-POL.
2. **CPU-share costs speed at high hit rates.** At 10 GB (92% hit), code decode is 64.2 against 71.1 for share 0, because computing a few misses on the CPU costs more than uploading them.
3. **Prompt processing does not use the cache.** The stats cover only ubatch ≤ 8, so the TTFT penalty grows as static gains GPU layers.

On the K-curve, that is roughly +4–5% decode, against +12% (chat) and +27–40% (copy) for MTP. So MTP is the better use of about 0.9 GB here.
- **Qwen3.6 decodes faster than Qwen3-30B at similar VRAM** (46 t/s at 7.6 GB against 36 at 8.2 GB), despite having more parameters. Its experts are smaller (1.81 MiB against 2.72), so each token moves fewer bytes, and only 11 of its layers keep a KV cache.

## Limits
- One host and one model. Two rounds per arm.
- Synthetic copy prompts, and one chat prompt.
- MTP acceptance on the copy prompts was not recorded: the server returned `draft_n` only on the first pass, and the accepted count came back null.
- No logprob-equivalence test was run for chat. The matched-VRAM comparison against more GPU layers is predicted, not measured.

- Measure the matched-VRAM comparison (K28 none vs K30 mtp3).
- Extend `inspect_model` to hybrid layers (ssm state bytes and the attention-layer count).

**Factory rules:**
- For models that ship MTP heads, MTP speculation is a lever worth +11–14% on chat and +23–42% on copy-heavy text, for about 0.9 GB of VRAM.
- Prefer n-gram speculation for copy-heavy workloads; prefer MTP for general chat.
- Gate it with distributional equivalence, not text identity.

**Method lesson:** prompts must be formatted for each model. A raw prompt that works on one model can end at token 1 on another, so engagement (n > 0) must be checked per arm.

# Digest of x86 D041-D048 for the Jetson over-memory lane (2026-11-10)
Source: `origin/x86/c2-resume` (`START-HERE.md` section 0, `decisions/D041..D048`). x86 hardware is an RTX 5070 Ti (16 GB VRAM, discrete, PCIe 4.0) plus a Ryzen 7 3700X, models Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Do not pool t/s across hosts.
Jetson context: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B UD-Q4_K_XL (22.4 GB) on 7.4 GiB shared DRAM, ~570 MiB/s NVMe, `-lm mmap -ngl 99 -cmoe`, decode 1.2-1.36 t/s, disk-bound: decode ~ disk_BW / (615 MB x miss_rate); page-cache LRU hit ~62% (see Jetson D030-D033). Key structural difference: x86 "cache" is a VRAM cache over host RAM (PCIe-bound, 1.5-28 GB/s links); ours is page cache over NVMe (disk-bound, 0.57 GB/s) with no CPU/GPU split (UMA).

## D041 (indicative): upstream `--moe-cache-mib` on Qwen3-30B; ncu roofline
- Result: at 8 GB cache beats static `--n-cpu-moe` by +38% decode (51 vs 37 t/s), at 4 GB loses 34% (18 vs 28); upload-only cache needs ~70-75% hit rate. ncu: 222 GB/s, 40% of kernel time in tiny kernels.
- Jetson relevance: consistent with our Jetson D030 (upstream moe-cache loses on UMA at 64% hits). The "hit rate >= ~75% to win" threshold matches; we are below it at 62%. Nothing new to run.

## D042 (indicative): n-gram self-spec, perf, bpftrace, intake
- Result: `--spec-type ngram-mod` on Qwen3-30B K30: 2.4x (rewrite) / 3.0x (repeat), text identical, 0 drafts and +-0% on open chat. perf: no DRAM-bandwidth PMU on Zen 2. bpftrace: 0.79 ms/CPU layer. Rule: log `draft_n`/`draft_n_accepted`; benchmark bandwidth with working set >= 8x LLC.
- Jetson relevance: n-gram is a flag, no rebuild if our image's llama-server has `--spec-type` (pin 31288c9c6 is the same engine x86 used). Costs nothing on chat. Verify batch reads each expert once per batch, which is the lever for a disk-bound decoder (see analysis below). Bandwidth-microbenchmark rule applies to our fio ceiling (we already model 570 MiB/s, Jetson D031).

## D043 / D047: protocols (no results)
- Frozen overnight protocols; amendments: A1 download A/A (0.2% effect), A2 post-hoc decode-path KLD (ub 1). Rule: a batch-shape floor (KLD ~0.0058, top-1 ~96.5-97%) exists for the reference itself; gate equivalence against it, not text identity.
- Jetson relevance: adopt the same KLD floor language; our D025/D027 gates (KLD 2.7e-4) already well inside it. Add swap/page-fault monitoring to quiet checks, which our watchdog already does.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# om_run.sh — guarded over-memory engine run on jetson-arm.
# usage: om_run.sh OUTDIR IMAGE "ENV_FLAGS" TOOL ARGS...
#   e.g. om_run.sh experiments/jetson/OM/b1-r1 campaign/llamacpp:jetson-c1-p03 "" llama-bench -m /om/model.gguf -lm mmap -ngl 99 -cmoe -p 64 -n 32 -r 2
# Model dir ~/models/campaign/qwen36-35b-a3b is mounted read-only at /om. Watchdog kills ONLY this container
# when MemAvailable < OM_MIN_AVAIL_MIB (default 700) or zram swap used > OM_MAX_SWAP_MIB (default 1536).
set -u
OUT=$1; IMG=$2; ENVF=$3; TOOL=$4; shift 4
R=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.." && pwd); mkdir -p "$OUT"
NAME="om-$(date +%s)-$$"
MODELDIR=${OM_MODELDIR:-$HOME/models/campaign/qwen36-35b-a3b}
DATADIR=$HOME/models/campaign/data/wikitext/wikitext-2-raw
DP=${DOCKER_CMD_PREFIX:-}
dk(){ if [ -n "$DP" ]; then $DP "docker $*"; else docker "$@"; fi; }
printf '%s\n' "$IMG" "$ENVF" "$TOOL $*" > "$OUT/cmd.txt"
dk run -d --name "$NAME" --runtime nvidia --network none --label campaign=c1 --label om=1 $ENVF \
   -v "$MODELDIR":/om:ro -v "$DATADIR":/d:ro "$IMG" /app/$TOOL "$@" > "$OUT/container.id" || { echo "START_FAIL" > "$OUT/status"; exit 2; }
if [ -n "$DP" ]; then KILLCMD="$DP 'docker kill $NAME'"; else KILLCMD="docker kill $NAME"; fi
python3 "$R/cc/resource_observe/resource_observe.py" watchdog --min-available-mib ${OM_MIN_AVAIL_MIB:-600} \
   --max-swap-used-mib ${OM_MAX_SWAP_MIB:-2560} --max-swap-rate-mibs ${OM_MAX_SWAP_RATE:-1000} --interval-ms 250 --kill-cmd "$KILLCMD" --out "$OUT/watchdog.jsonl" & WD=$!

T0=$(date +%s.%N)
RC=$(dk wait "$NAME"); T1=$(date +%s.%N)
kill $WD $SM 2>/dev/null; wait $WD 2>/dev/null; WDRC=$?
dk logs "$NAME" > "$OUT/stdout.txt" 2> "$OUT/stderr.txt"
OOM=$(dk inspect "$NAME" --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}')
dk rm "$NAME" > /dev/null
TRIP=$(grep -c watchdog_trip "$OUT/watchdog.jsonl" 2>/dev/null); TRIP=${TRIP:-0}
python3 - "$OUT" "$RC" "$T0" "$T1" "$OOM" "$TRIP" <<'PY'

o,rc,t0,t1,oom,trip=sys.argv[1:]

  status="watchdog_killed" if int(trip) else ("ok" if rc.strip()=="0" else "failed")),open(o+"/result.json","w"),indent=1)
print(open(o+"/result.json").read())

# Campaign c1 — start here (wrap-up snapshot, 2026-11-09)
Goal (user, latest): methodology + tools for fitting a very large MoE (~500 GB weights -> 128 GB unified memory + 4 TB SSD) at similar accuracy and acceptable tokens/s. Proxy: ibm-granite/granite-3.1-1b-a400m-instruct on llama.cpp (commit 31288c9c6), RTX 5070 Ti (discrete). Every result is labelled transferable / discrete-only / prediction (D012).

## What is here
- `decisions/D001..D020` — chronological decisions with evidence (read D012-D020 first).
- `LAB-FEASIBILITY.md`, `MANAGER-DESIGN.md`, `cc-inventory.csv` — Lab Manager findings and the CC inventory (observed vs inferred).
- `bin/` — `run_op` (recorded commands), `lab` (image/job/attempt/cancel/reconcile/register/image-load/chaos), `perf_summary`, `index_evidence`, `cost_report`, `cuda_compile_check`.
- `cc/` — Build CC (`build_engine`), `engine_handoff`, `routing_trace` (patch + replay), `memory_pareto`, `hybrid_expert` (Opus harness), `q8_reuse` (UNTESTED speed patch), `gpu_budget` (memory-restriction shim, may be incomplete), tests (`pytest` in each dir).
- `evidence/*.jsonl` — raw per-agent streams (intent/started/outcome); `index/ops.jsonl` merged; `lab/jobs/*` job/attempt state + results; `experiments/` summaries; `claims/paper-claims.md` (15 source-supported claims, none tested yet).
Not committed (reproducible/bulky): llama.cpp clone (`ref/`), image archives, nsys/ncu reports, base logits, traces (regenerate with the lab tests), Codex scratch trees. Models live in `~/models/campaign` (Granite pin 0da7a48b; GGUFs bf16/Q8_0/Q4_K_M/mixE4K/3K/2K).

## Findings to trust (with caveats in the D-notes)
1. Experts are 90.4% of weight bytes; mixed precision (experts Q4_K, rest Q8_0) halves Q4_K_M's quality loss at equal memory (D013).
2. Static layer offload (`--n-cpu-moe`) cuts GPU MiB linearly but decode collapses (discrete-only, D014). Page-cache-as-expert-cache has a sharp cliff when RAM < working set (D015, contaminated by concurrent compiles).
3. Granite routing skew is real vs a uniform control (D017), mild, weaker pooled across workloads.
4. Hybrid hit/miss dispatch is bitwise-exact; the serial cost model holds (33 us/miss); perfect-overlap upper bound NOT supported (D019).
5. Engine-native `--moe-cache-mib` (LRU, upload-on-miss) is slower than no cache until ~60% coverage (job-d50c052f94). The matched static-offload comparison in the same tool did not finish (D020) — rerun `lab/tests/static1.json`.
6. Build CC: failures recorded (3 failed attempts), ccache makes patched rebuilds ~10-20 s; image identity bug found by independent observation (D016); real handoff `accepted` for the corrected record (experiments in `cc/engine_handoff/example-real5`).
7. Lab core bugs found by testing recovery per phase (D006, D020); duplicate delivery, sandbox kill, retry-as-new-attempt, stale/conflicting result rejection all demonstrated (LAB-FEASIBILITY.md, MANAGER-DESIGN.md).

## Unfinished (honest list)
Hard GPU-memory restriction shim (T-L) not compiled/tested by me; Strata concepts not yet applied end-to-end (only studied + CPU tests, and the single-layer harness); static hot-set expert placement (managed-memory idea, D018) not started; no end-to-end speed/memory result beats the baselines in a way I would call an engine win; q8_reuse patch not compiled; Opus/Codex outputs only partly reviewed; Claude-side token cost not captured.

## Host state to restore (I changed these with your approval, D002)
Stopped: container `euaaa-llm-gpu-1` (`docker start euaaa-llm-gpu-1`) and user unit Sunshine (`systemctl --user start app-dev.lizardbyte.app.Sunshine.service`). GPU lock removed (D007). No host-wide driver/profiling change was made. Campaign containers are labelled `campaign=c1` (none should be running).

## Resume
`pip`-free: python3 stdlib + PyYAML/pytest. Re-create the lab: `bin/lab image add llamacpp-31288c9 ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp@sha256:395d01bb47eb23d5e967129c6ebd2b5969365401621e16dd3db33e50fa7462e3`; build an engine: `python3 cc/build_engine/build_engine.py --source <llama.cpp> --commit 31288c9c6 [--patch P] [--extra-target T] --tag X --out builds/results/Y` (needs BASE_RUNTIME digest, see cc/build_engine/README.md).

## Jetson lane (jetson-arm, branch jetson/c1) — added 2026-11-10
Read `handoff/jetson-checkpoint-1.md`, `experiments/jetson/SUMMARY.md`, decisions D021–D025. Headline: **first measured full-engine gain** — on Orin Nano (sm_87, bf16, batch-1 decode) the env-gated component `cc/moe_dispatch_sm87` (`GGML_CUDA_J_MMF_IDS=1`) raises decode 50.3 → 60.1 t/s (+19%) with mean KLD 2.7e-4 (D025). # D021 — Jetson lane start: per-host evidence streams; run_op non-UTF-8 echo crash (2026-11-09, host jetson-arm)
- Context: the Jetson clone at f0e676b (== origin/main) ran the same `.claude/settings.json` hook, which appended Jetson events to the git-tracked `evidence/claude-code.jsonl` — host conflation and guaranteed merge conflicts with x86.
- Change: `bin/cc_hook` and `bin/run_op` read host id from untracked `~/.config/siminfeng/host_id`; any host other than `x86-main` (or unset, = legacy x86 behaviour unchanged) writes to `evidence/<host_id>/`. Records carry `host_id`. The 4 Jetson lines already appended were moved to `evidence/jetson-arm/claude-code.jsonl`.
- Fixture run (ops in evidence/jetson-arm/opus-jetson.jsonl, task J-EV1): success, nonzero exit, non-UTF-8 stdout, background child (captured as `survivors`), timeout (status=timeout) all recorded.
- Defect found: run_op recorded the non-UTF-8 outcome correctly but then crashed echoing stdout as text, returning exit 1 for a command that exited 0 (same class as D020's lab runner bug, different file). Fix: echo raw bytes via `sys.stdout.buffer`. Regression re-run: bytes `\xff\xfe bad` passed through, rc=0.
- Limits: the hook still logs full tool payloads (no secret redaction beyond what existed); `survivors` lists descendants only at outcome time.
- x86 action requested: none required (default unchanged); adopt `evidence/<host>/` for new hosts.
# D022 — Jetson container path qualified; GPU visibility must be explicit (2026-11-09, jetson-arm)
- Owner action (user-authorized): docker.io 29.1.3, ccache 4.5.1, `nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker` (wrote /etc/docker/daemon.json with `nvidia` runtime), muk added to group docker (current session uses `sg docker -c`). No JetPack/driver/nvpmodel change.
- Test: host-compiled sm_87 CUDA smoke (`cc/smoke/cuda_smoke.cu`, nvcc 12.6, cudart static) bind-mounted read-only into `ubuntu:22.04@sha256:076e7bf8…`, `--network none`.
  - `--runtime nvidia` alone: exit 1, "CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version" (misleading: driver libs simply not injected).
  - `--runtime nvidia -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all -e NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=all`: PASS, Orin CC 8.7, integrated=1, 0/1024 mismatches.
- Consequence for the job/launch contract: on Jetson the GPU request is the env pair + runtime, not `--gpus`; a missing request yields a CUDA error that looks like a driver mismatch. Admission/launch must set it explicitly and the result classifier must not label this "driver incompatible". l4t base images set these env vars by default; generic arm64 images do not.
- Own error noted: an earlier check piped through `tail`, which masked the exit status; exit codes must come from run_op records, not pipelines.
# D023 — llama.cpp auto-fit context consumes Jetson shared DRAM; pin -c in test policy (2026-11-10, jetson-arm)
- Observation: lab test `gen_smoke` (no -c; 24 tokens) on jetson-c1 picked `n_ctx = 45568` (stderr of lab/jobs/job-4433960e61/att-1). Shared-DRAM high-water 6568 MiB vs 1634 MiB baseline (tegrastats RAM used, scope system-shared-dram) on a 7607 MiB device; earlier gen_smoke 5647 MiB. 
- Cause (source-supported): the fit logic sizes context from device free memory (cudaMemGetInfo / ggml_backend_cuda_get_available_uma_memory — the log prints "final available_memory_kb"); on Tegra this is system-available DRAM, so engine residency competes with OS/controller/agent headroom. On x86 the same default only consumes VRAM.
- Decision: Jetson test policies pin context explicitly. Added `lab/tests/jetson.json` (`gen_smoke_c2k`, `ppl2` unchanged since it already passes -c 512). x86's `lab/tests/quality.json` untouched (changing it would change x86 test identity) — x86 owner to decide whether gen_smoke should pin -c too, since its result also depends on free VRAM.
- Applicability rule for Manager/test CCs: on shared-memory platforms any engine default derived from "free device memory" is a host-memory policy; admission must declare it (memory.domain: shared-dram) and the test policy must fix it. A cudaMemGetInfo-interposing budget (x86 cc/gpu_budget, T-L) is the natural cap here — untested on Jetson.
- Also fixed: J-T4b treated J-T4-era admission records without a hash as "mismatch"; now "recorded-unhashed (pre-J-T4b)" and still re-checked (old rejected job still refused).
# D024 — Build CC outputs nearly pushed; history rewritten before publication (2026-11-10, jetson-arm, Opus own error)
- What happened: `git add campaign/cc/build_engine` (commit d1100a8) captured results/jetson-c1/ while that build was still running (in-progress build/ tree + staging snapshot), and a later `git add campaign` (ae82973) captured the running candidate build jetson-c1-j3 plus the finished 1.39 GB engine-image.docker.tar. .gitignore covered only builds/results/*, not cc/build_engine/results/*.
- Detected at `git push` (upload stalled); push killed; `git ls-remote` confirmed no jetson/* ref on origin, so nothing was published.
- Fix: the 4 unpushed local commits after f0e676b were rewritten with `git filter-branch --index-filter` from a clean side worktree (main worktree held a running build), dropping results/*/build, staging-*, engine-image.docker.tar, builds/jetson-native, the nsys .sqlite. Largest object now 3 MB. Commit messages/order preserved; old local SHAs c9e7a29.. superseded (c9e7a29 itself unchanged).
- Rules added: .gitignore for cc/build_engine/results/*/{build,staging-*,engine-image.docker.tar}; never stage a directory a running worker/build writes to (also stated in the campaign prompt — violated here); check `git diff --cached --stat` before commit.
- Retained on disk only (not git): image archives (identity via build-record sha256), native build trees.
# D025 — Full-engine decode gain on Jetson: route bf16 MoE gate/up (batch 1) to MMF instead of fused MMVF (2026-11-10, jetson-arm)
Claim category: **full-engine code gain (local to jetson-arm, sm_87, bf16 Granite-3.1-1b-a400m, batch-1 decode)**. Not transferred to x86 (untested there).
- Candidate: llama.cpp 31288c9c6 + cc/moe_dispatch_sm87/patches/combined-01-02.patch (sha256 9cd5745b…), env-gated, default = upstream. Image campaign/llamacpp:jetson-c1-j3 (Build CC record cc/build_engine/results/jetson-c1-j3/build-record.json, archive b730a81f…). Same image for all arms → only the env switch differs.
- Mechanism (J-T3 source analysis + independent review): the fused gate/up+GLU pattern asks the MMVF heuristic ("src0 rows ≤ 512" → vector kernel, 256 threads, F32 activations); standalone NVIDIA bf16 MUL_MAT_ID uses MMF (tensor-core MMA). `GGML_CUDA_J_MMF_IDS=1` declines that fusion on cc 870 when MMF is eligible. nsys (J-P002): gate/up per layer-token 385 µs fused MMVF → 2×131 µs MMF (+GLU kernel); kernel count +3120/64 tok (nothing skipped); GPU time −8.8% under tracing.
- Speed (J-E005, counterbalanced base,P1,P2,F,F,P2,P1,base; tg128 r5; steady = samples 2-5): base 50.48/50.20, **P1 60.07/60.05 (+19.3%)**, P2 (128-thread MMVF) 59.56/59.30 (+18.0%), all-fusion-off 57.34/57.33 (+13.9%). Depth 1024: base 48.7/48.6 → P1 57.8/57.8 (+19%). Prefill pp512 unchanged (1105–1149 both arms, base inert = same as unpatched image 50.4).
- Quality: batch-512 ppl20 identical (path not exercised there — prefill unaffected by design). Decode path (perplexity -ub 1, c128 x 8): base 8.0332, P1 8.0163, P2 8.0358. KL vs saved base logits: A/A mean ≈0 (max 6e-5 storage floor); **P1 mean KLD 2.7e-4, 99% 4.2e-3, max 9.1e-3, top-1 99.6%**; P2 2.0e-4, top-1 99.2%. For scale x86 Q8_0 vs bf16: 3.4e-3, 97.0% (D010). 64-token greedy text byte-identical for all arms.
- Precision note: MMF rounds F32 activations to bf16 before MMA (mmf.cuh:202-212) — a small numerics change, same class the down-projection already has in the base. Not "bit-exact"; passes the D005 smoke gate and a token-level check.
- Limits: one host, one model/precision, batch 1 decode, MAXN_SUPER with dynamic GPU devfreq (not pinned); only 2 runs per arm (each 5 reps) — effect (≈+10 t/s) ≫ A/A spread (≤0.3 t/s). Unknown on quantized weights (Q8_0/Q4 take MMVQ, different path), on multi-sequence decode, on other cc.
- Next discriminating experiment (x86): drop the `cc == 870` guard (or add cc 1200) and run the same A/B on the 5070 Ti — whether discrete Blackwell has the same MMVF-vs-MMF gap is unknown.
# D026 — Build CC rebuilds now hit ccache (22x faster); binaries are NOT bit-reproducible across attempts (2026-11-10, jetson-arm)
- ccache (J-T1b fix: CCACHE_BASEDIR=staging source, NOHASHDIR, compilercheck=content, build dir inside base): build jetson-c1-p01 (patch 01) populated cache (0/360 hits); baseline rebuild jetson-c1-rebuild: 348 hits / 360, wall 141 s vs 3154 s for the original jetson-c1 (same inputs). .cu objects are cached (most compile time is nvcc).
- Reproducibility: jetson-c1 vs jetson-c1-rebuild (identical commit, no patch, same toolchain/flags/base digest): all 7 tool hashes and all app_files differ. Likely cause: embedded build paths (`strings` finds a `staging-…` path in libllama-common of the rebuild; original used a different random staging dir and a different build-dir layout). Functional check: ppl2 = 7.5479 ± 0.84898 on both (identical to 4 decimals).
- Consequences: (1) release identity = source commit + patch sha + toolchain + base digest + build record + archive sha; binary hash equality must NOT be used to claim "same build" or to deduplicate; (2) Manager/handoff should compare records + functional checks; (3) a deterministic staging path (or -ffile-prefix-map / -fdebug-prefix-map) would be needed for bit-reproducibility — not attempted (x86 decides if needed).

## Upstream cf34d311 moe-cache (llama-completion, 800-char wiki prompt, -n 64, -lm mmap -ngl 99 -cmoe) — up-20261110-0436 (clean) + upv-20261110-0519 (with -lv 4 counters; TIMING CONTAMINATED: a CPU-heavy replay simulation ran at nice 0 for part of it)
| config | decode t/s (clean / upv) | decode hit rate | uploaded |
|---|---|---|---|
| no cache | 1.18, 1.19 / 1.21, 1.16 | — | — |
| cache 512 MiB | – / 0.98 | 37.7% | 23.0 GB |
| cache 1024 MiB | 0.91 / – | – | – |
| cache 2048 MiB | 0.98 / 0.98 | **64.0%** | 13.8 GB |
| 2048 + cpu-share 0.5 | 1.13 / – | – | – |

Interpretation: the cache achieves real hit rates (64% at 2 GiB ≈ 10% of experts — consistent with replay-sim LRU locality) yet decode is 17–23% slower than no cache. On UMA every miss still page-faults from NVMe AND is then copied into a separate device bank (~215 MB/token of copies at 2 GiB) while the bank's DRAM is subtracted from the page cache that serves misses. On discrete GPUs the upload buys PCIe-free GPU compute; on unified memory it is pure overhead + double residency. CPU-share (misses computed on CPU in place) recovers most of the loss but not more.
## Design consequence (hypothesis to test)
For unified-memory targets: do not copy experts into a separate cache. Keep each byte once (page cache / pinned host memory), let the GPU read hot experts in place (zero-copy mapped memory; Orin: pageableMemoryAccess=0, so pages must be registered/pinned), and spend DRAM on hit rate. Candidates: J-OM5 dedupe (release page-cache copy after upload) and a zero-copy hot set (J-OM6). Pinned vs upstream same-tool comparison pending (cmp sweep).
# D031 — Upstream llama.cpp +7% over-memory decode; NVMe is a 570 MiB/s budget drive; first-order decode model (2026-11-10, jetson-arm)
## Engine version (dependency update, not our code) — experiments/jetson/OM/cmp-20261110-0534

Caveat: runs partly overlapped a nice-19 replay simulation; pin arms show larger spread. Category: engine-version change (upstream moe/mmq/graph work between Oct 18 and Nov 8), local to Jetson.
## NVMe ceiling (fio on the model file, O_DIRECT, read-only) — experiments/jetson/OM/fio
rand4k qd1 19.6 MiB/s (181 µs) · rand4k qd32 74 MiB/s · rand128k qd8 475 · rand576k qd1 416 · rand576k qd8 536 · rand2m qd4 543 · seq1m qd8 573 MiB/s · 576k psync×4 535.
PCIe link is Gen3 x4 (8 GT/s, x4 — /sys current_link_*), so the limit is the drive: "X15 Lite SSD 128GB" (budget, small capacity). max_hw_sectors 128 KiB, read_ahead 128 KiB. The 825 MiB/s peak seen in D029 telemetry is likely a sampling-interval artefact (to verify).
## First-order model (prediction tool, validated loosely)
decode_tps ≈ disk_BW / (routed_expert_bytes_per_token × miss_rate). With 615 MB/token (layout) and 570 MiB/s: miss_rate 1.0 → ~1.0 t/s; measured 1.27–1.36 → implied miss ≈ 0.70–0.75 (page cache acting as a ~30% hit cache). Replay LRU at 1300–2048 expert slots (2.5–3.9 GB): miss 0.38–0.27 → predicted 2.4–3.4 t/s if the cache holds bytes ONCE and misses read at full drive bandwidth. Our UMA components (dedupe / direct-fill) target exactly that gap. Belady bound at 2048: miss 0.12 → ~7.8 t/s (prefetch headroom).
## Consequences
- For the 128 GB unified + 4 TB SSD target, SSD read bandwidth and access granularity are first-order design inputs; record drive model + fio matrix in every host inventory (added to NEEDS-MAP).
- Page-fault reads (≈20 KB) vs expert-sized reads (576 KB qd8 = 536 MiB/s) matter less on this drive than on a fast NVMe (both near the ceiling); on fast drives large aligned reads should matter more — x86 to measure.

# D033 — Readahead wastes 57% of NVMe bytes but disabling it halves speed: the drive is IOPS-bound for small reads (2026-11-10, jetson-arm)
Patch cc/mmap_advice/patches/01-mmap-advice-random.patch (env LLAMA_MMAP_ADVICE=random: no FADV_SEQUENTIAL, no WILLNEED prefetch, MADV_RANDOM on the mapping), image jetson-up1108-ra (152 s build). llama-completion p1, -n 64, -lm mmap -ngl 99 -cmoe. experiments/jetson/OM/ra-20261110-0635, order base,rand,rand,base; switch verified active by log line (advice_log=1 only in rand arms).
| arm | prompt t/s | decode t/s | NVMe read/run | avg KiB per IO | output |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| base-a / base-b | 5.68 / 5.69 | 1.19 / 1.20 | 56.6 / 55.7 GiB | 93 / 95 | 7a1541… |
| random-a / random-b | 1.42 / 1.47 | 0.56 / 0.59 | 24.1 / 23.5 GiB | 4 / 4 | 7a1541… (identical) |
Interpretation:
- ~57% of the bytes the default reads are readahead the computation never uses ("H-RA" readahead pollution: confirmed as byte waste).
- But without readahead every fault is a 4 KiB random read; the drive does ~20 MiB/s at 4K qd1 (D031 fio) → speed halves. The waste was buying IO size. Both extremes are wrong.
- Target design (component J-OM7): MADV_RANDOM on expert tensors + router-informed exact prefetch: when a layer's top-k ids are known, madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) exactly those experts' gate/up/down byte ranges (≈1.9 MB/expert, contiguous slices) so the kernel issues large async reads for useful bytes only. Expected: ~24 GiB useful at expert-sized IO (fio 576K qd8 ≈ 536 MiB/s) ≈ 46 s IO vs 56 GiB at ~400 MiB/s ≈ 140 s → up to ~2x decode if IO dominates (prediction).
- Methodology: "zero-code switch" (--numa) was inert (D032 addendum); the real switch needed a log line to prove it applied.

- Designs ARE model×hardware specific (D027: unfuse helps bf16/q4_K, hurts q8_0 on Orin). So the factory's product is: components with declared applicability + cheap per-platform qualification screens + a reproducible measurement method — not one universal engine config.

## 1. Tools (operations agents invoke)
| Need | Status | Notes / evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Build CC (identified source+patch → native image + record; amd64 & Jetson) | HAVE | D016, J-T1/J-T1b; ccache 22x (D026). Gap: binaries not bit-reproducible (D026) → identity by record+functional check; add `-ffile-prefix-map` NEXT |
| Model identity (`gguf_manifest`: tensor-data hash vs metadata) | HAVE | J-E001 file sha differs from x86; tensor compare pending x86 |
| Quantize/representation recipes as recorded ops | HAVE | J-E006 via Build CC `--extra-target llama-quantize` |
| Kernel microbench screen (`test-backend-ops perf -o MUL_MAT_ID` per type/shape/fusion) | **NOW** | would have found D027's per-type rule in minutes; required before porting dispatch rules to x86/other boards |
| Expert routing trace capture (per token/layer, prompt vs generated) | **NOW** | x86 cc/routing_trace patch exists (Granite); must qualify on qwen35moe + record completeness (Strata trace reader silently dropped truncated tails) |
| Expert-cache replay simulator (LRU/LFU/decay/static/Belady, generic L×E) | NOW (J-OM2 running) | Strata pattern, hardcoded 48×512 there |
| Static hot-set placement generator (profile → `-ot` tensor-override args / cache profile) | **NOW** | turns a routing profile into an engine placement; needs per-expert tensor split support check in llama.cpp (experts are fused 3-D tensors → may need a component) |
| Result acceptance / perf_summary with A/A-aware gate | NEXT | adopt Strata autotune rule: median per-round ratio > max(3%, 2×A/A gap, 2×drift); byte-identical outputs auto-accept, else KL gate |
| CUDA register-spill / static checks in Build gate | NEXT | Strata tools/check_cuda_spills.py pattern |
| Launch identity (effective argv/env/config hashed per attempt) | NEXT | Strata serve/launch_identity.py pattern; our run_op records argv, not engine-effective config |
| nvpmodel/clock pinning helper | NEXT (needs owner sudo authorization) | GPU devfreq 306–1020 MHz unpinned; we rely on warm-up discard + A/B interleave |

## 2. Profiling / tracing / observability
| Need | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| nsys timeline + kernel inventory (sm_87, sm_120) | HAVE | J-P001..P003; gotcha: stale .sqlite → 0-byte CSV, use `--force-export=true` |
| ncu counters on Jetson | NO (for now) | RmProfilingAdminOnly=1; needs root — use derived bytes/time instead (done) |
| Resource telemetry with scopes (tegrastats/proc/cgroup/sysfs/nvml) | HAVE | cc/resource_observe; never sum scopes; unavailable-with-reason |
| I/O + fault telemetry (vmstat majfault/refault, NVMe MiB/s, per-pid/cgroup faults, io.stat) | **NOW** (J-OM1 running) | over-memory runs are I/O bound; current telemetry blind to it |
| Safety watchdog (MemAvailable/swap trip → kill only the owned run) | **NOW** (J-OM1) | required before any oversubscription run on an 8 GB host |
| Quality: ppl smoke + paired KL + **decode-path (ub=1) KL** | HAVE | methodology counterexample J-E005: batch-512 ppl blind to decode kernels |
| Quality reference when the full model cannot be resident | NOW | same GGUF, placement-invariant reference run (slow but exact) + a resident smaller-quant reference; KL top-k file for 20 GiB model must be bounded (c128 × few chunks) |
| Engine-internal counters (cache hit/miss, bytes uploaded, stall time) | NOW | llama.cpp `--moe-cache-mib` exists (LRU upload-on-miss) — need its counters exposed or an nsys NVTX range |

## 3. Methodologies (agent procedures / decision rules)
| Rule | Status |
|---|---|
| Counterbalanced ABBA/ABAB, ≥2 runs/arm, discard first sample, steady mean | HAVE (J-E004/5/7) |
| A/A before trusting a delta; same image, env-switch arms (isolates code path) | HAVE |
| Classify every result (code gain / placement / representation / memory-fit / screen / prediction) | HAVE |
| Decode-only changes need ub=1 KL; prefill unaffected must be shown | HAVE |
| Shared-memory hosts: pin `-c`; never trust free-memory-derived engine defaults (D023); `-lm auto` disables mmap on Orin iGPU (llama-model.cpp:1590, ggml-cuda.cu:5473) → over-memory baseline must say `-lm mmap` | HAVE (new) |
| Fair "default" baseline for over-memory = what a competent user runs (`-lm mmap`, `-cmoe`/`-ncmoe N`, `--moe-cache-mib`), not the broken auto default; report the auto default's failure separately | NOW |
| Benchmark protocol IDs + corpus sha in every result; `nonconforming` status; cache-hit prompt check | NEXT (Strata BENCHMARK_PROTOCOL.md) |
| "Measured on:" line before every number; contract doc per component | NEXT (Strata docs style) |
| Per-platform applicability table per component (type × cc × batch) | HAVE (cc/moe_dispatch_sm87) |

## 4. Build tools / dependency management
| Need | Status | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Docker + Buildx (amd64), host-native JetPack builder + l4t runtime image (Jetson) | HAVE | one CC, two native targets |
| ccache with stable basedir | HAVE | D026 |
| Python deps: stdlib-first; venv for heavy converters (torch/transformers) | HAVE | ~/venvs/convert; system numpy broken on Jetson |
| Pinned upstream sources (llama.cpp 31288c9c6, Strata 504b1433 ref-only) | HAVE | record pins in decisions |
| Nix | NO | Strata's flake is x86_64-only; JetPack is apt/L4T-bound |
| Multi-platform registry index | NEXT | only after both native outputs + a registry exist |

## 5. Code fragments / functional modules (component CCs)
| Component | Status |
|---|---|
| moe-gateup-unfuse by type (patch 03) | HAVE (Orin qualified; x86 untested) |
| Static hot-expert placement (resident hot set + streamed cold experts) | **NOW** — main candidate for "better than default" over-memory |
| Router-aware next-layer prefetch / async read of cold experts (madvise WILLNEED / readahead on mmap ranges) | NEXT — needs trace + I/O telemetry first |
| Expert tiering policy (LFU-decay swap) à la Strata exchange rotation | NEXT — simulator first (J-OM2) |
| gpu_budget shim (cudaMemGetInfo/cudaMalloc cap) | NEXT on Jetson — natural cap for D023; x86 X3 owns qualification |
| x86 hybrid hit/miss dispatch (D019) | x86-owned; Jetson relevance low (no PCIe; CPU weak: 6×A78AE) |

## 6. Isolation / lab / Manager
| Need | Status |
|---|---|
| Admission by declared host capabilities; rejected/needs_information; hashed admission | HAVE (Jetson live) |
| Sandbox kill / runner death / reconcile / new attempt | HAVE (Jetson live) |
| Memory-cap isolation for over-memory tests (cgroup memory.max on container: charges page cache; does it charge nvmap/CUDA? unknown) | **NOW** — qualify with a bounded test before the 20 GiB runs |
| External evidence endpoint off-host | NEXT (git-only today; protects against sandbox loss only) |
| Storage admission (model files 20+ GiB, page cache effects, free-disk check) | NOW (62 GB free; 22 GB model) |
| GPU slot per host; no concurrent builds during timing windows | HAVE (rule), not enforced by code |

# J-SPEC1 — window-union replay: does speculative decoding help a disk-bound over-memory decoder?
Owner: Codex (bounded, CPU-only; no GPU, no docker, no builds, no network). Branch: work in tree, do not commit.
## Inputs
- Routing traces (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 40 layers x 256 experts, top-8): experiments/jetson/OM/trace-20261110-0504/{chat,code,math,wiki}/routing.jsonl (format: cc/routing_trace/README.md).
- Simulator: cc/expert_replay/expert_replay.py (+ tests). Per-expert bytes 1,900,544 (589,824+589,824+720,896).
- x86 context: `git show origin/x86/c2-resume:campaign/research/x86-c2-digest.md` is NOT there; read campaign/research/x86-c2-digest.md (ours) for T-SPECM/MTP numbers.
## Task
Add a `specwin` subcommand to expert_replay.py: for decode tokens only, group consecutive tokens into verify windows of size W (W=1,2,3,4,6,8), take the union of experts per layer per window, and replay that union stream through the existing cache policies (LRU, Belady) at capacities 650/1300/2600 slots (expert-slot = 1,900,544 B).
