versioned release; improved from telemetry and replay
Judged by
correct outputs, latency, failure rate

Skill

Is
A procedure: how to carry out a task using tools.
Test
“Does it say how to do X?”
Lifecycle
revised when runs show agents stumbling (turns, repairs)
Judged by
task success and turns per task in telemetry

Method

Is
Decision rules: what counts as better, how to measure, when to stop.
Test
“Does it say how to judge X?”
Lifecycle
changed rarely; a change means a new contract revision
Judged by
the operator
Fixed core: deliberately not CCs. The evidence store, controller, Manager with its frozen correctness contract, jobq wrapper, lab runner, telemetry writer and monitor (about 4.5k lines of Python). These are what the agent must not be able to change. Because they sit outside the CC layer, “output identical” and “1.13×” can be trusted.

Where each kind sits in the loop

Today the agent enters at “component”: we hand it finished patches. The observe and hypothesize stages are the gap. With them filled, the agent can propose its own components.

Show

Components

Ship in the engine. All of them carry depends_on, switches that default to off, engagement checks, a hypothesis, a correctness obligation and a rollback.

engine.components

mmap_advice

built
run 4: 0.49× → dormant

Patch 01. Sets madvise(MADV_RANDOM) on the model mapping, so the kernel stops sequential readahead when sparse expert pages are touched.

Switch
LLAMA_MMAP_ADVICE=random; any other value keeps default advice
Depends on
nothing; the root of the stack
Engagement
stderr llama_mmap: LLAMA_MMAP_ADVICE=random
Evidence
0.49× (893.7 vs 1,894 ms/token in run 3; same order in run 4), A/A 0.06, output identical. On this NVMe, readahead was helping: cutting it doubles per-token time.
Why dormant
router_prefetch, expert_fill and expert_pregate all patch the code it adds. The agent kept the commit with the switch off and checked needed_by against the dependency graph. The component's own rejection stands.
engine.components

router_prefetch

built
run 4: 0.62× → dormant

Patch 02. Hooks the CPU consumer of the MoE router output and issues MADV_WILLNEED on the selected experts' host ranges before they are read. An optional mode guesses that the next layer will use the same expert IDs.

Switches
LLAMA_EXPERT_PREFETCH=1, LLAMA_EXPERT_PREFETCH_NEXT=0|1
Depends on
mmap_advice (source)
Engagement
expert_prefetch: CPU host-consumer hook enabled; advise calls=N with N > 0
Evidence
0.62×, A/A 0.09, output identical. Advice is asynchronous and too late: the reads still block at compute time.
Lesson
It led to expert_fill: do the read yourself, in parallel, instead of asking the kernel to.
engine.components

expert_fill

built
run 4: 1.11× → keep

Patches 03–05 (about 670 changed lines). Before a node computes, a worker pool reads the routed experts' pages that aren't yet resident, using buffered parallel pread in 2 MiB chunks. The faults become sequential large reads, and the compute thread no longer stalls in D-state.

Switches
LLAMA_EXPERT_FILL=1, _THREADS=16 (1..64), _CHUNK_KIB=2048, _RANDOM=decode, _MAX_TOKENS=1, _DIAG, _POPULATE
Depends on
mmap_advice, router_prefetch (source)
Engagement
expert_fill: active, random advice applied at decode, stats calls=N with N > 0
Evidence
1.11×, A/A 0.03, output identical. Page faults per token fall from about 5,000 to about 490 (J-OM12/13 thread sampler).
engine.components

expert_pregate

built
run 4: 1.13× → keep

Patches 06–08 (about 840 changed lines). Predicts the next layer's top-K experts from the current hidden state (recall@8 0.81) and schedules bounded asynchronous fills ahead of demand. Patch 08 adds strict validation of every LLAMA_EXPERT_* variable, plus the expert_config: effective … line that the inspector checks.

Switches
LLAMA_EXPERT_PREGATE=1, _K=8 (1..32), _ORDER=after|before, _MAX_INFLIGHT=4 (1..64), _LOOKAHEAD=1 (1..2)
Depends on
expert_fill
Engagement
expert_pregate: active; effective … pregate=1; stats predictions=N with N > 0
Evidence
1.13× on top of fill (831 → 739 ms/token), A/A 0.016, output identical. Lookahead 2 was measured worse (J-OM11).
engine.components

thread_names

built
run 4: 1.01× → reverted (misjudged)

Patch 09 (6 lines). Names the fill workers xfill-N, so the thread sampler can attribute D-state and page faults to them. It is an observability component and has no speed hypothesis.

Switch
none; always on when built
Depends on
expert_fill, expert_pregate (applies to the worker context from patch 06)
Engagement
thread sampler sees threads matching ^xfill-[0-9]+$
Evidence
1.01×, gate not_measured, output identical, engagement passed. The agent reverted it because the only method it had was a speed method.
Fix
Judge it by methodology_observability (below): engaged, overhead within noise, signal present → keep.
engine.tuning

runtime_tuning

new · material only
expected ≈1.28× (measured by hand)

A config component: no patch, only shipped defaults for runtime knobs, each with its safe range and known interactions. The agent never tried -t 4 because no CC offered it. Anything that isn't a CC doesn't exist for the agent.

Knobs
-t CPU threads; -b/-ub batch sizes; -c; -ngl, -cmoe, -ot offload split; fill threads and chunk size (taken from expert_fill's env_ranges)
Evidence
J-OM13: factory engine 711.4 ms/token, with -t 4 659.3 (1.18× → 1.28× vs stock). J-OM12: -t 6 704.8, worse than -t 4.
Gate
methodology_ab, one knob per experiment; outputs must stay byte-identical. Knobs that can change output (KV type) belong in kv_quant.
Needs
lab_client.ab_submit to accept extra_argv per arm; abrun already supports it
engine.tuning

kv_quant

new · config
changes outputs → accuracy gate

KV cache in q8_0 (-ctk/-ctv q8_0), plus the micro-batch size, to free memory for weights or context. Kept apart from runtime_tuning because it changes outputs, so byte-identical can't be its gate.

Evidence
Model ladder: Qwen3.5-9B full GPU with kvq8 and ub128 runs at 10.6 tok/s
Gate
methodology_accuracy (non-inferiority on a frozen item set) plus a speed A/B

moe_cache

repackage
never built

A profile-pinned MoE expert cache: pin the most-routed experts (from a profile) in a fixed GPU or host budget. --moe-cache-mib 1024 --moe-cache-profile p.json --moe-cache-pin-frac 0.75.

Source
siminfeng/cc/moe_cache_profile; standalone patch at cf34d311, the factory's own base. Packaging it is just a component.yaml.

repackage + rebase
for Q8_0 models

Reuses one activation quantisation across consecutive Q8_0 mat-vec calls on the same input tensor. It has a strict hit rule: same tensor, pointer, type, dimensions, strides and CUDA stream.

Source

repackage + rebase
for BF16 MoE

Fixes a kernel-selection asymmetry on sm_87. The fused gate/up+GLU path asks the MMVF heuristic while MUL_MAT_ID asks MMF, so BF16 expert matmuls take a slow kernel during decode.

Source
siminfeng/cc/moe_dispatch_sm87 (analysis and patches at 31288c9c); kernel_screen can check it in isolation first

BF16 MoE models (Granite-class); low priority for Q4 Qwen

model_choice

new · artifact
where 2–10 tok/s is met

The model and quant file is part of the product. The agent proposes, for example, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B UD-Q4_K_XL, Qwen3.5-9B or Gemma-4-E4B. The component pins the file's sha256, size and recommended run mode.

Evidence
35B: 1.52 tok/s best, 62.9% on MMLU-Pro70. 9B: 10.6 tok/s. Gemma-4-E4B: 17.8 tok/s.
Gate
methodology_ladder: must fit, must meet the speed floor, then highest accuracy
Needs

Tools

Native capabilities behind grants. Each call returns in seconds; long work becomes a durable job that outlives the agent's turn.

factory.tools

builder

built
7 builds in run 4, ~130 s each

Turns a clean commit in the agent's own checkout into a container image, as a durable jobq build job.

Calls
submit (idempotency key), status, cancel, result
Guarantees
Source must be clean, with HEAD equal to the commit. The same key with a different request conflicts. Prep records the toolchain (nvcc, cmake, docker), the pinned l4t-cuda base digest, ccache and disk. It writes a schema-2 build record (source tree, patch sha, image ID). Staging trees are pruned after success.
Wraps
siminfeng/cc/build_engine
factory.tools

engine_inspector

built
caught K=48 in the demo

Checks source, binary and runtime config before GPU time is spent.

Calls
inspect: commit, dirty state, applied patches, host facts. preflight: are the flags supported by this image's binary (cached by image ID, not tag)? verify_effective_config: runs the binary briefly, parses expert_config: effective and any LLAMA_* line, and compares them with the request.
Wraps
siminfeng/cc/abrun/preflight.py and the patch 08 config line
factory.tools

lab_client

built
9 lab jobs, all output-identical

Runs real inference through the deterministic Manager. The agent never touches the GPU directly.

Calls
submit / status / cancel / result for one contract run; ab_submit / ab_status / ab_result for a full ABBA experiment in one gpu job
Guarantees
Admits only an image whose ID matches a build receipt and targets jetson-orin. The model is mounted read-only. The workload is fixed by the contract. Watchdog floor 600 MiB. Results go through an idempotent spool. Outcomes are distinct: candidate_failed, measurement_failed, wrong_target, bad_digest, cancelled.
Returns
gate, ratio, aa_gap, output_class, per-arm ms/token, evaluation ID
Wraps
cc/om_run, cc/abrun, cc/thread_sampler, cc/resource_observe/io_watchdog
factory.tools

evidence

built
most-called capability

The task's shared memory: observations, artifacts, attempts, evaluations and versioned decisions.

Calls
query (filters, cursor, limit ≤ 50), read (full record plus a 64 KiB verified preview), publish (a decision revision, compare-and-swap on expected_rev)
Guarantees
Task-scoped; cross-task reads need an explicit grant. Append-only. The same artifact ID with different bytes is rejected. No acknowledgement before fsync and commit.
Telemetry
Every call emits cc.call with duration_ms, bytes and task evidence size. A good first target for an RSI pass.

Attaches to a lab run and reports where time goes. Today the agent only sees ms/token, so it can rank components but not explain them.

Captures routed expert IDs and weights per token and layer through llama.cpp's graph callback. That is the data the prefetch, pregate and cache ideas came from.

Simulates cache, pin and prefetch policies over a routing trace on the CPU. It screens an idea in seconds before it costs a two-hour integrate-build-A/B cycle.

Applies a proposed change to a tool or skill CC in a scratch copy. It then replays recorded read-only calls and runs the test suite, and reports whether outputs stayed byte-identical and how latency moved.

Calls

Skills

Procedures the agent reads as material. They grant no authority; the host enforces that.

factory.skills

integration_skill

built
INTEGRATE · REPAIR · PREFLIGHT

How to take a component into the agent's own checkout, and how to recover when evidence says something went wrong.

Integrate
Work only in the owned checkout. Verify every patch sha and the base commit. Apply dependencies in order, one commit per component. Revert only that commit on rejection, and never touch unrelated work.
Repair
Diagnose from the actual rejection record, never from an arm name or an old success. Requested K is not effective K. Change exactly one thing per repair. Write a new decision revision citing evidence IDs. Never edit a scored contract.
Proven
Demo run 2: K=48 → CONFIG_REJECTED → K=8, with the failure kept

repackage

over_memory_run

repackage

new
the agent invents components

The missing step from evidence to a new component. Profile a run, trace routing, screen candidate policies in expert_replay, write the patch with its switch off by default, then write component.yaml: hypothesis, depends_on, env_ranges, engagement regexes, measure type and rollback.

Uses
profiler, routing_trace, expert_replay, component_schema

A new component enters the normal loop and gets no shortcut: build, admission, A/B and the frozen contract.

Source
c2/skills/codex-delegation, c2/launch_codex.sh

Methods

Rules of judgement. Each component declares which one judges it.

factory.methods

methodology_ab

built
speed, output unchanged

Ten steps for growing an engine with counterbalanced evidence: one component per experiment, bare build first, ABBA rounds, keep only on a clear win.

Gate
threshold = max(0.03, 2·aa_gap, 2·drift); improvement needs ratio − 1 > threshold (equality is null). Every base stdout must equal the frozen reference; a faster wrong answer is candidate_failed.
Decisions
keep_component, revert_component, and keep_dormant (rejected, but its source is needed by components not yet measured, with the switch off everywhere)
Scope
“identical greedy continuation of a fixed prompt; not an accuracy benchmark”
factory.methods

component_schema

built · rename
today: engine_component

Defines what a component must declare: base, ordered patches with sha256, depends_on, enable_env, env_ranges, engagement_checks, hypothesis, measure (perf | none | accuracy), correctness_obligation, rollback. Filed today as a component; it is really the contract every component is judged against.

methods

methodology_observability

new · small
fixes thread_names

For measure: none components. Keep if all three hold: it engaged (its declared regex matched), it costs nothing measurable (ratio ≥ 1 − threshold from the same ABBA), and the promised signal appears in evidence (for example, xfill-* threads in the sampler summary).

methods

methodology_accuracy

new · operator sets margin

For changes that may alter outputs: quant, KV type, model. It fixes the item set and seed, non-thinking greedy decoding, sample size, a Wilson interval, and a non-inferiority margin the operator chooses. It says when a speed gain may cost accuracy and how much. It also records that published thinking-mode scores are context, not substitutes.

methods

methodology_ladder

new
encodes your targets

Choosing a model for an 8 GB machine, in order: fits (model_registry) → meets the speed floor of 2 tok/s minimum, 5 goal, 10 stretch → highest accuracy among the rest, preferring models with published benchmarks. This is the rule the hand-run ladder used, written down so the agent can apply it.

methods

methodology_rsi

new

How to prove a tool or skill improvement is real. Replayed outputs are byte-identical. The targeted metric (for example p95 duration_ms of one capability) improves beyond run-to-run noise and stays flat as the task grows. The test suite passes. No integrity guarantee is weakened: tamper tests must still fail reads.

Build order

  1. Tag the kinds and fix the misfiles.Add x-factory-kind, rename engine_component → component_schema, add methodology_observability. thread_names stops being judged as a speed patch. About half a day for Codex.
  2. runtime_tuning plus extra_argv in lab_client.Material only. J-OM13 says this alone takes the engine from 1.18× to about 1.28×.
  3. accuracy_lab, methodology_accuracy, kv_quant.Turns the goal from “faster” into “better for 8 GB”, which is the stated priority.
  4. model_registry, methodology_ladder, model_choice.The agent picks the model and quant. This is where the 2 / 5 / 10 tok/s targets are actually met.
  5. profiler, routing_trace, expert_replay, component_authoring, moe_cache.The observe and hypothesize stages: the agent proposes components rather than only integrating ours.
  6. telemetry, capsule_revision, methodology_rsi.The RSI package: the same loop, aimed at the tools and skills.

CC v2 has no kind field, and we agreed not to add top-level fields. The kind goes under existing metadata. The factory's component loader enforces it, so only component CCs can be integrated and only method CCs can be cited as a gate.

JiuwenSwarm factory · Satay (Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB) · 2026-11-12

Satay CC Catalog

A capsule is a package: one functional category of the factory, such as building, measuring, or streaming experts from SSD. Inside it are modules, and each module is one of four kinds: a component ships in the engine, a tool is called, a skill says how to act, a method says how to judge. Below are 9 capsules and 38 modules: what each is called today, what it has already done, and what is still to build.

9capsules (functional packages)
12modules built in the factory
16built in the campaign, not yet a CC
10new to write
1.18× / 1.28×factory engine vs stock (J-OM13), without / with tuning

Capsule, module, kind

One capsule, as packaged
factory.lab
lab_client · tool accuracy_lab · tool methodology_ab · method methodology_accuracy · method methodology_observability · method

One release, one version, one hash. Capabilities are the tool modules; materials are the component, skill and method modules. The agent discovers the whole category with one cc_list entry.

Recorded in ccv2 (commit 608656eb, pushed)
cc: '2' id: factory.lab version: 2.0.0 capabilities: lab.ab_submit: kind: tool # capabilities may only be tool does: Submit one complete ABBA experiment … materials: ab: kind: method # component | skill | method | reference path: AB.md

The parser and JSON schema validate kind. cc_list now reports each module's kind. The factory refuses to integrate a material unless it is declared kind: component. All 12 current factory CCs are tagged.

Component

Is
Code, config or an artifact that ends up in the engine the user runs.
Lifecycle
integrate → build → measure → keep / dormant / revert
Judged by
the method it names

Tool

Is
A capability the agent calls, behind grants. It acts or returns data.
Lifecycle
versioned release; improved by RSI from telemetry and replay
Judged by
correct outputs, latency, failure rate

Skill

Is
A procedure: how to carry out a task with tools.
Lifecycle
revised when runs show agents stumbling
Judged by
task success, turns and repairs per task

Method

Is
Decision rules: what counts as better, how to measure, when to stop.
Lifecycle
changed rarely; a change is a new contract revision
Judged by
the operator
Fixed core: not in any capsule.The evidence store, controller, Manager with its frozen correctness contract, jobq, lab runner, telemetry writer and monitor. The agent must not be able to change these. That is why “output identical” and “1.13×” can be trusted.

Today vs target. The factory currently ships 12 single-module CCs with IDs like factory.builder and factory.components.expert_fill. The target packaging below merges them into category capsules. Module names stay the same and capability names gain a prefix (builder.submit), which the ccv2 name pattern already allows.

Status
Kind

absorbs factory.builder, factory.engine_inspector, factory.integration_skill

Turns a component into a verified engine image: put the patch into the agent's own checkout, check it, build it durably, and confirm the binary does what the config says.

toolbuilt
factory.builder · wraps cc/build_engine

Durable image build from a clean commit, as a jobq build job. Calls: submit (idempotency key), status, cancel, result.

Guarantees
HEAD must equal the commit and the tree must be clean; the same key with a different request conflicts. Prep records nvcc, cmake, docker, the pinned l4t-cuda base digest, ccache and free disk. Writes a schema-2 build record with source tree, patch sha and image ID. Prunes staging after success.
Did
Built 7 images in evolve run 4 (~130 s each, every one survived the agent's turn ending), plus the bare reference a9a0c71c and om12. The campaign's build_engine recorded 3 failed attempts honestly and found the image-identity bug (D016); warm ccache rebuilds take 10–20 s.

engine_inspector

toolbuilt
factory.engine_inspector · wraps cc/abrun/preflight

Checks before GPU time is spent. inspect: commit, dirty state, applied patches, host facts. preflight: does this image's binary accept the flags (cached by image ID, never by tag)? verify_effective_config: runs the binary briefly and compares the expert_config: effective … line and any LLAMA_* line against the request.

Did
Caught the labelled bad setting in demo run 2: CONFIG_REJECTED: LLAMA_EXPERT_PREGATE_K=48 (range 1..32), which the agent repaired to K=8. In run 4 it confirmed the effective config before every A/B: k=8 · pregate=1 · fill=1 · chunk_kib=2048 · matches request.

integration_skill

skillbuilt
factory.integration_skill · INTEGRATE / REPAIR / PREFLIGHT.md

How to integrate: work only in the owned checkout, verify each patch sha and the base, apply dependencies in order, one commit per component, and on rejection revert only that commit. How to repair: diagnose from the actual rejection record, never from an arm name or an old success. Requested K is not effective K. Change one thing per repair, write a new decision revision citing evidence IDs, and never edit a scored contract.

Did
Guided run 4 through 5 integrations (patches 01–09, one commit each), 2 reverts with restoration builds, and 2 dormant keeps, with no human input. In demo run 2 it guided the K=48 → K=8 repair, keeping the failure on record.

Written from real failures. Build-om12 failed with “nvcc not found” because jobq captures the submitting shell's PATH; the fix is now a Builder prep check.

Measures an admitted engine on real inference and decides whether a change is better. It covers speed, accuracy and observability, each with its own rules.

factory.lab_client · wraps om_run, abrun, thread_sampler, io_watchdog

Runs inference through the deterministic Manager. submit/status/cancel/result for one contract run, and ab_submit/ab_status/ab_result for a full ABBA experiment in one gpu job. The Manager admits only an image whose ID matches a build receipt and targets jetson-orin. The model is mounted read-only, the workload is fixed, and the watchdog floor is 600 MiB. A capsule is a package: one functional category of the factory, such as building, measuring, or streaming experts from SSD. Inside it are modules, and each module is one of four kinds: a component ships in the engine, a tool is called, a skill says how to act, a method says how to judge. Below are 9 capsules and 38 modules: what each is called today, what it has already done, and what is still to build.

lab_client · tool accuracy_lab · tool methodology_ab · method methodology_accuracy · method methodology_observability · method

JiuwenSwarm factory · Satay (Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB) · 2026-11-12

Satay CC Catalog

Every capsule (CC) the inference factory has, and every one it should have, sorted by what it is to the agent. There are four kinds. A component ships in the engine. A tool is called. A skill says how to act. A method says how to judge. Each entry gives its interface, evidence, gate and source.

12CCs built
13to repackage from existing campaign code
10new to write
1.18×factory engine vs stock llama.cpp (J-OM13)
1.28×with the missing tuning CC (-t 4)

Four kinds, and what each one is for

The kind decides the lifecycle. Only components go through integrate → build → A/B. Tools and skills are what an RSI system improves. Methods are the rules of judgement, so nobody, RSI included, changes them casually.

Component

Is
Code, config or an artifact that ends up in the engine the user runs.
Test
“Is it in the shipped image or its default config?”
Lifecycle
integrate → build → measure → keep / dormant / revert
Judged by
a method: A/B, accuracy or observability

Tool

Is
A capability the agent calls. It acts or returns data, behind grants.
Test
“Does the agent invoke it and get a result?”
Lifecycle
versioned release; improved from telemetry and replay
Judged by
correct outputs, latency, failure rate

Skill

Is
A procedure: how to carry out a task using tools.
Test
“Does it say how to do X?”
Lifecycle
revised when runs show agents stumbling (turns, repairs)
Judged by
task success and turns per task in telemetry

Method

Is
Decision rules: what counts as better, how to measure, when to stop.
Test
“Does it say how to judge X?”
Lifecycle
changed rarely; a change means a new contract revision
Judged by
the operator
Fixed core: deliberately not CCs. The evidence store, controller, Manager with its frozen correctness contract, jobq wrapper, lab runner, telemetry writer and monitor (about 4.5k lines of Python). These are what the agent must not be able to change. Because they sit outside the CC layer, “output identical” and “1.13×” can be trusted.

Where each kind sits in the loop

Today the agent enters at “component”: we hand it finished patches. The observe and hypothesize stages are the gap. With them filled, the agent can propose its own components.

Show

Components

Ship in the engine. All of them carry depends_on, switches that default to off, engagement checks, a hypothesis, a correctness obligation and a rollback.

engine.components

mmap_advice

built
run 4: 0.49× → dormant

Patch 01. Sets madvise(MADV_RANDOM) on the model mapping, so the kernel stops sequential readahead when sparse expert pages are touched.

Switch
LLAMA_MMAP_ADVICE=random; any other value keeps default advice
Depends on
nothing; the root of the stack
Engagement
stderr llama_mmap: LLAMA_MMAP_ADVICE=random
Evidence
0.49× (893.7 vs about 1,825 ms/token), A/A 0.06, output identical. On this NVMe, readahead was helping: cutting it doubles per-token time.
Why dormant
router_prefetch, expert_fill and expert_pregate all patch the code it adds. The agent kept the commit with the switch off and checked needed_by against the dependency graph. The component's own rejection stands.
engine.components

router_prefetch

built
run 4: 0.62× → dormant

Patch 02. Hooks the CPU consumer of the MoE router output and issues MADV_WILLNEED on the selected experts' host ranges before they are read. An optional mode guesses that the next layer will use the same expert IDs.

Switches
LLAMA_EXPERT_PREFETCH=1, LLAMA_EXPERT_PREFETCH_NEXT=0|1
Depends on
mmap_advice (source)
Engagement
expert_prefetch: CPU host-consumer hook enabled; advise calls=N with N > 0
Evidence
0.62×, A/A 0.09, output identical. Advice is asynchronous and too late: the reads still block at compute time.
Lesson
It led to expert_fill: do the read yourself, in parallel, instead of asking the kernel to.
engine.components

expert_fill

built
run 4: 1.11× → keep

Patches 03–05 (about 670 changed lines). Before a node computes, a worker pool reads the routed experts' pages that aren't yet resident, using buffered parallel pread in 2 MiB chunks. The faults become sequential large reads, and the compute thread no longer stalls in D-state.

Switches
LLAMA_EXPERT_FILL=1, _THREADS=16 (1..64), _CHUNK_KIB=2048, _RANDOM=decode, _MAX_TOKENS=1, _DIAG, _POPULATE
Depends on
mmap_advice, router_prefetch (source)
Engagement
expert_fill: active, random advice applied at decode, stats calls=N with N > 0
Evidence
1.11×, A/A 0.03, output identical. Page faults per token fall from about 5,000 to about 490 (J-OM12/13 thread sampler).
engine.components

expert_pregate

built
run 4: 1.13× → keep

Patches 06–08 (about 840 changed lines). Predicts the next layer's top-K experts from the current hidden state (recall@8 0.81) and schedules bounded asynchronous fills ahead of demand. Patch 08 adds strict validation of every LLAMA_EXPERT_* variable, plus the expert_config: effective … line that the inspector checks.

Switches
LLAMA_EXPERT_PREGATE=1, _K=8 (1..32), _ORDER=after|before, _MAX_INFLIGHT=4 (1..64), _LOOKAHEAD=1 (1..2)
Depends on
expert_fill
Engagement
expert_pregate: active; effective … pregate=1; stats predictions=N with N > 0
Evidence
1.13× on top of fill (831 → 739 ms/token), A/A 0.016, output identical. Lookahead 2 was measured worse (J-OM11).

built
run 4: 1.01× → reverted (misjudged)

none; always on when built

thread sampler sees threads matching ^xfill-[0-9]+$

Methods

Rules of judgement. Each component declares which one judges it.

factory.methods

methodology_ab

built
speed, output unchanged

Ten steps for growing an engine with counterbalanced evidence: one component per experiment, bare build first, ABBA rounds, keep only on a clear win.

Gate
threshold = max(0.03, 2·aa_gap, 2·drift); improvement needs ratio − 1 > threshold (equality is null). Every base stdout must equal the frozen reference; a faster wrong answer is candidate_failed.

It says when a speed gain may cost accuracy and how much. It also records that published thinking-mode scores are context, not substitutes.

new
encodes your targets

Choosing a model for an 8 GB machine, in order: fits (model_registry) → meets the speed floor of 2 tok/s minimum, 5 goal, 10 stretch → highest accuracy among the rest, preferring models with published benchmarks. This is the rule the hand-run ladder used, written down so the agent can apply it.

new

How to prove a tool or skill improvement is real. Replayed outputs are byte-identical. The targeted metric (for example p95 duration_ms of one capability) improves beyond run-to-run noise and stays flat as the task grows. The test suite passes. No integrity guarantee is weakened: tamper tests must still fail reads.

Build order

  1. Tag the kinds and fix the misfiles.Add x-factory-kind, rename engine_component → component_schema, add methodology_observability. thread_names stops being judged as a speed patch. About half a day for Codex.

  4. model_registry, methodology_ladder, model_choice.The agent picks the model and quant. This is where the 2 / 5 / 10 tok/s targets are actually met.
  5. profiler, routing_trace, expert_replay, component_authoring, moe_cache.The observe and hypothesize stages: the agent proposes components rather than only integrating ours.

"""Translate capsule capability names to the task-scoped factory native API."""
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys

from jiuwenswarm.factory.telemetry import set_turn_env
set_turn_env()

PREFIX = 'builder'
packet = json.load(sys.stdin)
cap = packet['capability']
packet['capability'] = PREFIX + '.' + cap
try:
    process = subprocess.run([os.environ.get('FACTORY_PYTHON', sys.executable), '-m', 'jiuwenswarm.factory.api', packet['capability']],
                             input=json.dumps(packet), capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=49)
    result = json.loads(process.stdout)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    result = {'outcome': 'error', 'error': {'code': 'TIMEOUT', 'message': 'Factory API exceeded the bounded call deadline'}}
except (ValueError, TypeError):
    # Surface the cause to the agent: the last stderr lines (the API redacts its own messages).
    detail = ' | '.join(process.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-3:])[-600:] if process.stderr else 'no stderr'

JiuwenSwarm factory · Satay, a Jetson Orin Nano with 8 GB · November 2026

Satay CC Catalog

An AI agent improves a language-model engine on a small machine. Everything it can use comes packaged as a capsule: a box of related parts for one job, such as “build the engine” or “measure it”. This page lists every capsule we have and every one we still need. For each part it explains what it does, what it has already done, and how we check that it works.

The idea in one minute

The agent starts with plain llama.cpp and a 35-billion-parameter model that is almost three times larger than the machine's memory. Its job is to make the engine faster without changing a single word of what the model says.

It cannot touch anything directly. It can only use the parts inside capsules. Each part is one of four kinds:

Component

A piece of the engine itself: a code patch or a setting. If we keep it, the user gets it.

e.g. expert_fill, a patch that loads model weights in parallel

Tool

Something the agent can run, and which reports back.

e.g. builder, which turns source code into a runnable engine

Skill

Written instructions on how to do a job well.

e.g. how to apply a patch, and how to recover when it fails

Method

Written rules on how to judge a result: what counts as better, and when to give up.

e.g. keep a change only if it is faster by more than the noise

Since this week, ccv2 records the kind on every part (kind: tool, kind: component, …). The factory checks it: the agent can only build what is declared a component.

A few things are deliberately not in any capsule: the evidence database, the job queue, and the referee that runs the model and compares its output with a frozen reference. The agent must not be able to change these. That is why its results can be trusted.

How one improvement moves through the factory

This is what happened for each component in run 4, which ran for 175 minutes with no human input.

  1. The agent reads a component: the patch, what it should do, what it depends on, and how to tell it is switched on.engine.expert_streaming · component
  2. It applies the patch to its own copy of llama.cpp and makes one commit, following the integration instructions.factory.build · integration_skill
  3. It asks the builder for an engine image. The build runs about two minutes in the background, inside Docker, and survives the agent pausing.factory.build · builder
  4. It checks that the new binary accepts the settings and really applies them.factory.build · engine_inspector
  5. It asks the lab to run the old engine and the new one on the real model, in the order old-new-new-old, twice. Each output is compared with the frozen reference.factory.lab · lab_client
  6. It applies the judging rules: keep it, revert it, or keep the code switched off because a later component needs it.factory.lab · methodology_ab
  7. It writes the decision, citing the evidence, and moves on to the next component.factory.evidence · evidence

Result, measured afterwards against stock llama.cpp: 1.18× faster with the agent's choices, 1.28× with one more setting it had no way to try. All outputs were identical to the reference.

What runs where, right now

Every tool capsule is native: a small Python launcher on the host. None uses ccv2's Docker (image) binding. Three of them start Docker containers underneath, because the engine itself lives in a container.

Capsule partHow the agent calls itWhat actually runs
buildernativePython queues a build job; the job runs docker buildx build to produce the engine image
engine_inspectornativePython, plus a few seconds of docker run --rm on the candidate image to read its flags and settings
lab_clientnativePython queues a GPU job. The referee runs the engine with docker run, model mounted read-only, then removes the container.
evidencenativePython and SQLite only; no Docker
components, skills, methodsread as filesNothing runs; the agent reads them. Components end up inside the engine image after a build.

Why native: the launcher must reach the job queue, the evidence database and Docker on the host, so wrapping it in its own container would add nothing. The engine is what needs isolation, and it gets it.

Who manages expert placement, right now

No capsule does. Placement is fixed by the referee's frozen command line, so the agent cannot change it.

The model is a mixture of experts: for each word it uses 8 of 256 small sub-networks per layer. The command line -ngl 99 -cmoe -lm mmap places everything that is not an expert on the GPU, and leaves all expert weights on the CPU side, read from the SSD on demand. On this machine the CPU and GPU share the same 8 GB, so “placement” really means which processor does the work, and what has to be in memory at the time.

The two components we kept only manage timing. expert_fill reads the chosen experts into memory in parallel just before they are needed. expert_pregate predicts the next layer's experts and starts reading them early. Neither one moves an expert to the GPU.

Parts that would manage placement exist, but none is in the factory yet:

PartStatusWhat it would do
moe_cachecampaignKeeps the most-used experts in a fixed memory budget. Tested slower on this machine, because shared memory means a double copy. Better suited to machines with a separate GPU.
hybrid_expertcampaignTest harness: runs cached experts on the GPU and the rest on the CPU, at the same time. It measured how much overlap is possible.
expert_placementproposedA setting component for the tuning capsule. It would expose llama.cpp's own placement controls (--n-cpu-moe, -ot) so the agent can try “first N layers' experts on the GPU”, judged like any other component.
Status
Kind
Capsule 1 of 9

factory.build

Turns a code change into a working engine, and proves the engine is what we think it is.

Getsa component, from engine.* capsulesGivesan engine image with a fingerprint (image ID) to factory.labRecordsevery build, success or failure, in factory.evidence

builder

toolin the factory
today: factory.builder · native, runs docker build in a queued job · uses cc/build_engine
Does
Takes a commit from the agent's copy of llama.cpp and builds a container image for the Jetson. The build runs in the background, so the agent submits it, ends its turn, and checks back later.
How
Before compiling, it checks the toolchain, the pinned CUDA base image and free disk space. After compiling, it writes a build record: source, patches, compiler and image ID. Then it deletes about 1.9 GB of temporary files.
Did
Built 7 engines in run 4 at about 130 seconds each, and the frozen reference engine. In the earlier campaign it caught a bug where two different builds got the same name.
Verifier
  • submit: refuses a dirty checkout or a commit that isn't checked out. The same request twice returns the same job; a different request under the same key is refused.
  • submit: the worker re-hashes the build script and patch, and stops with INPUT_CHANGED if anything moved after submission.
  • status: a finished job can never go back to “running”.
  • cancel: records the intent, stops the job, then confirms no process is left behind.
  • result: “success” only if the build record says success and contains an image ID.

Automated: tests/factory/test_builder.py (9), test_jobs.py (11).

engine_inspector

toolin the factory
today: factory.engine_inspector · native, short docker run · uses cc/abrun/preflight
Does
Answers three questions before any GPU time is spent. What is in this source? Does this engine accept these flags? Will it really use the settings I asked for?
How
Starts the image for a few seconds and reads its help text and its expert_config: effective … line, which patch 08 prints. Results are remembered per image ID, never per name, because names can be reused.
Did
In the first demo it caught a deliberately bad setting (K=48, allowed range 1–32). The agent read the rejection and fixed it to K=8. In run 4 it confirmed the settings before every comparison.
Verifier
  • inspect: reports the commit, whether there are uncommitted changes, and which patches are applied.
  • preflight: every requested flag must appear in the image's own help output.
  • verify_effective_config: each requested LLAMA_* value must match what the engine prints. A mismatch or crash is recorded as CONFIG_REJECTED, never ignored.

Automated: test_lab.py, test_review_fixes.py. Live: demo run 2 rejection record.

integration_skill

skillin the factory
today: factory.integration_skill · files INTEGRATE.md, REPAIR.md, PREFLIGHT.md
Does
Tells the agent how to add a component safely, and what to do when something fails.
How
Integrate: work only in your own copy, check every patch fingerprint, apply dependencies first, one commit per component, and undo only that commit if rejected. Repair: read the actual failure record, not a guess. Change one thing at a time, and write down why before trying again.
Did
Guided run 4 through five components with two reverts and two “keep but switch off” decisions, all without help.
Verifier
  • The file fingerprints are part of the capsule release, so the agent reads exactly the reviewed text.
  • Behaviour is checked from the record: one commit per component, every decision citing evidence IDs. Both are visible in run 4's story.

engine_build

skillbuilt, not packaged
c2/skills/engine-build
Does
A troubleshooting guide for builds: compiler not on PATH, base image not pinned, disk nearly full, cache warm or cold.
Did
Written from real failures, such as a build that failed because the job queue didn't see the CUDA compiler.
Verifier
  • Each failure it describes has a matching error code from builder, so the advice can be checked against real records.
Capsule 2 of 9

factory.lab

Runs the real model on the engine and decides, by fixed rules, whether a change is better.

Getsengine images from factory.buildGivesspeed, output check and verdict to factory.evidenceUsesthe referee in the fixed core, which the agent cannot change

lab_client

toolin the factory
today: factory.lab_client · native, queues a GPU job that uses docker run · uses om_run, abrun, thread_sampler
Does
Runs Qwen3.6-35B on an engine image and reports speed and whether the output matched. It can run a single check, or a full old-versus-new comparison.
How
The referee only accepts an image whose ID matches a build record made for this Jetson. It runs a fixed prompt and settings with the model mounted read-only, and a watchdog stops the run if memory gets dangerously low. For a comparison it runs old-new-new-old twice, so drift over time cancels out.
Did
Ran all of run 4's measurements. Every one of the 9 lab jobs produced output identical to the reference, and every container was cleaned up.
Verifier
  • submit / ab_submit: refused unless the image ID matches its build record, the architecture is arm64 and the target is the Jetson. Otherwise the result is bad_digest or wrong_target.
  • result: the output fingerprint must equal the frozen reference 7a154179…. A faster engine with different output counts as a failure.
  • ab_result: the component's own “is it on?” checks must show up in the engine log. The referee takes these from the component file; the agent can't supply them.
  • ab_result: also reports the noise between identical runs, so a small speedup can't be mistaken for a real one.
  • cancel: the container is removed and the removal confirmed.

Automated: test_lab.py (26), test_evolve.py (14). Faults covered: bad fingerprint, wrong target, tampered reference, upload failure, cancellation.

accuracy_lab

toolbuilt, not packaged
cc/acc · would run docker (llama-server) through the referee
Does
Asks the model a fixed set of exam questions (MMLU-Pro and others) and scores the answers. This is how we judge changes that are allowed to alter the output, such as a smaller model file.
Did
Scored the model ladder. Qwen3.6-35B got 62.9% (70 questions; the true score is likely between 51% and 73%). Qwen3.5-9B got 45.7% and Gemma-4-E4B 40.7%. It also found a server setting that made answers unstable.
Verifier
  • The question set is frozen by fingerprint; scoring a different set is refused.
  • Every score comes with its uncertainty range and the per-question answers.
  • A known-answer sample run must reproduce its stored score before a real run counts.

methodology_ab

methodin the factory
today: factory.methodology_ab · file AB.md
Does
Sets the rules for speed comparisons: test one change at a time, start from the plain engine, and keep a change only if it is clearly faster.
How
“Clearly faster” means faster by more than 3%, and by more than twice the noise seen between identical runs. If the output changes at all, it is a failure. If a rejected part is needed by a later one, its code may stay with its switch off.
Did
Run 4: kept expert_fill (1.11×) and expert_pregate (1.13×). Kept mmap_advice (0.49×) and router_prefetch (0.62×) switched off. Removed thread_names. The agent also refused to multiply the numbers into one headline figure.
Verifier
  • The pass/fail threshold is computed by the referee's code, not by the agent.
  • “Keep switched off” is only accepted if the dependency files show a later part really needs it.

methodology_accuracy

methodto write
Does
Sets the rules for changes that alter output: how many questions, how to compare two versions fairly, and how much accuracy we are willing to lose for speed. That last number is yours to set.
Verifier
  • Every accuracy verdict cites a frozen question set, a sample size and an uncertainty range.

methodology_observability

methodto write · small
Does
Rules for parts that add visibility instead of speed. Keep the part if it switches on, costs nothing measurable, and the new information appears.
Why
thread_names was removed in run 4 only because the speed rules were the only rules available.
Verifier
  • The promised signal (for example, named worker threads) must appear in the profiler output of the same run.
Capsule 3 of 9

factory.evidence

The factory's memory: what happened, what was decided and why, and what gets handed on at the end.

Getsrecords from every other capsuleGivesthe full history to the agent, the monitor, the story view and the RSI team

evidence

toolin the factory
today: factory.evidence · native, SQLite
Does
Lets the agent search the task's history, read any record in full, and publish its next decision.
How
Everything is append-only and scoped to one task. Files are stored by content fingerprint. A decision must name the version it replaces, so two writers can't overwrite each other.
Did
Held run 4's 696 records, 599 files (478 MB) and 25 decisions. It is the most-used tool, so its speed matters most as the history grows.
Verifier
  • query: only returns records from tasks you are allowed to read.
  • read: re-checks the file's fingerprint and refuses a tampered file.
  • publish: refused if the decision is stale, or if it cites evidence that doesn't exist.
  • No write is acknowledged until it is safely on disk.

Automated: test_store.py (13), test_api.py (7), test_review_fixes.py.

engine_handoff

toolbuilt, not packaged
cc/engine_handoff · native, never runs the image
Does
Writes the delivery sheet for a finished engine: fingerprints, architecture, labels and model-file compatibility. It checks the sheet against what the receiver needs.
Did
Produced a real accepted handoff, and exposed the bug where builds were tracked by name instead of fingerprint.
Verifier
  • The archive fingerprint on the sheet must equal the delivered bytes.
  • Every receiver requirement is marked met or unmet, never skipped.

component_schema

methodin the factory · to rename
today: factory.engine_component
Does
Says what every component must declare: the base version, its patches with fingerprints, what it depends on, its switches and their safe ranges, how to tell it is on, what it should improve, and how to undo it.
Did
These declarations let the agent work out the build order and the “keep switched off” rule by itself in run 4.
Verifier
  • The factory refuses a component unless its capsule declares kind: component.
  • Each patch fingerprint is re-checked before it is applied.
Capsule 4 of 9

engine.expert_streaming

Lets a model three times larger than memory run anyway, by bringing the needed pieces in from the SSD just in time. All of today's speedup comes from here.

Goes tofactory.build (applied as patches) and then factory.lab (measured)NoteThese parts manage when expert weights are read, not where they run. See expert placement above.
  1. Each word only needs 8 experts per layer, but which 8 is only known at the last moment.
  2. Without help, the engine stalls each time it touches an expert that isn't in memory yet.
  3. These parts read those experts earlier, in bigger and parallel chunks, so the stalls shrink.

mmap_advice

componentin the factory
today: factory.components.mmap_advice · patch 01 · switch LLAMA_MMAP_ADVICE=random
Does
Tells the operating system to stop reading ahead in the model file, on the theory that expert reads are scattered.
Did
Made it twice as slow (0.49×). Reading ahead helps on this SSD. Its code is kept, switched off, because three later parts are built on top of it.
Verifier
  • When on, the engine log says LLAMA_MMAP_ADVICE=random.
  • Patch fingerprint 1554b5b6… checked before applying.
  • Output identical to the reference.

router_prefetch

componentin the factory
today: factory.components.router_prefetch · patch 02 · needs mmap_advice
Does
As soon as the model picks its 8 experts, asks the operating system to start loading them.
Did
Slower (0.62×): the request arrives too late to help. Kept switched off. The lesson led to the next part: read the data directly instead of asking.
Verifier
  • When on, the log shows the hook enabled and a non-zero count of requests.
  • Output identical.

expert_fill

componentin the factory · kept
today: factory.components.expert_fill · patches 03–05 · 16 reader threads, 2 MB chunks
Does
Before an expert is used, 16 helper threads read its missing parts from the SSD in parallel, in large chunks. The main thread no longer waits on many small reads.
Did
1.11× faster, output identical. Memory page misses per word fell from about 5,000 to about 490.
Verifier
  • The log shows expert_fill: active and a non-zero count of fill calls.
  • Settings are checked against their safe ranges (threads 1–64, chunk 64 KB–64 MB).
  • Output identical.

expert_pregate

componentin the factory · kept
today: factory.components.expert_pregate · patches 06–08 · needs expert_fill
Does
Guesses which 8 experts the next layer will want (right about 81% of the time) and starts reading them while the current layer is still working. Patch 08 also makes the engine check all expert settings and print what it is actually using.
Did
1.13× faster on top of expert_fill, output identical. Time stuck waiting on the disk dropped from 43% to under 1%.
Verifier
  • The log shows expert_pregate: active, an effective-config line with pregate=1, and a non-zero prediction count.
  • Out-of-range settings (for example K=48) stop the engine with a clear message.
  • Output identical.

thread_names

componentin the factory
today: factory.components.thread_names · patch 09 · 6 lines
Does
Gives the helper threads readable names (xfill-1, xfill-2, …), so the profiler can tell who is waiting on what.
Did
Was the first demo's change. In run 4 it worked, at no cost (1.01×), but was removed because only speed rules existed. methodology_observability fixes that.
Verifier
  • The profiler sees threads named xfill-N during the run.
  • Output identical.

moe_cache

componentbuilt, not packaged
cc/moe_cache_profile · tested as image jetson-up1108-mc
Does
Keeps the most-used experts permanently in a fixed memory budget, chosen from a usage profile. This one does manage placement.
Did
Slower on this machine: CPU and GPU share memory, so caching makes an extra copy. It also changes output slightly. Worth packaging for machines with a separate GPU.
Verifier
  • The log reports cache size and hit rate.
  • Because output changes, it is judged by accuracy and KL-divergence checks, not identical output.

over_memory_run

skillbuilt, not packaged
c2/skills/over-memory-run
Does
Explains how to run a model bigger than memory: which flags, how low free memory may go, how to read the waiting and page-miss figures, and why the order of runs matters.
Did
Written from twelve rounds of experiments, including two dead ends: offloading whole layers made speed collapse, and relying on the OS file cache falls off a cliff when memory runs short.
Verifier
  • Its memory floors match the referee's watchdog settings.
Capsule 5 of 9

engine.kernels

Makes the GPU's arithmetic faster, and tests a change on its own in minutes before paying for a full engine comparison.

Goes tofactory.build and factory.lab, like expert_streamingStatusAll four parts exist from the campaign; none is packaged yet. Two need moving onto the factory's llama.cpp version.

moe_dispatch_sm87

componentbuilt, not packaged
cc/moe_dispatch_sm87 · patch 03 · switch GGML_CUDA_J_UNFUSE_IDS_TYPES
Does
Fixes a case where llama.cpp picks a slow GPU routine for experts on this chip, by choosing per weight type.
Did
On this Jetson: +23.6% for 4-bit experts with identical output, and +19.3% for 16-bit experts. It must stay off for 8-bit weights, where it is 6.2% slower. The best ready candidate for the next run.
Verifier
  • kernel_screen confirms the faster routine is selected for the target weight type.
  • Output identical for 4-bit models; KL check for 16-bit.

q8_reuse

componentwritten, never built
cc/q8_reuse
Does
Avoids repeating the same conversion step when several 8-bit operations read the same input.
Did
Designed and reviewed, but never compiled or measured. An honest unknown: exactly what the factory's keep-or-revert loop is for.
Verifier
  • Reuse only happens when the input, its shape and its GPU stream are all identical; the patch counts hits and misses.

kernel_screen

toolbuilt, not packaged
cc/kernel_screen · runs test-backend-ops in the engine image (docker)
Does
Times individual GPU operations by type, so a kernel idea can be ranked in minutes instead of a two-hour cycle.
Did
Screened the dispatch candidates above. It also exposed its own bug, a type-name capitalisation slip, which has been fixed.
Verifier
  • Type names are checked against the engine's real list.
  • Each timing is repeated, and its spread reported.

kernel_profile

skillbuilt, not packaged
c2/skills/kernel-profile
Does
Explains how to find the slow GPU step with a profiler, screen a fix on its own, and only then build and compare the whole engine.
Did
The path that found the moe_dispatch win.
Capsule 6 of 9

engine.tuning

Turns the engine's settings into components the agent can see and test. The agent can't try what isn't in a capsule, which is why run 4 never tried 4 CPU threads.

Goes tofactory.lab directly: settings need no rebuildNeedslab_client to accept per-run command-line settings; the comparison tool already supports this

runtime_tuning

componentto write
Does
Lists the engine's speed settings with safe ranges: CPU threads, batch sizes, context length, and the helper-thread count and chunk size.
Evidence
Measured by hand: 4 CPU threads take the engine from 1.18× to 1.28× faster than stock, with identical output. 6 threads was worse than 4.
Verifier
  • Each value must be inside its declared range; the engine log must show the value in use.
  • Judged one setting at a time with the speed rules, and output must stay identical.

expert_placement

componentto write
Does
Exposes llama.cpp's own controls for where experts run: put the experts of the first N layers on the GPU and the rest on the CPU. This would be the first part that manages placement in the factory.

On this machine every byte moved to the GPU side is a byte taken from the shared memory the experts stream through. The campaign saw speed collapse when whole layers were offloaded the wrong way. The comparison decides, not the theory.
Verifier
  • The engine's startup log must show the requested split.
  • The watchdog must not trip.
  • Output identical.

kv_quant

componentto write
Does
Stores the model's working memory (the KV cache) at 8-bit to save space. Because this can change output slightly, it is judged on accuracy, not on identical text.

Used in the 9B model's 10.6 words-per-second result.
Verifier

Capsule 7 of 9

models

Chooses which model and file size to ship: it must fit, be fast enough, and be as accurate as possible. This is where your targets of 2, 5 and 10 words per second are actually met.

Getsspeed from factory.lab, scores from accuracy_labGivesthe chosen model file, as a component

cc/model_manifest, cc/gpu_budget, cc/memory_pareto · native, read-only
Does
Lists the models on disk with fingerprints and sizes. It predicts whether each will fit, and in which mode, and shows the trade-off between memory, speed and quality.

cc/ladder · runs each step as a queued GPU job (docker)

Satay CC Catalog

An AI agent improves a language-model engine on a small machine. Everything it can use comes packaged as a capsule: a box of related parts for one job, such as “build the engine” or “measure it”. This page lists every capsule we have and every one we still need. For each part it explains what it does, what it has already done, and how we check that it works.

The idea in one minute

The agent starts with plain llama.cpp and a 35-billion-parameter model that is almost three times larger than the machine's memory. Its job is to make the engine faster without changing a single word of what the model says.

It cannot touch anything directly. It can only use the parts inside capsules. Each part is one of four kinds:

Component

A piece of the engine itself: a code patch or a setting. If we keep it, the user gets it.

e.g. expert_fill, a patch that loads model weights in parallel

Tool

Something the agent can run, and which reports back.

e.g. builder, which turns source code into a runnable engine

Skill

Written instructions on how to do a job well.

e.g. how to apply a patch, and how to recover when it fails

Method

Written rules on how to judge a result: what counts as better, and when to give up.

e.g. keep a change only if it is faster by more than the noise

Since this week, ccv2 records the kind on every part (kind: tool, kind: component, …). The factory checks it: the agent can only build what is declared a component.

A few things are deliberately not in any capsule: the evidence database, the job queue, and the referee that runs the model and compares its output with a frozen reference. The agent must not be able to change these. That is why its results can be trusted.

How one improvement moves through the factory

This is what happened for each component in run 4, which ran for 175 minutes with no human input.

  1. The agent reads a component: the patch, what it should do, what it depends on, and how to tell it is switched on.engine.expert_streaming · component
  2. It applies the patch to its own copy of llama.cpp and makes one commit, following the integration instructions.factory.build · integration_skill
  3. It asks the builder for an engine image. The build runs about two minutes in the background, inside Docker, and survives the agent pausing.factory.build · builder
  4. It checks that the new binary accepts the settings and really applies them.factory.build · engine_inspector
  5. It asks the lab to run the old engine and the new one on the real model, in the order old-new-new-old, twice. Each output is compared with the frozen reference.factory.lab · lab_client
  6. It applies the judging rules: keep it, revert it, or keep the code switched off because a later component needs it.factory.lab · methodology_ab
  7. It writes the decision, citing the evidence, and moves on to the next component.factory.evidence · evidence

Result, measured afterwards against stock llama.cpp: 1.18× faster with the agent's choices, 1.28× with one more setting it had no way to try. All outputs were identical to the reference.

What runs where, right now

Every tool capsule is native: a small Python launcher on the host. None uses ccv2's Docker (image) binding. Three of them start Docker containers underneath, because the engine itself lives in a container.

Capsule partHow the agent calls itWhat actually runs
buildernativePython queues a build job; the job runs docker buildx build to produce the engine image
engine_inspectornativePython, plus a few seconds of docker run --rm on the candidate image to read its flags and settings
lab_clientnativePython queues a GPU job. The referee runs the engine with docker run, model mounted read-only, then removes the container.
evidencenativePython and SQLite only; no Docker
components, skills, methodsread as filesNothing runs; the agent reads them. Components end up inside the engine image after a build.

Why native: the launcher must reach the job queue, the evidence database and Docker on the host, so wrapping it in its own container would add nothing. The engine is what needs isolation, and it gets it.

Who manages expert placement, right now

No capsule does. Placement is fixed by the referee's frozen command line, so the agent cannot change it.

The model is a mixture of experts: for each word it uses 8 of 256 small sub-networks per layer. The command line -ngl 99 -cmoe -lm mmap places everything that is not an expert on the GPU, and leaves all expert weights on the CPU side, read from the SSD on demand. On this machine the CPU and GPU share the same 8 GB, so “placement” really means which processor does the work, and what has to be in memory at the time.

The two components we kept only manage timing. expert_fill reads the chosen experts into memory in parallel just before they are needed. expert_pregate predicts the next layer's experts and starts reading them early. Neither one moves an expert to the GPU.

Parts that would manage placement exist, but none is in the factory yet:

expert_placementproposedA setting component for the tuning capsule. It would expose llama.cpp's own placement controls (--n-cpu-moe, -ot) so the agent can try “first N layers' experts on the GPU”, judged like any other component.

tool_response.content:
JiuwenSwarm factory · Satay, a Jetson Orin Nano with 8 GB · November 2026

Satay CC Catalog

An AI agent improves a language-model engine on a small machine. Everything it can use comes packaged as a capsule: a box of related parts for one job, such as “build the engine” or “measure it”. This page lists every capsule we have and every one we still need. For each part it explains what it does, what it has already done, and how we check that it works.

The idea in one minute

The agent starts with plain llama.cpp and a 35-billion-parameter model that is almost three times larger than the machine's memory. Its job is to make the engine faster without changing a single word of what the model says.

It cannot touch anything directly. It can only use the parts inside capsules. Each part is one of four kinds:

Component

A piece of the engine itself: a code patch or a setting. If we keep it, the user gets it.

e.g. expert_fill, a patch that loads model weights in parallel

Tool

Something the agent can run, and which reports back.

e.g. builder, which turns source code into a runnable engine

Skill

Written instructions on how to do a job well.

e.g. how to apply a patch, and how to recover when it fails

Method

Written rules on how to judge a result: what counts as better, and when to give up.

e.g. keep a change only if it is faster by more than the noise

Since this week, ccv2 records the kind on every part (kind: tool, kind: component, …). The factory checks it: the agent can only build what is declared a component.

A few things are deliberately not in any capsule: the evidence database, the job queue, and the referee that runs the model and compares its output with a frozen reference. The agent must not be able to change these. That is why its results can be trusted.

How one improvement moves through the factory

This is what happened for each component in run 4, which ran for 175 minutes with no human input.

  1. The agent reads a component: the patch, what it should do, what it depends on, and how to tell it is switched on.engine.expert_streaming · component
  2. It applies the patch to its own copy of llama.cpp and makes one commit, following the integration instructions.factory.build · integration_skill
  3. It asks the builder for an engine image. The build runs about two minutes in the background, inside Docker, and survives the agent pausing.factory.build · builder
  4. It checks that the new binary accepts the settings and really applies them.factory.build · engine_inspector
  5. It asks the lab to run the old engine and the new one on the real model, in the order old-new-new-old, twice. Each output is compared with the frozen reference.factory.lab · lab_client
  6. It applies the judging rules: keep it, revert it, or keep the code switched off because a later component needs it.factory.lab · methodology_ab
  7. It writes the decision, citing the evidence, and moves on to the next component.factory.evidence · evidence

Result, measured afterwards against stock llama.cpp: 1.18× faster with the agent's choices, 1.28× with one more setting it had no way to try. All outputs were identical to the reference.

What runs where, right now

Every tool capsule is native: a small Python launcher on the host. None uses ccv2's Docker (image) binding. Three of them start Docker containers underneath, because the engine itself lives in a container.

Capsule partHow the agent calls itWhat actually runs
buildernativePython queues a build job; the job runs docker buildx build to produce the engine image
engine_inspectornativePython, plus a few seconds of docker run --rm on the candidate image to read its flags and settings
lab_clientnativePython queues a GPU job. The referee runs the engine with docker run, model mounted read-only, then removes the container.
evidencenativePython and SQLite only; no Docker
components, skills, methodsread as filesNothing runs; the agent reads them. Components end up inside the engine image after a build.

Why native: the launcher must reach the job queue, the evidence database and Docker on the host, so wrapping it in its own container would add nothing. The engine is what needs isolation, and it gets it.

Who manages expert placement, right now

No capsule does. Placement is fixed by the referee's frozen command line, so the agent cannot change it.

The model is a mixture of experts: for each word it uses 8 of 256 small sub-networks per layer. The command line -ngl 99 -cmoe -lm mmap places everything that is not an expert on the GPU, and leaves all expert weights on the CPU side, read from the SSD on demand. On this machine the CPU and GPU share the same 8 GB, so “placement” really means which processor does the work, and what has to be in memory at the time.

The two components we kept only manage timing. expert_fill reads the chosen experts into memory in parallel just before they are needed. expert_pregate predicts the next layer's experts and starts reading them early. Neither one moves an expert to the GPU.

Parts that would manage placement exist, but none is in the factory yet:

PartStatusWhat it would do
moe_cachecampaignKeeps the most-used experts in a fixed memory budget. Tested slower on this machine, because shared memory means a double copy. Better suited to machines with a separate GPU.
hybrid_expertcampaignTest harness: runs cached experts on the GPU and the rest on the CPU, at the same time. It measured how much overlap is possible.
expert_placementproposedA setting component for the tuning capsule. It would expose llama.cpp's own placement controls (--n-cpu-moe, -ot) so the agent can try “first N layers' experts on the GPU”, judged like any other component.
Status
Kind
Capsule 1 of 9

factory.build

Turns a code change into a working engine, and proves the engine is what we think it is.

Getsa component, from engine.* capsulesGivesan engine image with a fingerprint (image ID) to factory.labRecordsevery build, success or failure, in factory.evidence

builder

toolin the factory
today: factory.builder · native, runs docker build in a queued job · uses cc/build_engine
Does
Takes a commit from the agent's copy of llama.cpp and builds a container image for the Jetson. The build runs in the background, so the agent submits it, ends its turn, and checks back later.
How
Before compiling, it checks the toolchain, the pinned CUDA base image and free disk space. After compiling, it writes a build record: source, patches, compiler and image ID. Then it deletes about 1.9 GB of temporary files.
Did
Built 7 engines in run 4 at about 130 seconds each, and the frozen reference engine. In the earlier campaign it caught a bug where two different builds got the same name.
Verifier
  • submit: refuses a dirty checkout or a commit that isn't checked out. The same request twice returns the same job; a different request under the same key is refused.
  • submit: the worker re-hashes the build script and patch, and stops with INPUT_CHANGED if anything moved after submission.
  • status: a finished job can never go back to “running”.
  • cancel: records the intent, stops the job, then confirms no process is left behind.
  • result: “success” only if the build record says success and contains an image ID.

Automated: tests/factory/test_builder.py (9), test_jobs.py (11).

toolin the factory

How
Starts the image for a few seconds and reads its help text and its expert_config: effective … line, which patch 08 prints. Results are remembered per image ID, never per name, because names can be reused.
Did
In the first demo it caught a deliberately bad setting (K=48, allowed range 1–32). The agent read the rejection and fixed it to K=8. In run 4 it confirmed the settings before every comparison.
Verifier
  • inspect: reports the commit, whether there are uncommitted changes, and which patches are applied.
  • preflight: every requested flag must appear in the image's own help output.
  • verify_effective_config: each requested LLAMA_* value must match what the engine prints. A mismatch or crash is recorded as CONFIG_REJECTED, never ignored.

Automated: test_lab.py, test_review_fixes.py. Live: demo run 2 rejection record.

skillin the factory

Does
Tells the agent how to add a component safely, and what to do when something fails.
How
Integrate: work only in your own copy, check every patch fingerprint, apply dependencies first, one commit per component, and undo only that commit if rejected. Repair: read the actual failure record, not a guess. Change one thing at a time, and write down why before trying again.
Did
Guided run 4 through five components with two reverts and two “keep but switch off” decisions, all without help.
Verifier
  • The file fingerprints are part of the capsule release, so the agent reads exactly the reviewed text.
  • Behaviour is checked from the record: one commit per component, every decision citing evidence IDs. Both are visible in run 4's story.

Capsule 2 of 9

factory.lab

Getsengine images from factory.buildGivesspeed, output check and verdict to factory.evidenceUsesthe referee in the fixed core, which the agent cannot change

Does

How
The referee only accepts an image whose ID matches a build record made for this Jetson. It runs a fixed prompt and settings with the model mounted read-only, and a watchdog stops the run if memory gets dangerously low. For a comparison it runs old-new-new-old twice, so drift over time cancels out.
Did
Ran all of run 4's measurements. Every one of the 9 lab jobs produced output identical to the reference, and every container was cleaned up.
Verifier

  • result: the output fingerprint must equal the frozen reference 7a154179…. A faster engine with different output counts as a failure.
  • ab_result: the component's own “is it on?” checks must show up in the engine log. The referee takes these from the component file; the agent can't supply them.

Automated: test_lab.py (26), test_evolve.py (14). Faults covered: bad fingerprint, wrong target, tampered reference, upload failure, cancellation.

Scored the model ladder. Qwen3.6-35B got 62.9% (70 questions; the true score is likely between 51% and 73%). Qwen3.5-9B got 45.7% and Gemma-4-E4B 40.7%. It also found a server setting that made answers unstable.
Verifier

methodology_ab

methodin the factory
today: factory.methodology_ab · file AB.md
Does
Sets the rules for speed comparisons: test one change at a time, start from the plain engine, and keep a change only if it is clearly faster.
How
“Clearly faster” means faster by more than 3%, and by more than twice the noise seen between identical runs. If the output changes at all, it is a failure. If a rejected part is needed by a later one, its code may stay with its switch off.

Run 4: kept expert_fill (1.11×) and expert_pregate (1.13×). Kept mmap_advice (0.49×) and router_prefetch (0.62×) switched off. Removed thread_names. The agent also refused to multiply the numbers into one headline figure.

methodology_accuracy

JiuwenSwarm factory · Satay (Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB) · 2026-11-12

Satay CC Catalog

A capsule is a package: one functional category of the factory, such as building, measuring, or streaming experts from SSD. Inside it are modules, and each module is one of four kinds: a component ships in the engine, a tool is called, a skill says how to act, a method says how to judge. Below are 9 capsules and 38 modules: what each is called today, what it has already done, and what is still to build.

9capsules (functional packages)
12modules built in the factory
16built in the campaign, not yet a CC
10new to write
1.18× / 1.28×factory engine vs stock (J-OM13), without / with tuning

Capsule, module, kind

One capsule, as packaged
factory.lab
lab_client · tool accuracy_lab · tool methodology_ab · method methodology_accuracy · method methodology_observability · method

One release, one version, one hash. Capabilities are the tool modules; materials are the component, skill and method modules. The agent discovers the whole category with one cc_list entry.

Recorded in ccv2 (commit 608656eb, pushed)
cc: '2' id: factory.lab version: 2.0.0 capabilities: lab.ab_submit: kind: tool # capabilities may only be tool does: Submit one complete ABBA experiment … materials: ab: kind: method # component | skill | method | reference path: AB.md

The parser and JSON schema validate kind. cc_list now reports each module's kind. The factory refuses to integrate a material unless it is declared kind: component. All 12 current factory CCs are tagged.

Component

Is
Code, config or an artifact that ends up in the engine the user runs.
Lifecycle
integrate → build → measure → keep / dormant / revert
Judged by
the method it names

Tool

Is
A capability the agent calls, behind grants. It acts or returns data.
Lifecycle
versioned release; improved by RSI from telemetry and replay
Judged by
correct outputs, latency, failure rate

Skill

Is
A procedure: how to carry out a task with tools.
Lifecycle
revised when runs show agents stumbling
Judged by
task success, turns and repairs per task

Method

Is
Decision rules: what counts as better, how to measure, when to stop.
Lifecycle
changed rarely; a change is a new contract revision
Judged by
the operator
Fixed core: not in any capsule.The evidence store, controller, Manager with its frozen correctness contract, jobq, lab runner, telemetry writer and monitor. The agent must not be able to change these. That is why “output identical” and “1.13×” can be trusted.

Today vs target. The factory currently ships 12 single-module CCs with IDs like factory.builder and factory.components.expert_fill. The target packaging below merges them into category capsules. Module names stay the same and capability names gain a prefix (builder.submit), which the ccv2 name pattern already allows.

Durable image build from a clean commit, as a jobq build job. Calls: submit (idempotency key), status, cancel, result.

Built 7 images in evolve run 4 (~130 s each, every one survived the agent's turn ending), plus the bare reference a9a0c71c and om12. The campaign's build_engine recorded 3 failed attempts honestly and found the image-identity bug (D016); warm ccache rebuilds take 10–20 s.

Caught the labelled bad setting in demo run 2: CONFIG_REJECTED: LLAMA_EXPERT_PREGATE_K=48 (range 1..32), which the agent repaired to K=8. In run 4 it confirmed the effective config before every A/B: k=8 · pregate=1 · fill=1 · chunk_kib=2048 · matches request.

Guided run 4 through 5 integrations (patches 01–09, one commit each), 2 reverts with restoration builds, and 2 dormant keeps, with no human input. In demo run 2 it guided the K=48 → K=8 repair, keeping the failure on record.

methodbuilt
factory.methodology_ab · AB.md

Ten steps: one component per experiment, bare engine first, ABBA rounds. Gate: threshold = max(0.03, 2·aa_gap, 2·drift), and improvement needs ratio − 1 > threshold. Judged run 4: kept expert_fill (1.11×) and expert_pregate (1.13×), held mmap_advice (0.49×) and router_prefetch (0.62×) dormant, reverted thread_names. The agent also refused to multiply the per-component ratios into one headline number.

methodnew

For changes that may alter outputs (quant, KV type, model): a frozen item set and seed, non-thinking greedy decoding, sample size, Wilson interval, McNemar for paired comparisons, and a non-inferiority margin the operator sets. Published thinking-mode scores are context, not substitutes.

methodnew

For measure: none components. Keep if the module engaged, costs nothing measurable (ratio ≥ 1 − threshold in the same ABBA), and the promised signal appears in evidence. With this method, thread_names (1.01×, xfill-* threads seen) would have been kept instead of reverted.

A worker pool reads the routed experts' non-resident pages with parallel pread in 2 MiB chunks before the node computes, so page faults become large sequential reads. Switches LLAMA_EXPERT_FILL=1, _THREADS=16, _CHUNK_KIB=2048, _RANDOM=decode.

A capsule is a package: one functional category of the factory, such as building, measuring, or streaming experts from SSD. Inside it are modules, and each module is one of four kinds: a component ships in the engine, a tool is called, a skill says how to act, a method says how to judge. Below are 9 capsules and 38 modules: what each is called today, what it has already done, and what is still to build.

An AI agent improves a language-model engine on a small machine. Everything it can use comes packaged as a capsule: a box of related parts for one job, such as “build the engine” or “measure it”. This page lists every capsule we have and every one we still need. For each part it explains what it does, what it has already done, and how we check that it works.

How one improvement moves through the factory

+

This is what happened for each component in run 4, which ran for 175 minutes with no human input.

+
  • The agent reads a component: the patch, what it should do, what it depends on, and how to tell it is switched on.engine.expert_streaming · component

+
  • It applies the patch to its own copy of llama.cpp and makes one commit, following the integration instructions.factory.build · integration_skill

+
  • It asks the builder for an engine image. The build runs about two minutes in the background, inside Docker, and survives the agent pausing.factory.build · builder

+
  • It checks that the new binary accepts the settings and really applies them.factory.build · engine_inspector

+
  • It asks the lab to run the old engine and the new one on the real model, in the order old-new-new-old, twice. Each output is compared with the frozen reference.factory.lab · lab_client

+
  • It applies the judging rules: keep it, revert it, or keep the code switched off because a later component needs it.factory.lab · methodology_ab

+
  • It writes the decision, citing the evidence, and moves on to the next component.factory.evidence · evidence

+

Result, measured afterwards against stock llama.cpp: 1.18× faster with the agent's choices, 1.28× with one more setting it had no way to try. All outputs were identical to the reference.

Every tool capsule is native: a small Python launcher on the host. None uses ccv2's Docker (image) binding. Three of them start Docker containers underneath, because the engine itself lives in a container.

+ buildernativePython queues a build job; the job runs docker buildx build to produce the engine image
+ engine_inspectornativePython, plus a few seconds of docker run --rm on the candidate image to read its flags and settings
+ lab_clientnativePython queues a GPU job. The referee runs the engine with docker run, model mounted read-only, then removes the container.
